## Dīgha Nikāya
## Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā
## Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.
## 1. Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta
## Discourse Related to Past Lives

I pay homage to that Blessed One who possesses great compassion; who, based on compassion for all beings, renounced the most desirable bliss of Nibbāna attained at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara; who fulfilled the difficult perfections (pāramīs) for the sake of rescuing the world of beings from the current of Saṃsāra; who attained the noble Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa); and who leads veneyya beings to Nibbāna.

I pay homage to the tenfold Dhamma, which is praised by the Buddha, well-expounded by the Buddha, protects those who practice it well from falling into the four woeful states (apāya), and is capable of destroying defilements.

I pay homage to the assembly of the Ariya Saṅgha, who are the true sons of the Buddha, endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla), who protect the lineage of the virtuous, and who have been liberated from the dark house of Saṃsāra.

I pay homage with my head to my teacher, who is as glorious and radiant as the sun, who causes the wisdom of his disciples to increase, and who cools beings with the pure water of loving-kindness (mettā).

The great Elder renowned throughout the earth by the name Buddhaghosa has well-composed the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) on the Mahāvagga. I shall now write the word-for-word translation (nissaya) of that Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā. Let the virtuous look well with the eye of wisdom.

Although there exists an old nissaya of that Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā composed by former teachers, monks of little wisdom cannot easily utilize it due to its deterioration. Therefore, and also at the urging of my noble teacher, I shall write this new nissaya, comparing it with various scriptures and purging it of errors.

This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Mahāpadāna Sutta. In this sutta, the following is the explanation of new terms.

In the term "Karerikuṭikāyaṃ," Karerī is the name of the Varuṇa tree. Because a Karerī pavilion stood near the door of that cell, it is called "Karerikuṭikā," just as it is called "Kosambakuṭikā" because a Kosamba tree stood near the door of the cell. It is said that within the Jetavana Monastery, there were four great residences: Karerikuṭi, Kosambakuṭi, Gandhakuṭi, and Salalāgāra. Each of these residences was built with an expenditure of one hundred thousand (kahāpaṇas). Among these four great residences, King Pasenadi had the Salalāgāra built, while the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had the remaining residences built. Thus, the Blessed One dwelt in the Karerikuṭi, which was built upon pillars by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika and resembled a celestial mansion (devavimāna).

Regarding "pacchābhattaṃ" (after the meal): for monks who observe the dhutaṅga practices of ekāsanika (the one-sessioner's practice) and khalupacchābhattika (the practice of refusing later food) and have eaten early in the morning, even the period within midday is considered "pacchābhatta." However, in this context, "pacchābhatta" is intended as the period after the regular meal.

"Piṇḍapātapāṭikkantānaṃ" means those who have returned from the alms-round, having finished the business of the meal and risen from their seats.

"Karerimaṇḍalamāḷe" refers to the sitting hall (rest house) constructed not far from that Karerī pavilion. That Karerī pavilion was between the Gandhakuṭi and the hall...
2:
That building is in the middle; therefore, the Gandhakuṭi, the Karerikuṭi, and the hall are all called "Karerimaṇḍalamāḷa." "Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyuttā" refers to a discourse connected with the recollection of past lives, described as "one birth, two births," etc., which is the continuity of aggregates (khandhas) lived in previous existences. "Dhammī" means a discourse connected with the Dhamma.

"Udapādi" means [the following thought arose]: "How wonderful is the Blessed One's knowledge of the recollection of past lives! Who can recollect the continuity of aggregates lived in previous existences, known as Pubbenivāsa, and who cannot?" Ascetics of other sects (titthiyas), disciples (sāvakas), solitary Buddhas (paccekabuddhas), and Buddhas can all recollect them. Which titthiyas can recollect? Those titthiyas who are supreme proponents of the doctrine of Kamma (kammavādī) can recollect only forty aeons (kappas), and not beyond that. Disciples can recollect one hundred thousand aeons. The two Chief Disciples can recollect one incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) and one hundred thousand aeons. Paccekabuddhas can recollect two incalculable periods and one hundred thousand aeons. For the Buddhas, however, there is no such limitation; they can recollect as far back as they desire.

Titthiyas recollect by following the sequence of aggregates; they cannot recollect if they skip the sequence. Even while recollecting in sequence, when they reach the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), they cannot see the occurrence of mental aggregates. They become like a blind bird fallen into a net or a cripple fallen into a pit. Stopping there, they hold the false view: "There is only this much; there is nothing beyond this." Thus, the titthiyas' recollection of past lives is like a blind person walking by the tip of a staff. Just as blind people can walk only when there is someone holding the tip of the staff and must sit right there if there is no one, similarly, titthiyas can only recollect by following the sequence of aggregates and cannot do so if they skip the sequence.

Disciples also recollect only by following the sequence of aggregates; when they reach the realm of non-percipient beings, they do not see the occurrence of aggregates. Even so, for beings wandering in Saṃsāra, there is no such time when aggregates do not exist. Since beings remain in the realm of non-percipient beings for five hundred aeons, the disciples, after passing that period and relying on the method given by the Buddhas, can recollect further existences, as did the Venerable Sobhita. The two Chief Disciples and the Paccekabuddhas, however, can recollect by observing death (cuti) and rebirth (paṭisandhi). For the Buddhas, there is no need to observe death and rebirth; whatever place they wish to see, they see that very place.
3:
When sectarians (titthiyas) recollect their past lives (pubbenivāsa), they can only recollect what they themselves have seen, done, or heard. The same applies to disciples (sāvakas) and Paccekabuddhas. The Buddhas, however, can recollect everything that has been seen, done, or heard, whether by themselves or by others.

The knowledge of past lives of the sectarians is like the glow of a firefly. The knowledge of the disciples is like the light of a lamp. The knowledge of the chief disciples (aggasāvakas) is like the light of the morning star (osadhitāraka). The knowledge of the Paccekabuddhas is like the light of the moon. The knowledge of the Buddhas, however, is like the radiance of the sun's orb shining in the autumn month of Tazaungmon. For the Buddha, there is no limit such as this many hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of births, or this many hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of aeons (kappas). In recollecting all things, there is no stumbling and no obstruction or exhaustion in the object; it occurs merely by reflecting, merely by the arising of the thought of attention as desired. It proceeds without any attachment, like an arrow shot with force through a stack of weak leaves, or like Indra's thunderbolt (vajira) released upon the peak of Mount Sineru. Thus, a conversation arose, was born, and proceeded concerning the Blessed One himself, saying, "Oh, how great is the Blessed One's knowledge of past lives!" To show all of this in brief, it is stated in the Pāḷi text only as: "Thus also is the recollection of past lives, thus also is the recollection of past lives." In that Pāḷi, "itipi" means "it is also of such a nature."

2-3. In the passage "Assosi kho... pe... atha bhagavā anuppatto," everything that should be said is exactly as stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. The distinction here is that in the Brahmajāla Sutta, he heard through his omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), but in this sutta, he heard through the divine ear (dibbasota). In that sutta, the conversation regarding praise and dispraise was unfinished (when the Buddha arrived); in this sutta, the conversation regarding past lives was unfinished. Therefore, the Blessed One thought, "These monks are praising the virtues of my knowledge of past lives, but they do not yet know the perfection of my knowledge of past lives. Now, I shall show them the perfection of that knowledge by teaching it," and so he approached. According to the custom of the Buddhas, he sat on the noble Buddha-seat which had been dusted and spread by the monks at that moment, specifically prepared for the purpose of delivering a Dhamma discourse. After the question, "Monks, for what conversation are you gathered now?" and the conclusion of the reply, "Venerable Sir, it is for such a conversation," he said, "Would you like [to hear]?" and so on, wishing to deliver a Dhamma discourse related to past lives. In that context, "iccheyyātha no" means "do you wish?" Then the monks, with joyful minds, requested him, saying, "Blessed One, please deliver this Dhamma discourse," and so on. In that context, "etassa" means "of the making of this Dhamma discourse related to past lives."
4:
Then the Blessed One, accepting their request and wishing to teach, said, "Monks, in that case, listen," thus urging them to listen and pay proper attention. Wishing to reveal the recollection of the broken cycle of existence (chinnavaṭuma), which is not shared by others, he spoke the words beginning with, "Monks, from this [point back], that (Vipassī Buddha)..." In that context, "yaṃ Vipassī" means "in which aeon Vipassī [appeared]."

This word "yaṃ" is seen in the sense of the nominative case (paccattavacana) in sentences such as: "Venerable Sir, whatever (yaṃ) speech I have heard and received in the presence of the Tāvatiṃsa gods, I report that to the Blessed One." It is seen in the sense of the accusative case (upayogavacana) in sentences such as: "That which (yaṃ) we asked, you have explained to us; we ask another thing, please tell us that." It is seen in the sense of the instrumental case (karaṇavacana) in sentences such as: "Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that (yaṃ) in a single world system [two Buddhas should arise simultaneously]." In this context, however, it should be understood as being in the sense of the locative case (bummattha). Therefore, it means "in which aeon." "Udapādi" means he appeared, making the ten thousand world systems echo.

"Bhaddakappe" (In the Auspicious Aeon) means that the Blessed One spoke thus, praising this aeon as a good aeon, a precious aeon, because it is adorned by the appearance of five Buddhas. It is said that from the time our Blessed One made his aspiration (abhinīhāra) [under Dīpaṅkara Buddha], there has never been another single aeon in that interval where five Buddhas were born. Before our Blessed One's aspiration, however, four Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara were born in a single aeon. After those Buddhas, there was one incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya) that was entirely empty of Buddhas.

At the end of that incalculable aeon, a single Buddha named Koṇḍañña appeared in one aeon. After him, there was again an incalculable period empty of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, four Buddhas named Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita appeared in one aeon. After them, there was again an incalculable period empty of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, above the incalculable period that is one hundred thousand aeons beyond this [Auspicious Aeon], three Buddhas named Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada appeared in one aeon. After them, there was again an incalculable period empty of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, one hundred thousand aeons above this, the Blessed One Padumuttara alone appeared in one aeon. After that Buddha, thirty thousand aeons above this, two Buddhas named Sumedha and Sujāta appeared in one aeon. After that, eighteen thousand aeons above this, three Buddhas named Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī...
5:
The Buddhas appear in a certain kappa (aeon). Counting back from this Bhadda-kappa, ninety-four kappas ago, a single Buddha named Siddhattha appeared in one kappa. Ninety-two kappas ago, two Buddhas, Tissa and Phussa, appeared in one kappa. Ninety-one kappas ago, the Blessed One Vipassī appeared. Thirty-one kappas ago, two Buddhas, Sikhī and Vessabhū, appeared. In this Bhadda-kappa, four Buddhas have appeared: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Buddha, Gotama; and the Buddha Metteyya will also appear. Because this kappa is adorned with the appearance of five Buddhas, the Blessed One praised it as a Sundara-kappa (Beautiful Aeon) or Sāra-kappa (Essential Aeon), saying: "In this kappa, so many Buddhas have appeared or will appear."

When asked, "Is this matter known only to the Buddhas, or is it known to others as well?", it should be answered that it is known to others too. To whom is it known? It is known to the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas. At the time of the world's formation, when the world-system exists as a single vast space for one incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya), rain begins to fall for the sake of the world's establishment. Initially, it is like the falling of frost during the eight days between the months of Tabodwe and Tabaung. Thereafter, the streams of rainwater, initially the size of sesame seeds, broken rice, whole rice, mung beans, cowpeas, jujube fruits, wood-apples, cucumbers, pumpkins, and gourds, gradually increase in size to two usabhas, half a gāvuta, one gāvuta, two gāvutas, half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas... and so on, reaching the size of a hundred yojanas, a thousand yojanas, and a hundred thousand yojanas. These fill the interior of the hundred billion world-systems up to the Brahma realms that have not yet perished.

Then, that water gradually recedes. As the water recedes, the celestial realms are established in their natural locations. The manner of their establishment should be understood as described in the "Pubbenivāsakathā" (Talk on Past Lives) of the Visuddhimagga.

When the water reaches the place where the human world is to be established, it stays firm due to the force of the wind, as if the mouth of a water-strainer (dhamakaraṇa) were closed. On the surface of the water, the earth appears like a lotus leaf. The site of the Mahābodhi throne (Mahābodhi-pallaṅka) is the last to perish when the world is destroyed and the first to be established when the world is re-formed. At that site, as a preliminary sign, a single lotus bush arises. If a Buddha is to appear in that kappa, flowers will bloom. If not, they will not bloom. If one Buddha is to appear, one flower blooms. If two, three, four, or five Buddhas are to appear, five flowers bloom. These flowers bloom together on a single stalk, like a cluster of flowers. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas...
6:
"Friends, let us go and see the preliminary sign," they agree and come to the site of the Mahābodhi throne. In a kappa where no Buddhas appear, no flowers bloom. Seeing the flowerless bush, those Suddhāvāsa Brahmas become displeased, thinking, "Alas, friends, the world will be in darkness; beings will die and fill the woeful states; the six celestial realms and the nine Brahma realms will be empty."

However, when they see flowers blooming, they joyfully utter an exclamation (udāna), saying, "We shall witness miracles such as the shaking of the ten thousand world-systems when the Omniscient Bodhisattas descend into their mother's womb, renounce the world, realize the Four Noble Truths, turn the Wheel of Dhamma, perform the Twin Miracle, descend from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, relinquish the life-force, and attain Parinibbāna." They also think, "The four woeful states will diminish, and the six celestial realms and nine Brahma realms will be filled." Then they return to their respective Brahma realms. In this Bhadda-kappa, five lotuses have bloomed. By the power of those signs, four Buddhas have appeared, and the fifth (Arimetteyya) Buddha will also appear. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, seeing those lotuses, knew this matter. Therefore, it is said, "It is known to others as well."

## Āyupariccheda-vaṇṇanā

5-7. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the past lives (pubbenivāsa) by way of defining the kappas with the method beginning with "Bhikkhus, from this (ninety-one kappas ago)," now speaks the passage beginning with "Bhikkhus, the Buddha Vipassī..." to show them by way of defining the lineage and so forth of those Buddhas. In showing the life span, both terms 'paritta' (limited) and 'lahuka' (brief) are synonyms for 'small' (appaka). That which is small is both limited and brief.

"Appaṃ vā bhiyyo" means living slightly more than a hundred years, or not reaching a hundred years and living only twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years. Such a long-lived person is extremely rare. It should be noted by going to various places that "a person with such a name lives this long." Among them, the laywoman Visākhā lived for one hundred and twenty years. Similarly, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, the Brahmin Brahmāyu, the Brahmin Sela, the Brahmin Bāvariya, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Mahākassapa each lived for one hundred and twenty years. The Elder Anuruddha lived for one hundred and fifty years, and the Elder Bākula lived for one hundred and sixty years. This Elder Bākula was the longest-lived of all. Even he did not live up to two hundred years.
7:
All Bodhisattas, including Vipassī and others, take conception in their mother's womb with a mind that is unprompted (asaṅkhārika), associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta), and accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata), preceded by loving-kindness (mettā). Due to the conception taken with such a mind, the lifespan should last for an incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya); thus, all Buddhas should have an incalculable lifespan. Why, then, did they not remain for an incalculable period? It is because of the failure of climate (utu) and nutriment (āhāra). Indeed, by the power of climate and nutriment, the lifespan both decreases and increases.

Among those decreases and increases, when kings are unrighteous (adhamma), then the sub-kings, generals, wealthy merchants, the entire city, and the entire country become unrighteous. At that time, the guardian deities of those kings and others, the terrestrial deities (bhūma-devatā) who are friends of those deities, the celestial deities (ākāsa-devatā) who are friends of those deities, the heat-cloud deities (uṇha-valāhaka) who are friends of the celestial deities, the cloud-deities (abbha-valāhaka) who are their friends, the cold-cloud deities (sīta-valāhaka) who are their friends, the rain-cloud deities (vassa-valāhaka) who are their friends, the deities of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) who are their friends, the Tāvatiṃsa deities who are their friends, and the Yāma deities who are their friends, and so forth, all become unrighteous. In this way, up to the highest plane of existence (bhavagga), excluding the noble disciples (ariya-sāvaka), all the assemblies of deities and Brahmas become unrighteous.

Because of the unrighteousness of those deities, the moon and sun move irregularly. The wind does not blow according to its regular course; blowing off-course, it causes the celestial mansions (vimāna) in the sky to shake and tremble. When the mansions are shaken, the minds of the deities do not incline toward play and enjoyment. When the minds of the deities do not incline toward play and enjoyment, the seasons, characterized by cold and heat, do not occur at the proper time. When the seasons are not right, the rain does not fall properly; sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not; in some places it rains, in some it does not. Even when it rains, it does not benefit the crops, as it rains or ceases in a way that is unhelpful during the times of sowing, sprouting, stalk-forming, flowering, and the taking of milky sap. Therefore, the crops ripen irregularly and are devoid of fragrance, color, and taste. Even rice placed in a single pot to cook: in one part the rice remains raw, in another it is overcooked, and only in one part is it cooked evenly. When such food is consumed, it is digested in the stomach in three different ways. Consequently, beings become prone to many diseases and have short lifespans. In this way, by the power of climate and nutriment, the lifespan decreases.
8:
When kings are righteous, the sub-kings also become righteous. In this manner, as previously described, all beings up to the Brahma world become righteous. Because they are righteous, the moon and the sun rotate harmoniously. The wind blows according to its proper course. The wind blowing in its proper course does not shake the mansions (vimānas) situated in the sky. Because those mansions are not shaken, the devas feel inclined to enjoy themselves. Thus, in due time, the season becomes favorable and the rain falls rightly. Providing benefit to the crops from the time of sowing, it rains when it should rain and ceases when it should cease. Therefore, the crops ripen evenly and are endowed with fragrance, color, taste, and essence (ojā). When the food prepared from those crops is consumed, it is properly digested. Therefore, beings are free from disease and long-lived. Thus, by the power of the season and the food, the life span increases.

Regarding the increase and decrease of life span: the Blessed One Vipassī was born during the period when the life span was eighty thousand years. The Blessed One Sikhī was born during the period when the life span was seventy thousand years. This is presented as if it were a gradual decline; however, it should be understood that it did not decline in such a linear sequence alone, but declined after repeatedly increasing. How should this be understood? In this Bhadda-kappa, the Blessed One Kakusandha was born during the period when the life span was forty thousand years. Dividing the life span into five parts, he remained for four parts and attained Parinibbāna while the fifth part was still remaining. That life span declined until it reached the ten-year span, then increased again to become an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) span, and then declining from there, it stood at the thirty-thousand-year span; at that time, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana was born. When that Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, in the same manner, the life span reached the ten-year span, increased again to an incalculable span, and after declining, stood at the twenty-thousand-year span; at that time, the Blessed One Kassapa was born. When that Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, in the same manner, the life span reached the ten-year span, increased again to an incalculable span, and after declining, reached the hundred-year span; then our Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddha was born. Thus, it should be understood that it declined after repeatedly declining and increasing. Among those life spans, whatever the life span of the humans was when the Buddhas were born, the life span of those Buddhas was also the same as that of those humans.

## The Explanation of the Limitation of Life Span is Finished.

## Description of the Section on the Bodhi Tree (Bodhipariccheda-vaṇṇanā)

In the section on the Bodhi tree, the phrase "pāṭaliyā mūle" means at the foot of the Pāṭali tree. On that day (when Buddha Vipassī attained enlightenment), the trunk of that Pāṭali tree emerged reaching fifty cubits, and its branches also reached fifty cubits; thus, it was one hundred cubits in height. On that same day, that Pāṭali tree was simultaneously covered from its base with flowers as if they were arranged in clusters, and divine fragrances wafted abroad. At that time, not only did this Pāṭali tree bloom, but all Pāṭali trees in the ten thousand world systems also bloomed. Not only did the Pāṭali trees bloom, but in all the trees of the ten thousand world systems, lotuses bloomed on the trunks, lotuses bloomed on the branches, lotuses bloomed on the vines, and lotuses bloomed in the sky; great lotuses also emerged, breaking through the surface of the earth. The Great Ocean was also covered with five-colored lotuses, as well as blue and red lotuses.

The entire ten thousand world systems were filled with rows of banners and shone with various colored flowers scattered from flower garlands tied here and there, resembling the Nandana Grove, Cittalatā Grove, Missaka Grove, and Phārusaka Grove. Banners hoisted at the rim of the eastern world system touched the rim of the western world system. Banners hoisted at the rims of the western, southern, and northern world systems touched the rim of the southern world system. In this way, the world systems were endowed with mutual glory. "Abhisambuddho" means having penetrated and realized all the glory of the Buddha's qualities and having fully awakened to the Four Noble Truths.

In the Pali texts such as, "Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, was fully awakened at the foot of the Puṇḍarīka tree," the explanation of the terms should be understood in this same manner. Here, "Puṇḍarīka" refers to a white mango tree (setamba). The dimensions of that white mango tree were the same (as the Pāṭali tree). On that day, that white mango tree was also well-covered with flowers of divine fragrance. It was not only covered with flowers but also with fruits. On one side of that white mango tree, young fruits hung; on another side, medium-sized fruits; on another side, fruits that were not too ripe; and on another side, well-ripened fruits with a delicious taste as if divine essence had been infused into them. Just like that white mango tree, in all the ten thousand world systems, flowering trees were adorned with flowers, and fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits.

"Sāla" refers to the Sāla tree. Its dimensions were also the same, and the glory of its flowers should be understood in the same way. The same method applies to the Sirīsa tree. Regarding the Udumbara tree—
10:
On the Udumbara tree, there were no flowers, but the magnificence of its fruit should be understood according to the method mentioned earlier for the mango tree. The same applies to the Nigrodha tree and the Assattha tree. Thus, the throne (pallaṅka) of all Buddhas is one and the same, but the trees under which they awaken are different. Among those trees, whichever tree a Buddha sits under to penetrate the Bodhi—known as the Knowledge of the Four Paths—that specific tree is called a "Bodhi" tree. This is known as the Section on the Bodhi Tree.

## Description of the Section on the Pairs of Disciples (Sāvakayuga-pariccheda-vaṇṇanā)

In the section on the pairs of disciples, "Khaṇḍatissa" refers to Elder Khaṇḍa and Elder Tissa. Between those two, Khaṇḍa was the younger brother of the same father, and Tissa was the son of the royal chaplain. Elder Khaṇḍa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), and Elder Tissa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramī). "Agga" (Chief) means noble because they possessed qualities incomparable to others, excluding the Blessed One Vipassī. "Bhaddayuga" (Auspicious Pair) means a good pair precisely because they were the chief disciples. "Abhibhūsambhava" refers to Elder Abhibhū and Elder Sambhava. Between those two, Elder Abhibhū reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom. Together with the Blessed One Sikhī, he went from the city of Aruṇavatī to the Brahma world, and while performing various miracles before the assembly of Brahmas, he preached the Dhamma. He then filled the ten thousand world systems with darkness, and for the Brahmas who were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega) wondering, "Why is there this darkness?", he spread light. Having resolved, "Let all Brahmas see my form and hear my voice," he made his voice heard while reciting the two verses beginning with "Ārambhatha" (Strive!). Elder Sambhava reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration.

"Soṇuttara" refers to Elder Soṇa and Elder Uttara. Between those two, Elder Soṇa reached the perfection of wisdom, and Elder Uttara reached the perfection of concentration. "Vidhurasañjīva" refers to Elder Vidhura and Elder Sañjīva. Between those two, Elder Vidhura reached the perfection of wisdom, and Elder Sañjīva reached the perfection of concentration. That Elder Sañjīva frequently entered meditative attainments. While he was accustomed to dwelling in jhāna through the power of meditative attainment in night quarters, day quarters, huts, caves, pavilions, and so on, one day he entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) in the forest. Then, forest workers and others, perceiving him as "dead," cremated him. Having emerged from the attainment at the predetermined time, he shook his robes and entered the village for alms. Because of that incident, they recognized him as "Sañjīva" (The Living One). "Bhiyyosuttara" refers to Elder Bhiyyosa and Elder Uttara. Between those two, Elder Bhiyyosa was superior in wisdom, and Elder Uttara was chief in concentration. "Tissabhāradvāja" refers to Elder Tissa and Elder Bhāradvāja. Between those two, Elder Tissa reached the perfection of wisdom, and Elder Bhāradvāja reached the perfection of concentration.
11:
It was so. "Sāriputta and Moggallāna" refers to Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna. Among those two, Venerable Sāriputta was foremost in the field of wisdom, and Venerable Moggallāna was foremost in the field of concentration. This is called the Division of the Pair of Disciples (Sāvakayugapariccheda).

## Description of the Division of the Assembly of Disciples

In the division of the assembly of disciples, the first assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Vipassī was endowed with four factors. These four factors were: all the monks were "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks; all the monks possessed robes and bowls created by psychic power; all the monks arrived of their own accord without being invited; and those monks assembled on the fifteenth-day Uposatha. Then, the Teacher, seated while holding a fan, performed the Uposatha (recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha). The same method applies to the second and third assemblies. Likewise, it should be understood for all the assemblies of the other Buddhas. However, specifically for our Blessed One, the assembly of disciples occurred only during the early period of his Buddhahood, and this sutta was also preached at a later time; therefore, without concluding with "Monks, now there is only one assembly of my disciples," he preached using the words "It was so."

In that text, "one thousand two hundred and fifty monks" refers to the one thousand monks who were formerly matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas) and the two hundred and fifty monks who were the followers of the two chief disciples, totaling one thousand two hundred and fifty monks. Among those monks, the story should be told starting from the initial aspiration of the two chief disciples to explain their entry into the monkhood. Among those who had become monks, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained Arahantship on the seventh day. The General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, on the fifteenth day, while the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta (also known as the Dhammayāga) was being preached to his nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, in the Sūkarakhata Cave in the middle of the Gijjhakūṭa Mountain, sent forth his insight knowledge following the discourse and attained the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (Sāvakapāramīñāṇa). The Blessed One, knowing the Elder's attainment of Arahantship, rose into the air and stayed at the Veḷuvana Monastery itself. The Elder, reflecting, "Where has the Blessed One gone?" and knowing that he was at the Veḷuvana Monastery, also rose into the air himself and stayed at the Veḷuvana Monastery. Then, the Blessed One recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha. Referring to that assembly, the Blessed One said, "one thousand two hundred and fifty monks." This is called the Division of the Assembly of Disciples (Sāvakasannipātapariccheda).

## Description of the Division of the Attendant

In the Division of the Attendant, the word "Ānanda" is spoken with reference to the state of being a permanent attendant. To speak in detail, the Blessed One had non-permanent attendants during the early period of his Buddhahood (Paṭhamabodhi). At one time, Venerable Nāgasamāla took the bowl and robes and followed him; at one time, Venerable Nāgita; at one time, Venerable Upavāna; at one time, Venerable Sunakkhatta; at one time, Cunda the novice; at one time, Venerable Sāgata; and at one time, Venerable Meghiya (served as attendants).

Among those attendants, once, while the Blessed One was traveling on a long journey with Venerable Nāgasamāla, they reached a fork in the road. Then, the Elder stepped off the path and said, "Blessed One, I will go by this path." Then, the Blessed One said, "Come, monk, let us go by this path." That Elder said, "Here, Blessed One, take your bowl and robes; I will go by this path," and began to place the bowl and robes on the ground. Then, the Blessed One said, "Monk, take them," and taking the bowl and robes, he proceeded. As for that monk who went by the other path, robbers took away his bowl and robes and also broke his head. That monk, thinking, "Now the Blessed One is my only refuge, there is no other," went to the Blessed One with blood flowing. When asked, "Monk, what is this?" he reported the whole matter. Then, the Blessed One comforted him, saying, "Monk, do not worry; it was because I foresaw this matter that I forbade you."

At another time, the Blessed One went to Jantu village in the Pācīnavaṃsa Deer Park with Venerable Meghiya. There too, Venerable Meghiya, after wandering for alms in Jantu village, saw a delightful mango grove by the riverbank and said, "Blessed One, take your bowl and robes; I will strive for the Dhamma of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) in that mango grove." Although he was forbidden three times by the Blessed One, he went there and was oppressed and overcome by unwholesome thoughts. Having returned, he reported that matter. To him also, the Blessed One said, "It was because I foresaw this matter that I forbade you," and in due course, he went to Sāvatthī.

While staying on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Gandhakuṭi precinct in Sāvatthī, surrounded by the assembly of monks, he addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old. When some monks are told, 'Let us go by this path,' they go by another path; some drop my bowl and robes on the ground. Choose a monk who will be my permanent attendant." Spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in the monks. Then, Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and...
13:
"Venerable Sir, desiring only You, I have fulfilled the perfections for an incalculable period plus a hundred thousand aeons. Is it not fitting for a great and wise attendant like me to serve? I shall attend to You," he said. To the Venerable Sāriputta, the Blessed One replied, "Enough, Sāriputta. In whichever direction you dwell, that direction is not empty of Me. Your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas. Therefore, I have no need for the service of an attendant through you," and He refused him. In this manner, starting with the Venerable Mahā-moggallāna, the eighty great disciples stood up. The Blessed One refused all of them as well.

The Venerable Ānanda, however, sat in silence. Then the monks said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Friend Ānanda, the community of monks is requesting the position of attendant; you should also request it." The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Friends, what kind of service is it that is obtained by asking? Does the Teacher not see me? If He is pleased, He will say, 'Let Ānanda attend to Me.'" Then the Blessed One said, "Monks, Ānanda should not be urged by another; he will know by himself and will attend to Me." After that, the monks said, "Rise, friend Ānanda! Rise, friend Ānanda! Request the position of attendant to the One of Ten Powers." The Elder stood up and requested eight boons: four refusals and four requests.

The four refusals were: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will not give me the fine robes He Himself receives, will not give me the alms-food He receives, will not allow me to stay in the same Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), and will not take me along when He accepts an invitation, only then will I attend to the Blessed One." When asked, "Ānanda, what disadvantage do you see in this?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, if I were to receive these things, there would be those who say, 'Ānanda enjoys the fine robes received by the One of Ten Powers, enjoys His alms-food, stays in the Fragrant Chamber, and goes together with Him to invitations. Receiving such gains, he attends to the Tathāgata; what burden is there for one who attends in such a way?'" Thus he requested these four refusals.

The four requests were: "Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One will go to an invitation accepted by me; if I shall be allowed to present to the Blessed One the assembly that has come from other countries and other districts to see the Blessed One at the very moment they arrive; if I shall be allowed to approach the Blessed One at the very moment doubt arises in me; and if the Blessed One will come and repeat to me the Dhamma He has taught in my absence, then I..."
14:
"...will attend to the Blessed One." When asked, "Ānanda, what benefit do you see in this?" he replied, "Venerable Sir, in this Dispensation, there are sons of good family with faith who, not getting an opportunity with the Blessed One, say to me, 'Venerable Ānanda, please come to our house for alms tomorrow together with the Blessed One.' Venerable Sir, if the Blessed One does not go there, and if I am unable to provide the opportunity for the assembly to see Him at the desired moment or to dispel their doubts, there will be those who say, 'Why does Ānanda attend to the One of Ten Powers? The Blessed One does not show even this much favor to Ānanda.' Furthermore, in the absence of the Blessed One, people will ask me, 'Friend Ānanda, where was this verse, this discourse, or this birth story taught?' If I am unable to answer that question, there will be those who say, 'Friend, do you not even know this much? Why do you wander for a long time following the Blessed One like a shadow?' Therefore, I desire that the Dhamma taught in my absence be repeated to me." He requested these four requests. The Blessed One granted them to him.

Thus, having received these eight boons, he became the permanent attendant. It was for this very special position of attendant that he attained the fruit of the perfections fulfilled for a hundred thousand aeons. Referring to this state of being the permanent attendant, the Buddha said, "Monks, now the monk Ānanda is my attendant, the foremost attendant (aggupaṭṭhāka)." This is called the Upaṭṭhāka-pariccheda (Section on the Attendant).

The Piti-pariccheda (Section on the Father) has an obvious meaning.

Regarding the phrase "He entered the monastery," why did He enter the monastery? After teaching this much, the Blessed One thought, "I have not yet taught the lineage of the seven Buddhas continuously to the end. Today, when I enter the monastery, these monks will speak words of praise concerning my Knowledge of Past Lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) to a great extent. Then I shall come and teach the Buddhavamsa (Lineage of the Buddhas) continuously to the end." Giving the monks an opportunity for their turn to speak, He rose from His seat and entered the monastery.

In the sequence of the Pali text taught by the Blessed One, these nine sections (vāra) appear: the Section on the Aeon (Kappa-pariccheda), the Section on Birth (Jāti-pariccheda), the Section on Clan (Gotta-pariccheda), the Section on Life-span (Āyu-pariccheda), the Section on Enlightenment (Bodhi-pariccheda), the Section on the Pair of Disciples (Sāvaka-yuga-pariccheda), the Section on the Assembly of Disciples (Sāvaka-sannipāta-pariccheda), the Section on the Attendant (Upaṭṭhāka-pariccheda), and the Section on the Father (Piti-pariccheda). Although the Sambahula-vāra (Section on the Many) does not appear yet, it should be brought in and explained.

## Explanation of the Section on the Many
For all Bodhisattas, it is the lineage and tradition that they must renounce the world and become monks when a son suitable for their family lineage is born. Why? From the moment the Omniscient Bodhisattas enter their mother's womb, many miracles of various kinds, as previously mentioned, occur. If, while such miracles occur, the birthplace, father, mother, wife, and son of these Bodhisattas were not known, the people would think: "This person has no known birthplace, father, wife, or son. He must be a deva, or Sakka, or Māra, or Brahmā. For devas, having such miracles is not surprising." Thinking thus, they would not consider the Dhamma as something to be heard or believed. Because of such lack of listening and believing, the realization of the Truth (abhisamaya) would not occur. Without the realization of the Truth, the arising of a Buddha would be in vain, and the Dispensation (Sāsana) would not be a means for liberation from the round of suffering. Therefore, for all Bodhisattas, the tradition is that "they must renounce the world and become monks when a son suitable for their family lineage is born." Thus, the section on the many (Sambahulavāra) is presented by way of sons and so forth.

## Explanation of the Classification of the Many
In that section on the many—
Samavattakkhandha, Atula, Suppabuddha, Uttara,
Satthavāha, Vijitasena, and the seventh, Rāhula.

These seven sons should be known according to the sequence of the seven Bodhisattas.

Among those sons, when Prince Rāhula was born, they first brought a name-plate and placed it in the hand of the Great Being (Mahāpurisa). At that moment, love for the son arose, shaking his entire body. That Bodhisatta thought and said: "When one son is born, such love for a son arises. It is said that I will have over a thousand sons. If this bond of love increases in this way every time each one of those sons is born, it will be difficult to break. A Rāhu (captor) is born; a bond is born." On that very day, he renounced the kingship and went forth. This is the method to be understood regarding the birth of sons for all Bodhisattas. This is the classification of sons.
16:
Sutanā, Sabbakāmā, Sucittā, and also Rocinī, Rucaggatī, Sunandā, and the seventh, Bimbā. These were the mothers of those seven Bodhisatta sons. As for Bimbādevī, when she gave birth to Prince Rāhula, she became known as Rāhula-mātā (Rāhula's mother). This is the classification of wives.

These two Bodhisattas, Vipassī Buddha and Kakusandha Buddha, renounced the world for the Great Renunciation by mounting a chariot drawn by thoroughbred horses. These two, Sikhī Buddha and Koṇāgamana Buddha, renounced by mounting the back of a noble elephant. Vessabhū Buddha renounced while sitting in a golden palanquin. Kassapa Buddha, while sitting on the great upper terrace of his palace, attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), emerged from that jhāna, and using it as a basis, resolved: "May the palace fly up and descend at the Bodhi-maṇḍa." The palace traveled through the air and descended at the Bodhi-maṇḍa. The Great Being also descended from that palace and, standing on the ground, thought: "May the palace return to its original place." The palace returned to its original place. The Great Being then practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for seven days and, sitting upon the Bodhi-throne, realized Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Our Bodhisatta, however, renounced by mounting the noble horse Kanthaka. This is the classification of vehicles.

The monastery of the Blessed One Vipassī was established in a place one league (yojana) in extent. Sikhī's in a place of three gāvutas; Vessabhū's in half a league; Kakusandha's in one gāvuta; Koṇāgamana's in half a gāvuta; Kassapa's in twenty usabhas. The monastery of our Blessed One was established in a place of sixteen karīsas by standard measure, and eight karīsas by royal measure. This is the classification of monastery sites.

The ground for the monastery of the Blessed One Vipassī was purchased by making golden bricks one cubit long, one span wide, and eight fingers thick, and laying them on their edges to cover the area. Sikhī's monastery ground was purchased by covering it with golden rods. Vessabhū's monastery ground was purchased by making golden blocks the size of an elephant's foot and laying them on their edges to cover the area. Kakusandha's monastery ground was purchased by covering it with golden bricks in the manner already mentioned. Koṇāgamana's monastery ground was purchased by covering it with golden tortoises in the manner already mentioned.
17:
The monastery land of Kassapa Buddha was purchased by covering it only with gold pieces. However, the monastery land of our Buddha was purchased by covering it with stamped Kahāpaṇas laid edge to edge. This is the section on the amount of wealth used for acquiring the monastery land.

Among the donors who purchased those monastery lands, the attendant donor who purchased the land and built the monastery for Vipassī Buddha was named Punabbhasumitta. For Sikhī Buddha, he was named Siriwaḍḍhana. For Vessabhū Buddha, he was named Sotthiya. For Kakusandha Buddha, he was named Accuta. For Koṇāgamana Buddha, he was named Ugga. For Kassapa Buddha, he was named Sumana. For our Buddha, he was named Sudatta. All of them were wealthy householders (Gahapati-mahāsāla). This is the section on the attendant donors.

Furthermore, there are four kinds of unchanging places (Aviññahitaṭṭhāna) that are not abandoned by any of the Buddhas. The Bodhi-pallaṅka (throne of enlightenment) of all Buddhas is an unchanging place and occurs in only one single location. The place where the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, was preached is in the Isipatana Migadāya and is indeed an unchanging place. The place where the Buddha first set foot at the gate of Saṅkassa city when descending from the celestial realm is also an unchanging place. The places where the four legs of the bed stand in the Gandhakuṭi of Jetavana Monastery are also unchanging places. As for the monastery itself, it may be small or large. The location of the monastery is also unchanging; only the city changes and moves away. When the city is in the east, the monastery is in the west. When the city is in the south, the monastery is in the north. When the city is in the west, the monastery is in the east. When the city is in the north, the monastery is in the south. At the present time, the city is in the north and the monastery is in the south.

Among all Buddhas, there are five kinds of differences (Vematta): difference in lifespan, difference in height, difference in clan, difference in exertion, and difference in radiance. Regarding the difference in lifespan (Āyu-vematta), some Buddhas have a long lifespan, while some have a short lifespan. For instance, the lifespan of Dīpaṅkara Buddha was one hundred thousand years, while the lifespan of our Buddha was one hundred years.

Regarding the difference in height (Pamāṇa-vematta), some Buddhas are tall, while some are short. For instance, Dīpaṅkara Buddha was eighty cubits tall, Sumana Buddha was ninety cubits tall, and our Buddha was eighteen cubits tall.
18:
Regarding the difference in clan (Kula-vematta), some Buddhas are born in the Khattiya (warrior-noble) clan, while some are born in the Brāhmaṇa (priestly) clan. Regarding the difference in exertion (Padhāna-vematta), for some Buddhas, the period of exertion is very short, as it was for Kassapa Buddha. For others, it is for a long duration, as it was for our Buddha.

Regarding the difference in radiance (Rasmi-vematta), the bodily radiance of Maṅgala Buddha extended to ten thousand world systems. The radiance of our Buddha, however, extended to about one fathom around his body. This difference in radiance is connected to their wish (ajjhāsaya); to whatever extent they wish the radiance to spread, it spreads to that extent. In the case of Maṅgala Buddha, he had the wish that his radiance should always spread through the ten thousand world systems. However, regarding the qualities of realized virtues (paṭividdhaguṇa), there is no difference among any of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, the section on the co-borns and the section on the constellations of our Buddha were shown. It is said that together with the Omniscient Bodhisatta, these seven co-borns (Sahajāta) came into existence: (1) the mother of Rāhula, (2) the Elder Ānanda, (3) Channa the courtier, (4) Kaṇṭhaka the horse, (5) the four great jars of treasure, (6) the Maha Bodhi tree, and (7) Kāḷudāyī the courtier. The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) descended into his mother's womb, renounced the world, turned the Wheel of Dhamma, and performed the Twin Miracle under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation. He was born, attained Enlightenment, and entered Parinibbāna under the Visākhā constellation. The assembly of his disciples and his relinquishing of the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) occurred under the Māgha constellation. His descent from the celestial realm occurred under the Assayuja constellation. This much should be brought forth and shown. This is called the section on various details (Sambahula-pariccheda).

Now, in the passages beginning with "Atha kho tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ," those monks, being filled with great amazement, said: "Friends, this process of recollecting from death onwards to the ascending of rebirth is the scope of the knowledge of past lives (Pubbenivāsa). However, to send the knowledge backwards from rebirth to reach death is extremely difficult. The Blessed One has preached it as if showing footprints in the sky." Having said things such as "It is wonderful, friends," they spoke further to show another cause for wonder, beginning with "Yatra hi nāma Tathāgato." In that context, "Yatra hi nāma" is a particle used in the sense of wonder, meaning "The Blessed One who..." In the term "Chinnapapañca," the proliferations (papañca) are these three defilements: craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi). In the term "Chinnavaṭuma," the path (vaṭuma) refers to the cycle of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. "Pariyādinnavaṭṭa" is a synonym for that same term, meaning one who has exhausted the entire cycle of kamma. "Sabbadukkhavītivatta" means [one who has transcended] all suffering known as the cycle of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa)...
19:
When [the suffering known as the round of resultants] has been transcended. Regarding the word "anussarissati" (will remember), although it is a word with a future tense due to the power of the particle "yatra", it should be understood here only in the sense of the past tense. This is because the Blessed One has already remembered those Buddhas; he will not remember them only now. "Evaṃsīlā" (of such virtue) means they possessed such virtue through the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, and both mundane and supramundane virtue. In the word "evaṃဓမ္မာ" (of such qualities), the states associated with concentration are intended; it means "of such concentration" through the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and both mundane and supramundane concentration. "Evaṃpaññā" (of such wisdom) means they possessed such wisdom through the power of the wisdom of the path and so forth. Regarding the term "evaṃvihārī" (of such dwelling), since the states associated with concentration were already mentioned below, if one asks why "dwelling" (vihāra) is mentioned again when it was already included, it is not a mere repetition; this term is spoken to indicate the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: those Blessed Ones were accustomed to dwelling in such attainment of cessation.

In the term "evaṃvimuttā" (of such liberation), there are five kinds of liberation: liberation by suppression (vikkhamphana-vimutti), liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquillization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti). Among these five, the eight attainments are called "liberation by suppression" because they are liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth, which they themselves have suppressed. The seven contemplations, such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā), are called "liberation by substitution of opposites" because they are liberated from the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) and so forth, which are abandoned by the power of their respective opposing factors. The four noble paths are called "liberation by eradication" because they are liberated from the defilements (kilesa) which they themselves have completely eradicated. The four fruits of recluseship are called "liberation by tranquillization" because they arise at the end when the defilements have been tranquillized by the power and majesty of the path. Nirvana is called "liberation by escape" because it has escaped from all defilements, is free from them, and stands far away. Thus, the meaning of "evaṃvimuttā" should be understood by way of these five kinds of liberation.

"Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito" means having arisen from staying in solitude.

## Description of the Nature of a Bodhisatta
In the passage beginning with "Atha kho, bhikkhave, vipassī bodhisatto" (Then, monks, the Bodhisatta Vipassī), the name "Vipassī" is the name of that Bodhisatta. He received this name because of his skill in seeing various diverse meanings. "Bodhisatta" means a wise being, a being who understands cause and effect. Alternatively, he is called a Bodhisatta because his mind is attached to and fixed upon the four paths known as "Bodhi" (Awakening). In the phrase "sato sampajāno" (mindful and clearly comprehending), "sato" refers to mindfulness (sati) itself. "Sampajāno" refers to wisdom (ñāṇa). It means that having well-established mindfulness and having discerned with wisdom, he descended into the mother's womb (conceived). By the word "okkamī" (descended), the Pali text shows only the fact of the Bodhisatta's descent into the womb, not the sequence of the descent (the process of conception). However, since that sequence is presented in the Commentary (Atthakathā), it should be understood as follows:

Indeed, all Bodhisattas, having fulfilled the thirty perfections (pāramī), having made the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga), having reached the pinnacle of the conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), the conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), and the conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā), and while staying in the third existence similar to King Vessantara, having given the seven great gifts and having shaken the earth seven times, they pass away and are reborn in the Tusita heaven in the second thought-moment. The Bodhisatta Vipassī also did the same and was reborn in the Tusita heaven, staying there for fifty-seven crores and six million years. At other times, when their perfections are not yet complete, Bodhisattas reborn in long-lived celestial realms do not stay for the full lifespan. Why? Because it is difficult to fulfill the perfections in those long-lived celestial realms. Those Bodhisattas perform "adhimutti-kālakiriya" (voluntary death) and are reborn only in the human world. However, just as one is able to attain omniscience in a single existence after completing the perfections, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, having fully completed all perfections, stayed in that Tusita heaven until the end of the lifespan according to the human calculation.

For the deities, when it is said, "According to human calculation, passing away (cuti) will occur within seven days from now," five preliminary omens (pubbanimitta) appear: the flowers worn wither, the clothes worn become soiled, sweat drips from the armpits, a loss of beauty occurs in the body, and the deity cannot remain on his celestial throne. Among those five preliminary omens, "mālā" (flowers) refers to the flowers worn on the day of conception.
21:
The flower garlands worn [by the deities] remain unwilted for fifty-seven crores and six million years, but they wilt at that time when death approaches. The same applies to their garments. For such a long duration, the deities experience neither cold nor heat, but at the time of death, drops of sweat exude from their bodies, one by one. For this long duration, no disfigurement such as broken teeth or grey hair appears on their bodies; the goddesses appear as if sixteen years old, and the gods as if twenty years old. However, at the time of death, the physical form of those deities appears weary. For this long duration, there is no such thing as weariness in the celestial realm, but at the time of death, they sigh, stretch their limbs, and find no delight in their seats.

These premonitory signs (pubbanimitta) appear only to the great deities, just as in the world, signs such as falling meteors, earthquakes, and lunar eclipses appear only to powerful kings and great ministers, and not to everyone. Just as among humans, only those skilled in astrology and such know the premonitory signs, and not everyone, so too, not all deities know these signs; only the wise ones know. Among them, those gods who were reborn through meager wholesome kamma become afraid when these signs appear, thinking, 'Who knows where we shall be reborn now?' But those of great merit are not afraid, thinking, 'Based on the gifts we have given, the virtue we have guarded, and the meditation we have practiced, we shall enjoy prosperity in the higher celestial realms.' The Bodhisatta Vipassī, too, seeing these premonitory signs, was not afraid, thinking, 'Now, in the existence immediately following this, I shall become a Buddha.' Then, when those signs appeared, the deities from the ten thousand world-systems assembled and entreated him: 'O Great One, when you were fulfilling the ten perfections, you did not fulfill them desiring the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, Brahmā, or a Universal Monarch; you fulfilled them desiring Buddhahood for the sake of delivering the world. Now is the time, O Great One, for your Buddhahood; now is the moment, O Great One, for your Buddhahood.'

Then the Great Being, without yet giving his consent to those deities, made the Five Great Observations (pañcamahāvilokana) regarding the time, the island, the region, the family, and the lifespan of the mother. Among those five, he first observed the time, thinking, 'Is it now the time to become a Buddha, or is it not yet the time?' At that time, a period when the lifespan increases beyond a hundred thousand years is not the time. Why? Because at that time, for beings, birth, aging, and death...
22:
(When the lifespan of beings is extremely long, birth, aging, and death) are not apparent, and the Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas is never devoid of the Three Characteristics (tilakkhaṇa). When they are told, 'Impermanence, suffering, and non-self,' they do not think to listen or to believe, saying, 'What is this they are saying?' Because they cannot think thus, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) cannot occur. Without that realization, the Dispensation (Sāsana) cannot lead to liberation from suffering. Therefore, that is not the time. A period when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is also not the time. Why? Because at that time, beings are overwhelmed by defilements, and the advice given to beings overwhelmed by defilements does not remain as instruction; it vanishes quickly like a line drawn on water with a stick. Therefore, that period is also not the time. The period when the lifespan is between a hundred thousand years and a hundred years is called the time; at that time, humans had a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Then the Great Being observed the time, thinking, 'This is the time for me to be conceived.'

Then, observing the island, he looked at the four great islands along with their surrounding islands and saw: 'Buddhas are not born in the other three islands; they are born only in Jambudīpa.'

Then, thinking, 'Jambudīpa is vast, measuring ten thousand yojanas; in which region are Buddhas born?' he observed the region and saw the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa). The Middle Country is as described in the Vinaya: 'To the east is the market town named Gajaṅgala,' and so forth. That Middle Country is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in breadth, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. Only in this region are Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, Universal Monarchs, and other powerful warrior-nobles (Khattiya-mahāsāla), brahmins (Brāhmaṇa-mahāsāla), and householders (Gahapati-mahāsāla) born. 'In this region, there is a city named Bandhumatī; I should be born there,' he reached a final decision.

Then, observing the family: 'Buddhas are born only in a family esteemed by the world. At present, the warrior-noble (Khattiya) family is esteemed by the world; I shall be born in that family. The king named Bandhumā shall be my father.' Thus he saw the family.

Then, observing the mother: 'The mother of a Bodhisatta must not be flighty or addicted to liquor; she must have fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and must have kept the five precepts unbroken since birth. This queen named Bandhumatī is endowed with such qualities; she shall be my mother...'
23:
(Reflecting on the lifespan of the mother-to-be), he considered: "This queen shall be my mother; how long will her life last?" Upon reflection, he saw: "It will last for seven days beyond ten months."

Having thus made these Five Great Observations, he thought, "O deities, now is the time for me to become a Buddha." Intending to favor the deities, he gave his consent and dismissed them, saying, "You may go." Surrounded by the deities of the Tusita realm, he entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita celestial city. Indeed, in all celestial realms, there is a Nandana Grove. There, the deities wandered about, reminding him of the opportunities provided by his previously performed wholesome deeds, saying, "When you decease from this Tusita realm, may you go to a happy destination (sugati)." While wandering in that Nandana Grove, surrounded by deities who were thus reminding him of his merit, he passed away (deceased).

When he thus deceased, he knew, "I am deceasing," but he did not know the death-consciousness (cuti-citta). Even after taking rebirth, he knew it, but he did not know the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta) itself. However, he did know, "I have taken rebirth in this place." Some Elders, however, say: "It is appropriate to obtain the sequence of reflection; he will know it in the second or third thought-moment."

The Elder Tipiṭaka Mahāsīva, however, said: "The rebirth of Great Beings (Mahāsattas) is not like the rebirth of others; their mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) reach the highest pinnacle. However, because it is impossible to know that very consciousness with the same consciousness, he does not know the death-consciousness. Even at the moment of death, he knows, 'I am deceasing.' He does not know the rebirth-linking consciousness. He knows, 'I have taken rebirth in such and such a place.' At that time, the ten-thousandfold world system trembles."

Thus, being mindful and clearly comprehending, as he descended into his mother's womb, he took rebirth with a Great Resultant consciousness (mahāvipāka citta) similar to the unprompted wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge (somanassa-sahagata ñāṇa-sampayutta asaṅkhārika kusala citta), which is preceded by loving-kindness, out of the nineteen types of rebirth-linking consciousness. Elder Mahāsīva, however, said it was with a consciousness accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata). Just like our Blessed One, that Bodhisatta also took rebirth on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha.

At that time, it is said that from the seventh day before the full moon, the Bodhisatta's mother participated in the festival of the stars, which was free from intoxicants and endowed with the splendor of flowers and perfumes. On the seventh day, she rose early, bathed in scented water, and having adorned herself with all ornaments and eaten excellent food, she undertook the eightfold Uposatha precepts. She then entered the magnificent royal chamber and, while lying on her royal bed and falling asleep, she saw this dream— "Four..."
24:
The Four Great Kings, it is said, lifted the Queen together with her bed, carried her to Lake Anotatta, and bathed her. They dressed her in divine garments, anointed her with divine perfumes, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from that Lake Anotatta was a Silver Mountain, and inside it was a Golden Mansion. There, they laid her down with her head toward the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered on a Golden Mountain near that Silver Mountain. Descending from there, he ascended the Silver Mountain, entered the Golden Mansion, and after circumambulating his mother three times, he appeared to pierce her right side and enter her womb.

Then the Queen, having awakened, reported the dream to the King. When the night had turned to dawn, the King summoned sixty-four prominent Brahmins. On ground smeared with fresh cow-dung and prepared with auspicious offerings such as parched rice, he had costly seats prepared. To the Brahmins seated there, he served excellent milk-rice prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar in gold and silver bowls, covering them with other gold and silver bowls. He also satisfied them with gifts of new unwashed cloth and tawny cows.

Then, having satisfied them with all desirable objects, he informed them of the dream and asked, "What will happen?" The Brahmins said, "Great King, do not worry. A conception has taken place in the Queen's womb. It is a male child, not a female. You will have a noble son. If he lives the household life, he will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he leaves the household life and ordains, he will surely become a Buddha in the world, one who has removed the veil of defilements." This is the preliminary explanation of the phrase "He descended into his mother's womb."

In this context, "Dhammatā" (Natural Law) means that in this descent into the mother's womb, this is the natural order, this is the nature, this is the fixed law (niyāma). This law is fivefold: the law of kamma (kamma-niyāma), the law of seasons (utu-niyāma), the law of seeds (bīja-niyāma), the law of mind (citta-niyāma), and the law of nature (dhamma-niyāma).

Among these five, the law of kamma (kamma-niyāma) is the giving of desired results by wholesome kamma and undesired results by unwholesome kamma. To illustrate this kamma-niyāma, stories should be told using the verse beginning with "Na antalikkhe." To give another example: a woman, having quarreled with her husband, wished to die by hanging herself and put her neck into a noose. A man, while sharpening a knife, saw the woman and ran toward her, wishing to cut the rope, saying, "Do not be afraid!" At that moment, the rope turned into a highly venomous snake and remained there. The man fled in fear. The woman, however, died right there.
25:
A woman wishing to die put her neck into a noose. A man, while sharpening a knife, saw the woman's action and, wishing to cut the rope, ran towards her to comfort her, saying, "Do not be afraid, do not be afraid!" The rope turned into a venomous snake and remained there. The man fled in fear. The other woman died right there. Such stories should be shown here.

In various regions and at various times, the simultaneous bearing of flowers and fruits by trees, the blowing or non-blowing of the wind, the intensity or mildness of the sun's heat, the falling or non-falling of rain, the blooming of lotuses by day and their wilting by night—such a nature is called utuniyāma (the law of seasons/physicality).

The fact that only rice fruit comes from rice seeds, only sweet taste from sweet seeds, and only bitter taste from bitter seeds—this nature is called bījaniyāma (the law of seeds/biology).

The fact that preceding mental and mental-factor states (citta-cetasika) condition succeeding ones through the condition of decisive support (upanissaya-paccaya), such as the arising of receiving (sampaṭicchana) and so on immediately after eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa)—this nature is called cittaniyāma (the law of mind/psychic order).

The occurrence of events such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems during the Bodhisatta's descent into his mother's womb—this is called dhammaniyāma (the law of nature/Dhamma). Among these five, dhammaniyāma is intended here. Therefore, wishing to show that very meaning, [the Buddha] said, "Bhikkhus, this is the nature (dhammatā)," and so on.

In that context, "descends into the womb" means "has descended into the womb." This happens only after the Bodhisatta has descended, not at the moment of descending. "Appamāṇo" means having a great measure. "Vipulo" means extensive. "Uḷāro" is a synonym for that same term. In passages such as "They eat lofty (uḷāra) foods," the word "uḷāra" is used for what is sweet. In passages such as "The venerable Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty (uḷāra) praise," "uḷāra" is used for what is noble. Here, however, the meaning of "extensive" is intended. In the phrase "the divine majesty of the gods (devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ)," this majesty of the gods means the radiance of their worn garments spreads for twelve yojanas; likewise the radiance of their bodies, their ornaments, and their mansions. It means surpassing that [radiance of the gods].
26:
Lokantarika refers to the inter-world hell located in the space between every three world-systems, like the space in the middle of three cartwheels or three alms-bowls placed touching each other. This Lokantarika hell is eighty thousand yojanas in extent. "Agha" means constantly open. "Asaṃvuta" means having no ground below to stand on. "Andhakāra" means a realm of darkness. "Andhakāratimisa" means being endowed with extreme darkness that causes blindness because it prevents the arising of eye-consciousness. It is said that eye-consciousness does not arise there. The moon and the sun possess such great power because they can shine simultaneously over three great continents. They possess such great majesty because they can dispel darkness and show light for nine hundred thousand yojanas in each direction. "They do not shine with their radiance (ābhāya nānubhonti)" means they are unable to illuminate that hell with their own light. It is said that those suns and moons travel around the middle of the Cakkavāḷa mountain, and the Lokantarika hells are situated beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountain. Therefore, those suns and moons are unable to shine with their radiance in that hell.

"Even those beings who are there (ye pi tattha sattā)" refers to those beings who have been reborn in that great Lokantarika hell. By what kamma are they reborn there? They are reborn there because of committing heavy and cruel offenses against their parents and against righteous ascetics and brahmins, and because of committing daily acts of violence such as killing living beings, like the thieves Abhaya and Nāga in the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Their bodies are three gāvutas in height. They have long claws like bats. They cling to the Cakkavāḷa mountain with their claws like bats on a tree. When they move about and come within reach of each other's hands, they think, "We have found food," and as they struggle, they lose their grip and fall into the water that supports the world. Just as ripe Madhuka fruits fall into the water when the wind blows, they lose their hold and fall into the water. As soon as they fall, they dissolve and perish like lumps of flour in extremely salty water.

"Friends, it seems there are other beings who have come here to experience this suffering, just as we are experiencing great suffering," they say, seeing each other on the day the Bodhisatta is conceived. However, this light does not last even for the duration of drinking a cup of gruel. It flashes out like lightning for only a moment, such as a finger-snap, and disappears even while they are saying, "What is this?" "Saṅkampati" means shaking all around. The other two terms (sampakampati, sampavedhati) are merely synonyms for the first term. Again, the phrase beginning with "appamāṇo ca" is stated for the purpose of conclusion.
27:
“Four young deities approach from the four directions for protection”—in this statement, “four” refers to the Four Great Kings. In the ten thousand world systems, there are four Great Kings for each, totaling forty thousand. Among those ten thousand world systems, the Great Kings residing in this world system entered the auspicious chamber (siri-gabbha) holding swords to protect the Bodhisatta. The remaining Great Kings took up guard from the door of the chamber up to the edge of the world system, driving away the hosts of earth-dwelling demons (paṃsupisāca) and other yakkhas who might cause harm or oppression.

What is the purpose of this protection? From the moment of conception, starting from the embryonic stage (kalala), even if a hundred thousand Māras were to lift a hundred thousand Mount Sinerus and come to harm the Bodhisatta or his mother, all those dangers would vanish in mid-air. Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Ruhiruppāda story (the case of causing blood to flow): “Monks, it is impossible, it cannot happen, that one could deprive a Tathāgata of life by external effort. Monks, Tathāgatas attain final Nibbāna without external effort. Go, monks, to your respective dwellings; Tathāgatas, monks, do not need protection.” (Cullavagga 341). Likewise, there is no danger to the lives of the Bodhisatta and his mother through external effort. However, there are non-humans (amanussa) with deformed, unsightly, and terrifying appearances, as well as beasts and birds, whose sight or sound might cause fear or terror to the Bodhisatta’s mother. The protection was taken to prevent such fear and terror. Furthermore, out of reverence born from the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, the Great Kings provided protection, urged by their own respect.

Do the four Great Kings staying inside the chamber show themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother or not? They do not show themselves during times of bodily activities such as bathing, adorning, or eating. However, they show themselves when she enters the auspicious chamber and lies down on the noble bed. In that regard, although seeing non-humans is usually terrifying for humans, the Bodhisatta’s mother does not fear them upon seeing the Great Kings, due to the power of her own merit and that of her son. Her mind regards them just like ordinary palace guards.

“Naturally virtuous” (pakatiyā sīlavatī) means being endowed with virtue by her very nature. It is said that in times when no Buddha has appeared, people take precepts by bowing and sitting in a crouching position before ascetics and wanderers. Our Bodhisatta’s mother also took precepts from the ascetic Kāladevila. However, when the Bodhisatta was in her womb, it was not appropriate to sit at the feet of another. She merely reflected on the precepts she had already taken while remaining in her own place. Therefore, she undertook the precepts by herself. This is what is taught. Starting with humans...
28:
(Regarding whether the four Great Kings show themselves to the Bodhisatta’s mother or not) — they do not show themselves during times of bodily care such as bathing, adorning, or eating. However, they show themselves when she enters the auspicious chamber and lies down on the noble bed. In that regard, although seeing the appearance of deities is terrifying for humans, the Bodhisatta’s mother does not fear them upon seeing the four Great Kings, due to the power of her own merit and that of her son. Her mind regards those four Great Kings just like ordinary palace guards. She was naturally virtuous. It is said that in times when no Buddha has appeared, people take precepts by bowing and sitting in a crouching position before ascetics and wanderers. Our Bodhisatta’s mother also undertook virtue from the ascetic Kāladevila. In truth, while the Bodhisatta was in her womb, she was unable to sit at the feet of another; even sitting on an equal seat to take precepts would only amount to a mere reflection. Therefore, it means she undertook the precepts by herself.

“Regarding men” means that starting from the Bodhisatta’s father, lustful thoughts (desire for a man) did not arise in her towards any men. As for the appearance of the Bodhisatta’s mother, even highly skilled artists are unable to depict it in paintings or sculptures. It cannot be said that lust does not arise in a man upon seeing her; however, if a man with a lustful mind desires to approach her, his legs would fail to carry him, remaining stalled as if bound by divine shackles. Therefore, it is said “inviolable” and so on.

“With the five cords of sensual pleasure” refers to the previous statement “associated with the cords of sensual pleasure,” which showed the rejection of unchaste conduct through the power of desire for a man; here, it shows the acquisition of sense objects. At that time, hearing that such a son had been conceived in the Queen's womb, kings from all around sent gifts consisting of objects for the five sense doors, such as costly ornaments and musical instruments. Due to the abundance of the past kamma of the Bodhisatta and his mother, there was no limit to the amount of gains and honors.

“Having an untiring body” means that while other women become weary from carrying a pregnancy and experience swelling of the hands and feet, no such weariness occurred for her. “Abiding in the womb” refers to the child inside the belly. “She sees” means she sees him only after the embryonic stages (kalala, etc.) have passed and he has reached the state where his limbs and sense faculties are fully developed. For what purpose does she look? Only for the sake of his comfort. Just as a mother, while lying down or sitting, looks at her son to ensure his comfort, thinking, “If his hand or foot is hanging down, I will lift and place it well,” so too the Bodhisatta’s mother looks to see if her son is in distress during her rising, walking, turning, or sitting, or when she swallows hot, cold, salty, bitter, or pungent food. Looking for her son's comfort, she sees the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged. While other children in the womb sit crouching, pressing against the old food receptacle, carrying the new food receptacle, with the abdominal lining behind them, leaning against the backbone, and resting their chin on their two fists like a monkey in a tree hollow during rain, the Bodhisatta is not like that; he stays with his backbone behind him, like a Dhamma preacher on a preaching throne.
29:
Just as monkeys sit in a tree hollow when it rains, so do other children sit in their mother's womb.
