The Bodhisatta, however, is not like that; he sits with his back straight, cross-legged like a Dhamma preacher on a Dhamma throne, facing the East. The merit performed by the Bodhisatta's mother in previous lives cleanses the womb. When the womb is pure, a delicate skin-complexion arises. At that time, the abdominal skin is unable to conceal the Bodhisatta, and he is clearly visible to the mother who looks at him, as if he were outside. The Blessed One, wishing to clarify this meaning through a simile, taught the passage beginning with "Seyyathāpi." The Bodhisatta within the womb, however, does not see his mother. This is because eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) does not arise within the mother's womb.

"Passes away" (kālaṅkaroti) means that she passes away not because of the cause of childbirth, but solely because of the exhaustion of her life span. The place where a Bodhisatta has dwelt is like a shrine-room (cetiyakuṭi) and is not fit for use by others. It is also not appropriate to remove the Bodhisatta's mother and place another in the position of Chief Queen; therefore, the life span of a Bodhisatta's mother is only that long, and thus she passes away at that time. At what age does she pass away? She passes away in middle age (majjhima-vaya). In the first stage of life, the sensual desire (chandarāga) of beings for their own bodies is strong; therefore, a woman who becomes pregnant at that age cannot protect the fetus, and the fetus is prone to many ailments. However, after passing two parts of middle age and reaching the third part, the womb is clear. Children born in a clear womb are free from disease. Therefore, it is the natural law (dhammatā) here that the Bodhisatta's mother, having enjoyed pleasures in the first stage of life, gives birth in the third part of middle age and then passes away.

In the phrase "nine or ten months," by the power of the word "vā" (or) as a disjunctive, it should be understood that seven, eight, eleven, or twelve months, and so on, are also included. Among those, a child born at seven months lives but cannot endure cold or heat. A child born at eight months does not live. Children born in the remaining months live.

"The devas receive him first" means that the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, who are Arahants (khīṇāsava), receive him. How do they receive him? Some say, "taking the form of midwives." Rejecting that statement, this is said: At that time, the Bodhisatta's mother stood wearing a gold-threaded cloth and wrapped down to her feet in a white silk (dukūla) robe resembling a fish's eye. Then, her delivery was very easy, like water issuing from a water-strainer (dhamakaraṇa). Then, those Brahmas, approaching in their natural Brahma forms, first...
30:
(The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas) received him with a golden net. From the hands of those Brahmas, the Four Great Kings received him with an antelope-skin rug (ajinappaveṇi). From them, humans received him with a white silk cushion (dukūlacumbaṭaka). Therefore, it is said, "The devas receive him first, and afterwards humans."

"Four sons of devas" refers to the Four Great Kings. "Having received" means receiving with the antelope-skin rug. "Mahesakkha" means having great power, great retinue and fame, and being endowed with the marks (lakkhaṇa).

"He is born purely" means that unlike other beings who are born stuck in the birth canal, with limbs bent and twisted, he is not born that way; he is born without being stuck. "Udena" means with water (amniotic fluid). "By any impurity" means that while other beings, due to kamma-born winds (kammajavātā), are turned feet-up and head-down, falling into the birth canal as if falling into a hundred-fathom-deep hellish abyss, or like elephants being pulled through a small keyhole, experiencing great suffering and being born smeared with various impurities, the Bodhisatta is not like that. For kamma-born winds are unable to turn the Bodhisatta feet-up and head-down. Like a Dhamma preacher descending from a Dhamma throne, or like a man descending from a ladder, he stands stretching out both hands and both feet, and is born unsmeared by any impurity of the mother's womb.

"Streams of water" refers to masses of water. Among them, the cold water falls into a golden bowl, and the hot water falls into a silver bowl. This is said to show the drinking water and utility water for the Bodhisatta and his mother, which is unmixed with any impurity on the ground, as well as the play-water that is not shared with others. As for other water brought in gold and silver jars, and water in lotus ponds where swans and water-fowls frolic, there is no limit.

"Just born" (sampatijāta) means born at that very moment. Although in the Pali it is shown as if it were immediately upon leaving the mother's womb, it should not be viewed that way. In detail, the Brahmas first received the just-born Bodhisatta with a golden net; from the hands of those Brahmas, the Four Great Kings received him with an antelope-skin rug; from their hands, humans received him with a white silk cushion. Only after being released from the hands of humans did he stand upon the earth. "While the white parasol was held" means while the divine white parasol was being held appropriately. In this context, the attendants of the parasol...
31:
The five royal regalia, such as the sword and others, also arrived. In the Pāḷi text, however, only the parasol is mentioned, just as a king is mentioned when he travels. Among those five royal regalia, only the parasol is visible, but the one holding the parasol is not seen. Likewise, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-feather whisk, the yak-tail whisk, and the diadem are visible, but those holding them are not seen. It is said that deities with invisible forms held all those royal regalia. And it is said thus:

"Deities held in the sky a parasol with many branches and a thousand circles. Yak-tail whisks with golden handles waved to and fro. Yet, those holding the whisks and the parasol were not seen."

Regarding the phrase "He looked towards all directions," it is said as if the Bodhisatta, standing after taking seven steps, looked around at all directions. However, it should not be viewed in this way. In truth, when the Great Being (Mahāsatta) was released from the hands of humans and stood upon the earth, he looked towards the East. At that moment, many thousands of world-systems became like a single open space. There, deities and humans, making offerings with perfumes, garlands, and so on, said: "O Great Man, there is no one equal to you in this world, let alone anyone superior."

In this manner, having glanced at the ten directions—the four main directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—and seeing no one equal to himself, he recognized, "This is the North," and facing North, he proceeded by taking seven steps. Thus should the meaning be understood here.

"Āsabhi" means noble. "Aggo" means being the foremost and supreme of all through virtues. The other two words (Jeṭṭho and Seṭṭho) are merely synonyms of this word "Aggo." With the two phrases "This is the last birth" and "Now there is no more renewed existence," he proclaimed the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) to be attained in this very existence.

In this context, standing on the earth with level feet is the omen (pubbanimitta) for obtaining the four bases of power (iddhipāda). Facing the North is the omen for proceeding by overwhelming and overcoming the masses. Taking seven steps is the omen for obtaining the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The holding of the divine white parasol is the omen for obtaining the noble white parasol of liberation (vimutti). Obtaining the five royal regalia is the omen for being liberated through the five kinds of liberation. Looking towards all directions is the omen for obtaining unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). Uttering the noble speech is the omen for the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) which cannot be turned back by others. The lion's roar, "This is the last birth," is the omen for the final passing away (parinibbāna) into the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa nibbānadhātu).
32:
Thus it should be known. These sections (vāra) appear in the Pāḷi; however, the manifold section (sambahulavāra) does not appear and should be brought forth and shown.

Indeed, on the day the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) was born, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled. Deities from the ten-thousandfold world-system gathered in a single world-sphere (cakkavāḷa). First, the deities received him, and afterwards, humans. Lutes with strings and drums covered with skins sounded by themselves without being played by anyone. The shackles and bonds of humans broke into pieces. All diseases were calmed, disappearing like copper tarnish washed away by acid. Those blind from birth saw forms. Those deaf from birth heard sounds. The lame became endowed with speed. Even those born dull-witted or mute gained mindfulness. Ships sailing to foreign lands reached their ports safely. Jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shone with their own radiance. Enemies gained hearts of loving-kindness. The fire in the Avīci hell was extinguished. Light appeared in the inter-cosmic hells (lokantara). Water in the rivers did not flow. The water in the great ocean became sweet-tasted. The wind did not blow. Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees descended to the ground. The moon shone exceedingly. The sun was neither too hot nor too cold, becoming stainless and endowed with a temperate season. Deities, standing at the doors of their respective mansions, engaged in great celebration by clapping their hands, whistling, and tossing their garments. A great cloud rained, covering all four continents. The masses were not oppressed by hunger or thirst. Door-leaves opened by themselves. Trees bearing flowers and fruits took on their blossoms and fruits. The ten-thousandfold world-system became like a single array of banners and garlands.

In those events such as the earthquake, the omens should be understood as follows: The trembling of the ten-thousandfold world-system is the omen for obtaining Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññutañāṇa). The gathering of deities in a single world-sphere is the omen for their gathering all at once to receive the Dhamma when the Wheel of Dhamma is turned. The deities receiving him first is the omen for obtaining the four fine-material sphere jhanas (rūpāvacara jhāna). The humans receiving him afterwards is the omen for obtaining the four immaterial sphere jhanas (arūpāvacara jhāna). The lutes with strings sounding by themselves is the omen for obtaining the successive meditative attainments (anupubbavihāra). The sounding of the drums covered with skins is the omen for the proclamation of the great Drum of Dhamma. The breaking of bonds and shackles is the omen for the total eradication of the conceit "I am" (asmimāna). The disappearance of diseases among the masses is the omen for the realization of the Four Noble Truths. The seeing of forms by those blind from birth is the omen for obtaining the divine eye (dibbacakkhu).
33:
## Precursors
The hearing of sounds by the deaf is the precursor to the attainment of the divine ear element (dibba-sota-dhātu). The fulfillment of swiftness in the lame is the precursor to the attainment of the four bases of power (iddhipāda). The establishment of mindfulness in the dull-witted is the precursor to the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). The arrival at a good port of ships sailing to foreign lands is the precursor to the attainment of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The brilliance of jewels by their own power is the precursor to the light of the Dhamma that will be shown to the world.

The attainment of a mind of loving-kindness by enemies is the precursor to the attainment of the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra). The extinguishing of fires in the Avīci hell is the precursor to the extinguishing of the eleven fires. The light appearing in the Lokantarika hells, dispelling the darkness of ignorance, is the precursor to the vision of the light of knowledge. The sweetness of the great ocean is the precursor to the single taste of the flavor of Nibbāna. The ceasing of strong winds is the precursor to the shattering of the sixty-two views. The birds descending to the ground is the precursor to the taking of refuge for life by the masses after hearing the exhortation. The extreme brilliance of the moon is the precursor to being beloved by many people. The sun having a pleasant season free from heat and cold is the precursor to the attainment of physical and mental happiness. Deities standing at the doors of their mansions and playing by clapping their hands, etc., is the precursor to the uttering of an inspired utterance (udāna) upon reaching Buddhahood. The falling of a great rain over the four great islands is the precursor to the falling of the great rain of Dhamma. The absence of the affliction of hunger is the precursor to the attainment of the deathless through mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). The absence of the affliction of thirst is the precursor to being happy with the bliss of liberation (vimutti-sukha). The spontaneous opening of door-leaves is the precursor to the opening of the door of the Eightfold Path. Trees bearing flowers and fruits is the precursor to blooming with the flowers of liberation and being laden with the weight of the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). The presence of a single banner-garland throughout the ten thousand world-systems is the precursor to being adorned with the garlands of the banners of the Noble Ones (ariya). This is known as the Chapter of Various Occurrences (Sambahulavāra).

Here, they ask a question: "When the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) stood on the earth and walked facing north, uttering the lion's roar, did he go on the ground or through the air? Did he go while being visible or invisible? Did he go naked or adorned? Being in the form of a child..."
34:
"Did he go [walking], or did he go in the form of an elderly person? Later on, did he remain in that state, or did he become a young child again?" they asked. This question arose at the lower floor of the Lohapāsāda (Bronze Palace) and was answered by the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya. In this context, the Elder spoke extensively regarding the doctrines of fatalism (niyati), past deeds (pubbekata-kamma), and creation by a supreme lord (issara-nimmāna-vāda), and finally explained thus: "Although the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) walked on the ground, to the multitude it appeared as if he were traveling through the air. Although he walked visibly, to the multitude it appeared as if he were invisible. Although he walked without clothes, to the multitude he appeared as if he were well-adorned and dressed. Although he walked as a young child, to the multitude he appeared like a youth of about sixteen years of age. However, afterwards, he was just a young child and not like that [sixteen-year-old youth]." The assembly was delighted, saying, "Friends, the Elder has answered the question as if he were the Buddha himself." The section on the Lokantarika is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. It should be understood that all these natural phenomena (dhammatā) described from the beginning occur for all Bodhisattas.

## Dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavaṇṇanā

"Addasa kho" (He indeed saw) means he saw the Great Being who was brought while lying in a roll of fine cloth (dukūla-cumbaṭaka). "Mahāpurisassa" (Of the Great Man) means of a man who is great by way of birth, lineage, family, region, and so on. "Dve gatiyo" (Two destinies) means two kinds of outcomes (nipphatti) or two destinies. Indeed, this word "gati" is used in the sense of:

1. The destiny (gati) to be reached by beings, such as hell, etc., in the passage: "Sāriputta, there are these five destinies" (M. Ni. 1.153).
2. Inclination (ajjhāsaya) in the passage: "I do not know the coming or the going (gati) of these virtuous monks of good character" (M. Ni. 1.508).
3. Refuge (paṭissaraṇa) in the passage: "Nibbāna is the destiny (gati) of the Arahant" (Pari. 339).
4. Attainment or outcome (nipphatti) in the passage: "Brahma, I indeed know your destiny (gati) and I know your splendor; such is the great power of Baka Brahma" (M. Ni. 1.503).

It should be understood that here also, it is used in the sense of attainment or outcome (nipphatti). "Anaññā" (No other) means there is no other outcome.

"Dhammiko" (Righteous) means one who is endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action and is free from falling into the wrong paths (agati). "Dhammarājā" (Righteous King) is just a synonym for the preceding term. Alternatively, he is called Dhammarājā because he obtained kingship through Dhamma (righteousness).
35:
"Cāturanto" means the lord of the entire earth bounded by the four oceans, such as the eastern ocean. "Vijitāvī" means one who has conquered in battle. "Janapadatthāvariyappatta" means one whose realm has attained stability and firmness. Indeed, under a harsh king who oppresses the world with taxes, punishments, and so on, people abandon the central realm and live in the border regions, relying on mountains, seashores, and so on. Under an excessively soft king, people oppressed by the violence and robbery of thieves abandon the border regions and come to live in the center of the realm. Under such kings, the realm does not attain stability. But when this prince rules as king, his realm will be as firm as if placed on a stone slab and surrounded by iron bands; to show this, the fortune-telling brahmins said, "Janapadatthāvariyappatta."

In the term "Sattaratanasamannāgata" (endowed with the seven treasures), it is called a "treasure" (ratana) in the sense of producing delight and joy. Furthermore:

"Because it is cherished, of great value,
Incomparable, rare to see,
And used by noble beings,
It is called a treasure."

From the time the Wheel Treasure appears, there is no other place of worship; all people perform offerings with incense, flowers, etc., and pay homage to that Wheel Treasure alone. Thus, it is a treasure in the sense of being cherished (cittīkata). There is no price that can be set, saying the Wheel Treasure is worth this much wealth; thus, it is a treasure also in the sense of being of great value (mahaggha). The Wheel Treasure is unlike other treasures existing in the world; thus, it is a treasure also in the sense of being incomparable (atula). Since Universal Monarchs arise only in the aeons when Buddhas arise, and Buddhas arise only once in a long while, it is a treasure also in the sense of being rare to see (dullabhadassana). This treasure arises only for a noble and exalted being (anomasatta) endowed with [excellence in] birth, appearance, family, and power, and not for anyone else; thus, it is a treasure also in the sense of being used by noble beings. As with the Wheel Treasure, so it is with the remaining ones. One who is endowed with these seven treasures, both as a retinue and as all means of enjoyment, is called "Sattaratanasamannāgata."

Now, to show them by their nature, the fortune-telling brahmins said "Tassimāni," and so on. Among the terms "Cakkaratanaṃ," etc., this is the summary of the meaning: the Wheel Treasure appears, capable of bringing and bestowing the glory and wealth of the four great continents surrounded by two thousand small islands. Likewise, the Elephant Treasure appears, capable of traveling around the earth bounded by the oceans in just one morning, traveling through the air. The Horse Treasure is of the same nature. Endowed with the fourfold [army]...
36:
...the Gem-treasure appears, which is capable of dispelling darkness and providing light for the distance of one league (yojana) within the gloom. The Woman-treasure appears, who is free from the six defects and practices what is pleasing. The Householder-treasure appears, who is capable of seeing treasure-pots buried within the earth for the distance of one league. The Advisor-treasure appears, known as the eldest son, who is born from the womb of the chief queen and is capable of administering the entire kingdom.

Parosahassaṃ means a number exceeding one thousand. Surā means those who are fearless. Vīraṅgarūpā means those who have the nature of effort (vīriya), which is a characteristic of heroes. It means those sons, being of the nature of effort, do not become weary even if they fight in battle all day long. Sāgarapariyantaṃ means the earth which has the ocean as its boundary, established with the Cakkavāḷa mountains as the limit. Adaṇḍena means ruling without punishing beings who have committed offenses, whether by monetary fines or by weapons such as mutilation. This Wheel-turning King abandons both types of punishment and rules without punishment. Asatthena means not ruling by oppressing others with weapons such as swords; rather, without causing even as much blood as a small fly to flow, he conquers the aforementioned earth through Dhamma alone, being welcomed by rival kings with the words, 'Come, Great King,' and thus he dwells having overcome and become the lord.

Having thus stated the first achievement, to state the second achievement, the words beginning with 'Sace kho pana' were spoken. Therein, he is called 'Vivaṭacchado' (one who has opened the cover) because the covering or veil known as passion, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, defilements, and craving has been destroyed and opened. There is also a variant reading 'Vivaṭṭacchadā,' but the meaning is the same.

Having thus stated the second achievement, to show the marks (lakkhaṇa) which are the causes of those achievements, the words beginning with 'Ayañhi deva kumာရော' were spoken. Therein, 'Suppatiṭṭhitapādo' (one with well-planted feet) means that unlike other people whose toes, heels, or sides of the feet touch the ground first when placing the foot down, leaving a gap in the middle, or whose parts of the foot rise first when lifting the foot, it is not so for him. For him, the entire surface of the sole touches the ground all at once, like the surface of a golden sandal, and rises from the ground all at once. Therefore, he is 'Suppatiṭṭhitapādo'.
37:
Cakkāni — There are two wheels on the two soles of the feet. The spokes, rims, and hubs of these wheels have already been mentioned in the Pāḷi. The distinction should be understood by the phrase 'sabbākārapari-pūrāni' (complete in every aspect). In the center of the soles of those wheels, the hub is seen. The circular lines defining the hub, the rim surrounding the hub (or the encircling band), the axle hole, the spokes, the circular lines on the spokes, the rim, and the beads (or ruby-like engravings) on the rim are all visible. This has already appeared in the Pāḷi. Although not directly mentioned in the Pāḷi, the numerous characteristics of the wheels should be known as follows: a spear, the Sirivatsa, the Nandi (three-fold neck-line diagram), the Sovattika (Svastika), a wreath (vaṭaṃsaka), a food vessel (vaḍḍhamānaka), a pair of fish, an auspicious seat (bhaddapīṭha), an elephant goad, a palace, an archway, a white umbrella, a sword, a palm-leaf fan, a peacock-feather fan, a yak-tail whisk, a turban, a gem, an alms bowl, a jasmine garland, a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white lotus, a Paduma lotus, a Puṇḍarīka lotus, a full jar, a full bowl, the ocean, the world-system (Cakkavāḷa), the Himavā mountains, Mount Sineru, the moon and the sun, the stars, the four great islands, and the two thousand small islands. At the very least, everything up to the retinue of a Cakkavatti king is merely an accompaniment to the wheel-mark.

Āyatapaṇhī — Having long and full heels. While the forefeet of others are long and the leg bone (shin) rests on the top of the heel, making it appear as if the heel were cut off, it is not so for the Bodhisatta. If the foot of the Great Man is divided into four parts, two parts form the forefoot, the leg bone rests on the third part, and the fourth part is the heel, which is rounded as if turned with a lathe and resembles a red woolen ball.

Dīghangulī — Unlike others whose fingers are some long and some short, he has long fingers and toes like those of a monkey. They are thick at the base and gradually taper toward the tips, resembling sticks of orpiment that have been kneaded with resin oil and rolled smooth. Therefore, it is said, 'dīghangulī'.

Mudutalunahatthapādo — Having hands and feet as soft as a layer of cotton that has been struck a hundred times and dipped in clarified butter. Just as they are soft at birth, they remain soft and tender even in old age. Because he has such soft and tender hands and feet, he is called 'mudutalunahatthapādo'.

Jālahatthapādo — This does not mean that the spaces between the fingers are connected by skin. Such a condition is called 'phaṇahatthaka' (hood-hand), which is a human defect that prevents one from receiving ordination. For the Great Man, the four fingers (excluding the thumb) and the five toes are of equal length. That...
38:
Furthermore, the four fingers (excluding the thumb) and the five toes are of equal length. Because they are of equal length, the barley-grain marks (yava-lakkhaṇa) on the joints align with one another. Then, the hands and feet of that Great Man are like a lattice window (jāla-vātāpana) crafted by a skilled carpenter. Therefore, it is said, 'jālahatthapādo' (having net-like hands and feet).

Because his ankles are set high, he is called 'ussaṅkhapādo' (having high-set ankles). For other people, the ankles are on the sides of the feet; thus, their feet are as if fixed with bolts and cannot turn freely, and the soles are not visible when they walk. For the Great Man, however, the ankles are positioned high above the top of the foot. Consequently, from the navel upward, his upper body remains as still as a golden statue placed on a boat, while only the lower body moves. His feet turn easily, and the soles are clearly visible to those watching from the front, back, left, or right; it is not like elephants, whose soles are seen only from behind.

'Eṇijaṅgho' means having calves like those of the eṇī antelope, with calves full of flesh. The flesh is not bunched up on one side; rather, he is endowed with calves that are evenly surrounded by flesh, well-rounded, and resemble the shape of a grain of rice or barley.

'Anonamanto' means one who does not bend. By this term, the Great Man's state of being neither hunchbacked nor dwarfed is shown. Other people are either hunchbacked or dwarfed. In the hunchbacked, the upper body is incomplete; in the dwarfed, the lower body is incomplete. Because their bodies are incomplete, they are unable to stroke their knees without bending. The Great Man, however, because both his upper and lower body are complete, is able to stroke his knees (without bending his body).

'Kosohitavatthaguyho' means having the male organ concealed in a sheath, like that of a noble bull or a king elephant, resembling the calyx of a golden lotus. 'Vatthaguyha' refers to the organ that should be concealed by cloth.

'Suvaṇṇavaṇṇo' means having a complexion like a solid gold statue that has been polished with vermilion, rubbed with a tusker's ivory, and finished with red chalk. To show that he has a solid, smooth, and soft body, and to describe the color of his skin, it is said, 'kañcanasannibhattaco' (having skin like gold). Alternatively, this is a synonym for the preceding term.
39:
"Rajojalla" means dust or dirt. Just as a drop of water rolls off a lotus leaf, it does not adhere. Even though dust and dirt do not settle on them, the Buddhas perform acts such as washing their hands for the sake of the season's suitability and for the merit of the donors; they also do so out of duty (vatta). It is said: "A monk entering a monastery should wash his feet before entering."

"Uddhaggaloma" means having body hairs that, at the end of their rightward curl, point upwards as if looking up at the beauty of the face.

"Brahmujugatta" means having a straight body like a Brahma; he will have a body that is straight and tall. Generally, beings bend in three places: the neck, the waist, and the knees. When they bend at the waist, they bend backwards; in the other two places, they bend forwards. Some tall people are crooked at the sides; some walk with their faces tilted up as if counting the stars; some, having little flesh and blood, resemble a roasting spit; some lean forward and walk trembling. But this Great Man grows straight and tall, and it is shown that he will be like a golden gatepost erected in a celestial city. Just as the marks of a Great Man are not fully complete in every aspect at birth, it should be understood that they are described with reference to how they will become in the future.

"Sattussada" means having full flesh in seven places: the backs of the two hands, the backs of the two feet, the two shoulders, and the neck. In others, the network of veins is visible on the backs of the hands and feet, and the joints of the bones are visible on the shoulders and neck. Such people look like hungry ghosts (petas). The Great Man is not like that; because the flesh is full in those seven places, with the backs of the hands and feet where the network of veins is hidden, and with a neck like a well-fashioned golden drum, he appears like a stone statue or a painted image.

"Sīhapubbaddhakāya" means having a body like the front half of a lion. For a lion, only the front body is full, while the hind body is not. For the Great Man, however, the entire body is full like the front half of a lion. His body, like a lion's, in various places by way of indentation and elevation...
40:
(The Great Man's body) does not have a bad or distorted shape. It is long where it should be long. In places where it should be short, thick, thin, broad, or rounded, it is exactly so. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, when the result of wholesome kamma is present, it is indeed pleasing. Those limbs that are beautiful when long, stay long. Those limbs that are beautiful when short, stay short. Those limbs that are beautiful when thick, stay thick. Those limbs that are beautiful when thin, stay thin. Those limbs that are beautiful when broad, stay broad. Those limbs that are beautiful when rounded, stay rounded.” Thus, the physical form of the Great Man, produced by various wholesome thoughts and prepared by the ten perfections, cannot be replicated even by all the artisans or all the powerful beings in the world.

"Citantaraṃsa" means the area between the two shoulder blades is called "antaraṃsa." Because the Great Man has that space between the shoulders filled and full, he is called "Citantaraṃsa." In others, that place is hollow, and the two shoulder blades appear separately. For the Great Man, however, a layer of flesh rises evenly from the waist to the neck, covering the back like a well-placed golden slab.

"Nigrodhaparimaṇḍala" means having a body as symmetrical as a banyan tree. Just as a banyan tree, whether fifty or a hundred cubits high, with its trunk and branches in proportion, is equal in height and width, so too the Great Man is equal in height and arm span. It means his proportions are not uneven like others whose bodies might be long or have a wide span but are not equal. Therefore, it is said, “How great is the extent of his body,” and so on. In that context, “yāvatako assa” is expressed as “yāvatakvassa.”

"Samavaṭṭakkhandha" means having a well-rounded neck. Some people have necks like cranes, herons, or pigs—long, crooked, or thick. When they speak, the network of veins becomes visible. For the Great Man, it is not so. The Great Man has a neck like a well-rounded small golden drum. When he speaks, the network of veins is not visible. He has a powerful voice like the sound of thunder.
41:
(20) Some people have long necks like cranes, curved necks like herons, or thick necks like pigs. When such people speak, a network of veins becomes clearly visible. Their voices also come out faintly. But it is not so for the Great Man (Mahāpurisa). The neck of the Great Man is like a well-rounded golden drum. When he speaks, no network of veins appears, and he possesses a powerful voice like the roar of thunder.

(21) "Rasaggasaggī" is the name for the nerves that carry taste. In the Great Man, seven thousand taste-carrying nerves, turned upwards, are gathered and fixed in the throat. Even a portion of food the size of a sesame seed placed on the tip of the tongue spreads throughout the entire body. For this reason, while he was practicing the great austerities (dukkara-cariyā), he was able to sustain his body with just a single grain of rice or a spoonful of mung bean soup. In others, because such nerves do not exist, the essence (ojā) does not spread through the entire body. Because the essence does not spread, those people are prone to many diseases.

(22-23) He is called "Sīhahanu" because he has a jaw like that of a lion. In a lion, only the lower jaw is full, not the upper. But in the Great Man, both the upper and lower jaws are full, like the moon on the twelfth day of the waxing phase. At that time, the fortune-telling Brahmins, looking at the edges of the jaws, observed that in these jaws, twenty teeth below and twenty above, totaling forty, would be even and close-set. They predicted, "O King, this prince will have forty teeth," and so on. While others with a full set of teeth have only thirty-two, this Great Man will have forty.

(24-26) While others' teeth may be uneven, with some high and some low, this Great Man's teeth will be even like a conch shell sliced with a saw. While others' teeth may be wide-spaced like a crocodile's, causing fish or meat to get stuck between them when eating, this Great Man's teeth will be close-set like a row of diamonds set on a golden plate. They will appear clearly demarcated as if marked with a brush. While others may develop decayed teeth, causing the canines to be black or discolored, this Great Man will have perfectly white canines. He will have canines endowed with a radiance that surpasses even the morning star (osadhitāraka).

(27) "Pahūtajivho" means having a broad tongue. While others' tongues may be thick, thin, short, stiff, or uneven, the Great Man's tongue is soft, long, broad, and beautiful in color. To dispel the doubts of those who come to examine this mark, because of its softness, he rolls that tongue like a needle and touches both nostrils; because of its length, [he touches] both ear-holes...
42:
...and because of its breadth, it can cover the entire forehead up to the hairline. Thus, by demonstrating the softness, length, and breadth of his tongue, he dispels their doubts. Referring to the tongue endowed with these three characteristics, it is said, "He has a broad tongue (pahūtajivho)."

"Brahmassaro" means that while others have broken voices, cracked voices, or voices like a crow, this Great Man will be endowed with a voice like that of the Great Brahma. The Great Brahma's voice is clear because it is not obstructed by bile or phlegm. For the Great Man, his past meritorious deeds purify the source of his voice. Because the source is pure, the voice arising from the navel is clear and possesses the eight qualities. Because he speaks like a Karavīka bird, he is called "one who speaks like a Karavīka bird" (karavīkabhāṇī), meaning he has a sweet voice like the song of an intoxicated Karavīka bird.

"Abhinīlanetto" does not mean his eyes are entirely blue. Rather, in the places that should be blue, his eyes have an extremely pure blue color like the blue pea flower (umā). In the places that should be yellow, they have a yellow color like the kaṇikāra flower; in the places that should be red, a red color like the bandhujīvaka flower; in the places that should be white, a white color like the morning star; and in the places that should be black, a black color like a black bead (addāriṭṭhaka). They appear like jeweled lion-windows opened in a golden mansion.

In the term "Gopakhumo", "pakhuma" refers to the entire eye apparatus. That eye has the quality of a black calf's [eye] in its thickness, and a red calf's in its clarity. It means he has eyes like those of a tender red calf born that very moment. Others' eyes are incomplete. They are endowed with eyes that are either protruding or deep-set, like the eyes of elephants or mice. But the Great Man's eyes are surrounded by eyelashes that are soft, smooth, dark blue, and delicate, like polished and burnished jeweled spheres.

"Uṇṇā" refers to the uṇṇā hair. "Between the eyebrows" means it is born exactly in the middle of the two eyebrows, above the nose. It rises and stays in the middle of the forehead. "Odātā" means it is pure, with a color like the morning star. "Mudū" means it is like a tuft of cotton that has been carded a hundred times and dipped in clarified butter (ghee). "Tūlasannibhā" means it is like silk-cotton or vine-cotton. This is an analogy for the whiteness of that uṇṇā hair. If that uṇṇā hair is held by the tip and pulled, it is half an arm's length long.
43:
When released, it [the uṇṇā hair] curls to the right with its tip pointing upwards. It shines with a most captivating splendor, like a silver stud placed in the middle of a golden plate, like a stream of milk flowing from a golden jar, and like the morning star in the sky tinged with the glow of dawn.

The term 'Uṇhīsasīsa' is used in reference to two meanings: having a full forehead and having a full head. To explain in detail, from the edge of the Great Man's right ear, a fleshy protuberance rises, covering and filling the entire forehead, and ending at the edge of the left ear. This fleshy protuberance is as beautiful as a king's royal headband (uṇhīsa). It is said that kings made royal headbands after seeing this mark of the Great Man. This is the first meaning.

Other people have incomplete heads; some have heads like monkeys, some like fruits, some like skulls, some like elephant brows, some like gourds, and some with protruding backs of the head. The head of the Great Man, however, is perfectly full like a water bubble, as if it were turned on a lathe. Between these two, according to the first method, he is called 'Uṇhīsasīsa' because his head appears as if wrapped with a royal headband. According to the second method, he is called 'Uṇhīsasīsa' because his head is perfectly circular in all parts like a headband.

## Explanation of the Name of Prince Vipassī

Although the phrase 'sabbakāmehi' (with all desires/pleasures) is mentioned as if it occurred after the examination of the marks, it should not be understood in that way. It should be understood that first, those soothsayers were satisfied, and only then was the examination of the marks performed. The details of this matter have already been mentioned in the section on the descent into the womb (gabbhokkanti). 'Pāyentī' means suckling with milk. For that prince, sixty nurses provided with faultless and sweet milk were appointed for service. Likewise, sixty nurses each, skilled in various other tasks, were also appointed. There were sixty men to give orders to those nurses, and sixty ministers to inspect whether various tasks were completed or not. Thus, there were four groups of sixty women and two groups of sixty men, totaling six groups of sixty (360) attendants.

'Setacchattaṃ' refers to the divine white umbrella. The white umbrella given by his father, however, remained only in the auspicious chamber (sirigabbha). In the words 'mā naṃ sītaṃ vā' etc., the meaning should be understood as 'let [cold, etc.] not oppress him.' 'Svāssudaṃ' should be resolved into 'so assudaṃ.' 'Aṅkeneva aṅkaṃ' means carrying from one person's arm to another's arm, and from one person's shoulder to another's shoulder.
44:
From one person's shoulder-blade to another's shoulder-blade only; 'parihariyati' means being carried, and 'sampāpiyati' means being brought.

'Mañjussara' means having a voice that is not harsh. 'Vaggussara' means having a voice that is skillful, proficient, and perfect. 'Madhurassara' means having a melodious voice. 'Pemaniyassara' means having a voice that inspires love and affection.

Regarding the melodious voice of the Karavīka birds among those voices, to speak in detail: when a Karavīka bird pecks a delicious ripe mango with the tip of its beak, drinks the flowing juice, flaps its wings, and sings out, four-footed creatures begin to frolic in ecstasy as if intoxicated. Even four-footed creatures searching for food drop the grass from their mouths and listen to that sound. Beasts of prey, while chasing smaller animals, stand still without even putting down their raised feet. The hunted animals also stand still, forgetting the fear of death. Even birds flying in the sky stand still, spreading their wings and listening to that sound. Even fish in the water stand still, flapping their fins and listening to that sound. In this way, Karavīka birds have melodious voices.

Queen Asandhimittā, the consort of King Dhammāsoka, also asked the Saṅgha, "Venerable sirs, is there anyone whose voice is like the Buddha's voice?" When they replied, "The voice of the Karavīka bird is similar," she asked, "Venerable sirs, where do those birds live?" They replied, "They live in the Himālaya." The queen then said to the king, "Great King, I wish to see a Karavīka bird." The king released a golden cage, saying, "Let a Karavīka bird come and sit in this cage." The cage went and stood before a Karavīka bird. The bird thought, "This cage has come by royal command; I cannot help but go," and sat in the cage. The cage returned and stood before the king. However, they could not make the Karavīka bird sing. Then the king asked, "Friends, why does this bird not make a sound?" They replied, "Great King, it is because it does not see its kinsfolk." Then the king had the bird surrounded with mirrors. The bird, seeing its own reflection and thinking, "My kinsfolk have arrived," flapped its wings and sang with a melodious voice like one playing a jeweled flute. The people of the entire city frolicked as if intoxicated. Queen Asandhimittā thought, "If even the voice of this animal is this melodious, how much more melodious must be the voice of the Blessed One who has attained the splendor of Omniscient Wisdom?" She developed joy (pīti) directed towards the Buddha, and without letting go of that joy, she, along with seven hundred female attendants who followed on foot, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). In this way, the voice of the Karavīka bird is very melodious.
45:
The voice of the Karavīka bird is said to be melodious. It should be understood that the voice of Prince Vipassī was a hundred, even a thousand times more melodious than that of the king of Karavīka birds.

"Kamma-vipākaja" (born of the ripening of kamma) refers not to the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) produced by meditation, but to a physical eye (maṃsa-cakkhu) similar to that of the devas, resulting from the fruition of kamma. With this eye, he was capable of picking out a specific marked sesame seed from among seeds poured into a sesame cart, saying, "This is that seed."

Regarding the name "Vipassī", the derivative meaning is: he is called Vipassī because he sees clearly, free from the darkness caused by blinking at intervals, and because he sees with open eyes. In the second instance, he is called Vipassī because he sees after investigating and reflecting. It means he sees by examining repeatedly.

"Atthe panāyati" means he knows and sees the benefit (or justice), or he brings it about. One day, while King Bandhumā was sitting in the place of judgment and administering justice, they brought the adorned Great Being (the Bodhisatta) and placed him in his arms. While the King was fondling the prince in his lap, the ministers decided a case in favor of the non-owner against the rightful owner (unjustly). Then the Bodhisatta uttered a sound of displeasure. The King said, "What is this sound? Investigate it." Upon investigation, seeing no other cause, they thought, "It must be because the case was poorly decided," and so they decided in favor of the rightful owner again. Wanting to test whether the prince did this knowingly, they again decided against the rightful owner. The Bodhisatta uttered the same sound again. Then the King realized, "The Great Being knows," and from then on, he became heedful. With reference to this, it is said: "The prince sees the benefit (justice) by investigating and reflecting."

In the words beginning with "Vassika", a palace comfortable for living during the rainy season is called "Vassika". The same logic applies to the others. Here, the derivative meaning is: living in the rainy season is "vassa"; a palace worthy of living in during the rainy season is "vassika". The same applies to the others (Hemantika and Gimmhika).

Among those three, the Vassika palace is neither too high nor too low. Its doors and windows are neither too many nor too few. Floor coverings, bedspreads, and various foods are suitable here even when mixed. In the Hemantika (winter) palace, the pillars and walls are low. The doors and windows are small with fine openings. Projections are built into the walls to let in heat. In this palace, floor coverings, bedspreads, and garments to be worn...
46:
...warm woolen blankets and such are suitable (in winter). The foods are rich in oil, spicy, and undiluted. In the Gimmhika (summer) palace, the pillars and walls are high. In this summer palace, the doors and windows are numerous and large. Floor coverings and such made of fine silk (dukūla) are suitable. The foods are full of sweet flavors. Near the windows of that palace, new water jars are placed, filled with water, and covered with blue lotuses and such. In various places, water machines are made, from which streams of water flow out as if it were raining.

"Nippurisehi" means without men (only women being present). In this context, it is not only the musicians who are without men; in all places, there are no men. Even the doorkeepers are only women. Even those who perform services such as bathing are only women. It is said that the King thought: "If my son, who is enjoying such sovereignty, happiness, and prosperity, sees a man, he might develop thoughts of male behavior (purisāsaṅkā). Let such doubts not arise in my son." Thus, he placed only women in all affairs.

## The Explanation of the First Recitation Section is Finished.

## Explanation of the Old Man

43-4. In the second recitation section (bhāṇavāra), "gopānasivaṅka" means one who is bent like the curved rafters (gable-end) of a house. "Bhogga" means being bent in three places: the neck, the waist, and the knees. "Daṇḍaparāyana" means one who walks relying on a staff, one for whom a staff is the support. "Ātura" means one afflicted by old age. "Gatayobbana" means one whose youth has passed and who has reached the final stage of life. "Disvā" means seeing that old man manifested by the Suddhāvāsa Arahant Brahmas through their psychic power right in front of the chariot, at a time when the chariot was in front and the troops were behind, even though he was surrounded by an army of about half a league and well-guarded. It is said that the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas thought: "This Great Being is stuck in the five cords of sensual pleasure like an elephant in the mud; we shall arouse his mindfulness." Thus, they showed him that old man. Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw the old man thus shown. Indeed, the Brahmas showed him for the sake of the Bodhisatta's heedfulness (appamāda) and to provide an occasion for conversation with the charioteer. "Kiṃ paneso" means "What is the nature of this person called an old man? Friend... I have never seen such a person before," thus he asked.
47:
The phrase "Tena hi" means "If I too must have such hair and such a body." He said, "Friend charioteer, if that is so, there is no need to go to the park today," meaning that although he had set out with the intention of visiting the park, he saw no benefit in viewing it. He spoke thus in accordance with the spiritual urgency (saṃvega) that filled his heart. When the prince returned to the palace, he dismissed the women and sat alone in his royal chamber. He sat there as if struck in the heart by a first arrow, digging at the root of birth, thinking, "When there is birth (jāti), aging is manifest; that birth is contemptible and loathsome."

King Bandhuma had been listening attentively since the time the fortune-telling brahmins had made their prediction. When he heard that the prince had turned back midway while going to the park, he summoned the charioteer. His thought was: "Let him only rule the kingdom; let him not go forth into homelessness. May the words of the brahmins not come true."

## Description of the Sick Man
As mentioned before, he saw a sick person shown by the Suddhāvāsa deities. "Ābādhika" refers to being ill with an affliction that disrupts the postures. "Dukkhita" means being in a state of suffering due to the pain of the disease. "Bāḷhagilāna" means being severely ill. "Palipanna" means being overwhelmed (sunk). Here too, he sat as if struck by a second arrow, digging at the root of birth, thinking, "When there is birth, these two—aging and sickness—are manifest; that birth is contemptible; non-arising (Nibbāna) alone is safety."

## Description of the Dead Man
"Vilāta" refers to a palanquin (bier). "Peta" refers to one who has departed from this life. "Kālaṅkata" refers to one who has reached the end of their time, having completed the lifespan they were meant to live. The Brahmas also showed this dead person in the same manner as before. Here too, he sat as if struck by a third arrow, digging at the root of birth, thinking, "When there is birth, these three—aging, sickness, and death—are manifest; that birth is contemptible; non-arising alone is safety."
48:
## Description of the Recluse
"Bhaṇḍu" means shaven-headed. The Brahmas showed this recluse to that Great Being in the same manner as before. In the phrases beginning with "Sādhu dhammacariyā," the connection of the meaning of each word should be understood as: "O Prince, practicing such wholesome Dhamma is good," and thus he went forth. All these terms are synonyms for the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakamma-patha). "Avihiṃsā" (non-violence) at the end refers to the wholesome state of the sense sphere that is the preliminary stage of compassion (karuṇā). "Anukampā" (empathy) refers to the wholesome state of the sense sphere that is the preliminary stage of loving-kindness (mettā). The word "Tena hi" is a particle used in the sense of exhortation. Upon seeing the recluse, the prince's mind inclined toward renunciation. Then, wishing to speak with that recluse, he exhorted the charioteer and spoke the words beginning with "Tena hi."

## Description of the Bodhisatta's Renunciation
Monks, "Atha kho bhikkhave" means after hearing the words "The recluse's good practice of Dhamma" and many other Dhamma discourses. Having heard discourses concerning the danger of living in a house crowded with wife and children while being guarded by a great multitude, and the benefits of the seclusion of a recluse living at ease in the forest with a mind like a deer, he desired to go forth. Thus it is said, "Monks, then the Prince Vipassī summoned the charioteer."

Going forth after seeing these four signs is the lineage, tradition, and custom of all Bodhisattas. Other Bodhisattas also see these signs only after a long time, just as Prince Vipassī did. However, our Bodhisatta saw all four signs on the same day, made the Great Renunciation (Mahābhini-kkhamana), and went forth on the banks of the Anomā River. Because the signs appeared on a single day, when he reached Rājagaha and was asked by King Bimbisāra, "O Wise One, why have you gone forth?", he replied:

"Having seen the aged, and the suffering sick,
And having seen the dead whose life-span had ended,
And having seen the recluse wearing saffron-dyed robes,
Therefore, O King, have I gone forth."

## Description of the Great Multitude Following in Renunciation
"Sutvāna tesaṃ" means having heard the words of those eighty-four thousand beings, this thought occurred. "Orako" means inferior or low. "Anupabbajiṃsu" means they followed him into renunciation.
49:
They went forth following him. Why is it not stated here, as it is said later regarding the following of Khaṇḍa and Tissa, "having departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī"? It is because they heard the news while outside the city. All of them were indeed the attendants of Prince Vipassī. Although they had come early to serve him, they did not find the prince and went to have their breakfast. Having finished their breakfast, they returned and asked, "Where is the prince?" Hearing that he had gone to the park, they set out thinking, "We shall see him right there in that park." On their way, they met the returning charioteer and heard his words: "The prince has gone forth." Right at the place where they heard this, they removed all their ornaments, sent for saffron-dyed robes from the market, shaved off their hair and beards, and went forth. Thus, because they heard the news outside the city after having already departed from it, it is not said here, "having departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī."

"He wandered on a walking tour" means that in every place he reached, a great pavilion was constructed and offerings were prepared; he wandered on tour for four months, accepting only the alms-food requested by the multitude of people who had invited him for the following day.

"He was surrounded" means he was accompanied by this group of monks. When did this thought arise in the Bodhisatta? It was on the fourteenth day, thinking, "Tomorrow will be the full moon of Visākha." At that time, he became weary of the company of the group (gaṇasaṅgaṇikā), thinking, "These people surround me now while I wander, just as they did before when I was a layman; what is the use of this group?" He thought, "I shall go this very day," but then reconsidered, "Today is not the right time; if I go now, everyone will know. I shall go only tomorrow."

On that day, the villagers in a village similar to Uruvelā invited them for the next day. They prepared only milk-rice (pāyāsa) for the eighty-four thousand monks and the Great Being (Mahāpurisa). Then, on the following day, the Great Being, having completed the meal-service with those monks in that very village, went only to his own dwelling. There, those monks performed their duties toward the Great Being and then entered their respective quarters for the night and day. The Bodhisatta also entered his leaf-hut and sat down.

"When the midday hour has come,
And the birds have settled down,
The great forest rustles;
That fear appears to me."
50:
At such a time of fear for those who do not delight in seclusion, and at a time of distress for all beings, he thought, "This is the time [to depart]," and having gone out and closed the door of the leaf-hut, he headed toward the Bodhi-maṇḍa (Seat of Enlightenment). Although he had seen the Bodhi-maṇḍa while wandering in that place at other times, the thought of sitting there had never occurred to him before. But on that day, his knowledge had reached maturity; therefore, seeing the adorned Bodhi-maṇḍa, the thought to ascend it arose. That Vipassī Bodhisatta approached from the southern direction, performed a circumambulation (padakkhiṇa), and having prepared a fourteen-cubit seat on the eastern side, he sat down after making a resolution and undertaking the fourfold effort (caturanga-vīriya): "As long as I have not become a Buddha, I shall not rise from this seat."

With reference to his dwelling in seclusion, it is said: "He lived alone, secluded from the group."

"By another way, those [monks]" means that those eighty-four thousand monks came in the evening to attend to the Bodhisatta and sat surrounding the leaf-hut. Saying, "It has become very late, let us investigate," they opened the leaf-hut, and although they did not see him, they did not pursue him, asking, "Where has he gone?" Thinking, "The Great Being seems to be weary of living in a group and wishes to live alone; we shall see him only when he has become a Buddha," they departed on a tour toward the interior of Jambudīpa.

## Explanation of the Bodhisatta's Insight

"To one who has approached for dwelling" means to one who has approached to stay for one night at the Bodhi-maṇḍa. "To one who has gone into seclusion" means to one who has reached a place secluded from people. "To one who is in retirement" means to one who is dwelling by way of singleness of mind. "Suffering" means dukkha. "Passes away and is reborn"—this pair is said with reference to the successive rounds of death and rebirth. In the phrase "of aging and death," because the Bodhisatta had gone forth after seeing only the aged, the sick, and the dead at the time of his renunciation, only aging and death appeared in his knowledge. That is why it is said, "of aging and death."

Thus, the reflection of the Vipassī Bodhisatta, who took aging and death as the root, was like one descending from the peak of existence, descending from the end to the root. Then, O monks, this thought occurred to the Vipassī Bodhisatta:

"Through wise attention" (yoniso manasikāra) means through attention to the means (upāya) and through primary attention. Indeed, the attention of one who attends to impermanence and so on as impermanent is called wise attention. And because this [reflection] proceeds by way of the contemplation of rise and fall (udayabbayānupassanā), such as "When what exists do birth and so on come to be? When what is absent do they not come to be?", it is included among those contemplations of impermanence and the like.
51:
It is one of those [types of attention] such as the reflection on impermanence. Therefore, for the Bodhisatta Vipassī, through wise attention in this proper manner, there arose a penetration by wisdom. The Bodhisatta's wisdom met with (fully understood) the cause of aging and death—that which being present, aging and death come to be. What is that cause? It is birth (jāti). Therefore, it was said: "When there is birth, aging and death come to be." The meaning here is that the Bodhisatta's wisdom met with the wisdom that grasps the cause of aging and death. In this manner, all terms should be understood.

In the context of "With name-and-form as condition, consciousness [comes to be]," although it could have been stated as "With volitional formations as condition, consciousness [comes to be]" or "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations [come to be]," neither of these was taken. Why? Because ignorance and volitional formations belong to the past life, and this insight (vipassanā) cannot be connected with those factors. For the Great Being (Bodhisatta) was intent on investigating by way of present phenomena. One might object: "Is it not impossible to become a Buddha without seeing ignorance and volitional formations?" True, it is not possible. However, this Bodhisatta saw those [ignorance and formations] only through the power of seeing existence (bhava), clinging (upādāna), and craving (taṇhā). Here, the discourse on Dependent Origination should be explained in detail. However, that discourse has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga.

"Paccudāvattati" means it turns back or retreats. Which consciousness turns back here? It is both the rebirth-linking consciousness and the insight-knowledge (consciousness). Between the two, the rebirth-linking consciousness turns back from the cause (formations), and the insight-knowledge turns back from the object (formations). Both cannot transcend name-and-form; they do not go beyond name-and-form. In the words "To this extent, one may be born," etc., whether consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, or name-and-form is the condition for consciousness—when these two are mutually conditioning each other—it is designated that by this much mutual support between consciousness and name-and-form, a being "may be born" or "may be born again and again." Beyond this consciousness and name-and-form, what other thing could be born or born again? Is it not only this combination of consciousness and name-and-form that is born and born again? Having thus shown the five terms such as "one may be born" along with the successive deaths and rebirths, and wishing to conclude the meaning expressed by the word "ettāvatā" (to this extent), he said: "With name-and-form as condition, consciousness [comes to be]; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form [comes to be]." Furthermore, by the power of the forward order of Dependent Origination, in order to show birth, aging, and death in the future life which has name-and-form (conditioned by consciousness) as its root, he said: "With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases [come to be]," and so on. In that statement, "there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering" means the arising of the entire mass of suffering consisting of various parts such as birth, aging, and so forth. In this way, the Great Being saw the arising of the entire suffering of the round of rebirths.
52:
“Samudaya, samudaya” (Origin, origin) means arising, arising. “Pubbe ananussutesu” means in things not heard before, not previously heard. In the phrases beginning with “cakkhuṃ udapādi” (the eye arose), the very insight wisdom (vipassanā-paññā) that contemplates arising is called “cakkhu” (eye) in the sense of seeing; “ñāṇa” (knowledge) in the sense of making known; “paññā” (wisdom) in the sense of knowing in various ways; “vijjā” (true knowledge) in the sense of arising by piercing through and penetrating; and “āloka” (light) in the sense of illumination.

Referring to this, the Elder Sāriputta taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: “The eye arose in the sense of seeing; knowledge arose in the sense of knowing; wisdom arose in the sense of knowing in various ways; true knowledge arose in the sense of penetration; light arose in the sense of illumination. The eye-dhamma has the meaning of the sense of seeing. The knowledge-dhamma has the meaning of the sense of knowing. The wisdom-dhamma has the meaning of the sense of knowing in various ways. The true knowledge-dhamma has the meaning of the sense of penetration. The light-dhamma has the meaning of the sense of illumination.” What is meant by these many terms? It means the mere recognition of conditions: “When this cause exists, this effect arises.” Alternatively, it refers to tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) that has just entered the course of insight.

“Adhigato kho myāyaṃ” should be resolved as “Adhigato kho me ayaṃ” (This has been attained by me). “Magga” refers to the path of insight (vipassanā-magga). “Bodhāya” means for the sake of knowing the Four Noble Truths, or for the sake of knowing Nibbāna. In another way, it is called “Bodhi” because it knows; this is a name for the Noble Path (ariya-magga), and thus it means for the sake of that Noble Path. This is because the Noble Path is rooted in the path of insight. Now, wishing to show that path of insight, the Buddha taught the passage beginning with “yadidaṃ nāmarūpanirodhā” (that is, from the cessation of mind-and-matter). Here, the terms in the nominative case such as “viññāṇanirodha” (cessation of consciousness) refer to Nibbāna itself. In this way, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) saw the cessation—the non-arising—of the entire suffering of the round of rebirth.

“Nirodha, nirodha” means “non-arising, non-arising.” The terms “cakkhu” and so on have the same meanings as previously mentioned. However, in this section on cessation (nirodha-vāra), all these terms mean the mere recognition of cessation: “When this cause is absent, this effect does not occur.” Alternatively, it refers to the powerful insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) which is the cause for reaching the Noble Path.

“Aparena samayena” means at another time after having known the conditions and the cessation of conditions. “Upādānakkhandhesu” means in the aggregates which are the objects of clinging. “Udayabbayānupassī” means repeatedly contemplating that arising and passing away which was previously seen. “Vihāsī” means he dwelt while maintaining the insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) that has reached its peak. Why is this said? All Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), in their final birth, go forth on the day their son is born, practice austerities (dukkharacariyā), then ascend the Bodhi-seat, defeat the army of Māra, and in the first watch of the night, attain the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsānussati-ñāṇa). In the middle watch, they purify the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). In the last watch, they contemplate dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), emerge from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), focus on the five aggregates of clinging, contemplate the fifty characteristics of arising and passing away, develop insight up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), and penetrate all the Buddha-qualities through the Noble Path. This Bodhisatta Vipassī, being one who had fulfilled the perfections, followed this same sequence: in the last watch, emerging from the fourth ānāpāna-jhāna, focusing on the five aggregates, he practiced the aforementioned insight into arising and passing away. To show this practice, the passage beginning with “aparena samayena” was taught.
53:
All Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections, in their final existence, depart on the day of their son's birth through the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) and become monks to practice. Having ascended the Throne of Enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka) and defeated the forces of Māra, in the first watch of the night, they recollect their past lives (Pubbenivāsa). In the middle watch, they purify the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu). In the last watch, they contemplate Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), and arising from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (Ānāpāna-catuttha-jhāna), they direct their minds to the five aggregates of clinging (Upādānakkhandha). By way of arising and passing away, they see the fifty characteristics, and developing insight (Vipassanā) up to the Change-of-lineage knowledge (Gotrabhū-ñāṇa), they penetrate all the qualities of a Buddha (Buddha-guṇa) through the Noble Path (Ariyamagga). This Bodhisatta Vipassī also, having fulfilled the perfections, performed everything in the aforementioned sequence, and in the final watch, arose from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, directed his mind to the five aggregates, and began the insight into arising and passing away as described. To show that contemplation of arising and passing away, this word beginning with "Aparena samayena" was spoken.

In that text, "This is form" (iti rūpaṃ) means: this is form, this much is form, there is no form beyond this; it refers to the comprehensive grasping of form without remainder by way of its nature of being deformed (ruppana), the distinction between the great primary elements (mahābhūta) and derived form (upādā-rūpa), and by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. By the words "This is the origin of form" (iti rūpassa samudayo), it means the seeing of the cause of form thus grasped. In that text, "thus" (iti) means that arising occurs in this manner. The detail of it is: "With the arising of ignorance, form arises; with the arising of craving, form arises; with the arising of kamma, form arises; with the arising of nutriment, form arises." One who sees the characteristic of birth also sees the arising of the aggregate of form—thus it should be understood. Regarding cessation: "With the cessation of ignorance, form ceases... (pe) ... One who sees the characteristic of change also sees the cessation of the aggregate of form." This is its detail.

In the passages beginning with "This is feeling" (iti vedanā), it likewise means: this is feeling, this much is feeling, there is no feeling beyond this; this is perception; these are mental formations; this is consciousness, this much is consciousness, there is no consciousness beyond this. It refers to the comprehensive grasping of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness without remainder by way of their nature of experiencing, perceiving, constructing, and cognizing, as well as the distinctions of feeling such as pleasure, the distinctions of perception such as perception of forms, the distinctions of formations such as contact, and the distinctions of consciousness such as eye-consciousness. By the words "This is the origin of feeling," etc., it means the seeing of the cause of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness thus grasped. There also, "thus" (iti) means that arising occurs in this manner. Their detail should be understood in the same way as stated for form: "With the arising of ignorance, feeling arises." However, there is this distinction: for the three mental aggregates, instead of saying "with the arising of nutriment," one should say "with the arising of contact" (phassa). For the aggregate of consciousness, one should say "with the arising of mind-and-matter" (nāmarūpa). The terms for cessation should also be joined by way of that contact and mind-and-matter. This is the summary found in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī. The full detail in all its aspects is...
54:
In the phrase "with the arising of mind-and-matter" (nāmarūpasamudayā), the term for cessation (atthaṅgama) should also be joined by way of that same mind-and-matter. This is the summary here; the full detail of the investigation of arising and passing away (udayabbaya-vinicchaya) in all its aspects has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. For that Bodhisatta Vipassī, dwelling thus contemplating arising and passing away in the five aggregates of clinging by way of the fifty characteristics, as the insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) was gradually developed, his mind was liberated without clinging to or grasping even a trace of the defilements known as taints (āsavas), which were being ceased by the cessation of non-arising. This mind is said to be "being liberated" at the moment of the Path (magga-khaṇa) and "liberated" at the moment of the Fruit (phala-khaṇa). Or, at the moment of the Path, it is both "liberated" and "being liberated," while at the moment of the Fruit, it is simply "liberated."

By this much, the Great Man (Mahāpurisa) was well-liberated from all bonds. With a mind-continuity as fully blossomed as a paduma lotus touched by the sun's rays, having attained the four path knowledges, the four fruit knowledges, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), the knowledge of the four modes of birth (yoni), the knowledge of the five destinations (gati), the six uncommon knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), and all the qualities of a Buddha, and with his aspiration fulfilled, while still sitting on the Throne of Enlightenment, he reflected:

"Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Sorrowful is birth again and again.
O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again. All your rafters (defilements) are broken, the ridge-pole (ignorance) is shattered. My mind has reached the unconditioned (Nibbāna); it has attained the destruction of cravings."

And also:

"Just as the destination of a fire, struck by a smith's iron hammer, glowing and then gradually going out, is not known;
Even so, there is no destination to be pointed out for those who are perfectly liberated, who have crossed the flood of the bond of sensual desires, and have reached the unshakable bliss (Nibbāna)."

Reflecting thus, he shone like the sun in autumn or like the full moon.

## The Explanation of the Second Recitation Section is finished.
55:
## Commentary on the Request of Brahmā

In the third recital section (bhāṇavāra), the thought "What if I were to teach the Dhamma?" means "If I were to teach the Dhamma (it would be good)." When did this thought arise? It arose in the eighth week (sattāha) after he had attained Buddhahood. It is said that after becoming the Buddha, he sat for seven days on the Throne of Enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka); for seven days he stood gazing at the Throne of Enlightenment; for seven days he walked on the Jeweled Walk (ratanacaṅkama); for seven days he sat in the Jeweled House (ratanaghara) contemplating the Dhamma; for seven days he sat at the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree; for seven days he sat at the foot of the Mucalinda tree; and for seven days he sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree. Rising from the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, in the eighth week, he returned to the Ajapāla Banyan tree, and as soon as he sat down, this thought arose—a thought that is the habitual practice of all Buddhas—and immediately following it, the thought beginning with "This Dhamma I have realized..." arose.

In that context, "adhigato" means penetrated or realized. "Dhammo" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths. The word "gambhīro" (deep) is a term that negates shallowness. "Duddaso" (hard to see) means that because it is deep, it is difficult to see; it must be seen with the eye of wisdom through great effort, and cannot be seen easily. Because it is hard to see, it is "duranubodho" (hard to understand), meaning it must be penetrated with difficulty and cannot be understood easily. "Santo" means peaceful, stilled from all types of heat (defilements). "Paṇīto" (sublime) means that which does not cause satiety (atappako). These two terms (santo and paṇīto) are spoken solely with reference to the supramundane (lokuttara) Dhamma. "Atakkāvacaro" means it is not within the sphere of reasoning or logic, but can only be entered into by wisdom. "Nipuṇo" means subtle. "Paṇḍitavedanīyo" means to be experienced only by the wise who have practiced the right path.

"Ālayarāmā" means that beings are attached to the five cords of sensual pleasure; therefore, those sensual pleasures are called "ālaya" (attachments). The one hundred and eight diversifications of craving (taṇhāvicarita) are also called "ālaya." Because they delight in these attachments, they are called "ālayarāma." Because they take pleasure in attachments, they are called "ālayarata." Because they greatly rejoice in attachments, they are called "ālayasammuditā." Just as a king who enters a well-prepared garden filled with trees laden with flowers and fruits delights in those various excellences, becomes joyful and gladdened, does not feel weary, and does not wish to leave in the evening; in the same way, beings delight in these attachments to sensual objects (vatthukāma-ālaya) and attachments to craving (taṇhā-ālaya), and they live in the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) with joy and without weariness. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show them the two kinds of attachments as if they were garden grounds, spoke the words beginning with "ālayarāmā."

"Yadidaṃ" is a particle; with reference to its place, it should be understood as "yaṃ idaṃ" (which is this), and with reference to Dependent Origination, it should be understood as "yo ayaṃ" (which is this). "Idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo" means: the causes of these effects (such as formations, etc.) are called "idappaccaya" (specific conditions); the state of these specific conditions is "idappaccayatā"; and that idappaccayatā, which is the arising of effects in dependence on causes, is called "idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo."
56:
This term (idappaccayatā-paṭiccasamuppādo) is a designation for ignorance (avijjā) and other causes of effects such as formations (saṅkhāra). The entire passage beginning with "sabbasaṅkhārasamatho" refers solely to Nibbāna. For it is in dependence on Nibbāna that all the fluctuations of formations are stilled and fully calmed; therefore, it is called "sabbasaṅkhārasamatho" (the stilling of all formations). And because it is in dependence on Nibbāna that all five kinds of acquisitions (upadhi), such as the acquisitions of the aggregates (khandhūpadhi), are relinquished, all cravings are exhausted, all lust of defilements fades away, and all suffering ceases, it is therefore called "sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho" (the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation). That craving is called "vāna" because it weaves or binds together one existence with another, or kamma with its fruit. Because of the departure from that craving called vāna, it is called "Nibbāna."

"It would be a weariness to me" means that teaching the Dhamma to those who do not understand would be a weariness to my body and a distress to my body. For the Buddhas, only physical weariness and distress can occur; in their minds, however, both of these are absent.

In the word "apissu," the syllable "api" is a particle used in the sense of conjunction (sampiṇḍana). It indicates: "Not only did this thought occur, but these verses also appeared in my knowledge." In the words beginning with "Vipassiṃ," it means "of the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, Vipassī." "Anacchariyā" means repeatedly wonderful or extraordinary. "Paṭibhaṃsu" means they became the objects of the intuitive knowledge (paṭibhāna-ñāṇa) and reached the state of being contemplated.

"Kicchena" means obtained with difficulty or hardship; it does not mean obtained through the painful practice (dukkhā paṭipadā). This is because all four paths of the Buddhas are only the pleasant practice (sukhā paṭipadā). However, this was said with reference to the practice for the attainment (āgamanīya-paṭipadā) of Buddhahood, during the time of fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) while still possessed of lust, hate, and delusion. At that time, he gave difficult gifts such as cutting off his adorned head, drawing blood from his throat, plucking out his well-anointed eyes, and giving away his son who was the light of his lineage and his wife who served him devotedly. He also endured sufferings such as the cutting and hacking of his limbs in births like that of Khantivādī the Hermit. It is with reference to this that it is said "obtained with difficulty."

In the word "halaṃ," the letter "ha" is merely a particle, and the meaning is "alaṃ" (enough/stop). "Pakaasituṃ" means to teach. Thus, it means: "It is enough; I am not able to teach this Dhamma obtained with such difficulty; what benefit would there be in teaching it?" "Rāgadosaparetehi" means by beings afflicted by lust and hate, or by beings followed by lust and hate.

"Paṭisotagāmiṃ" refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths which goes against the stream of views such as permanence (nicca), etc., and proceeds by way of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), non-self (anattā), and foulness (asubha). "Rāgarattā" refers to beings who are dyed with the lust for sensual pleasures (kāmarāga), the lust for existence (bhavarāga), and the lust for views (diṭṭhirāga). "Na dakkhanti" means they will not be able to see it through its true nature as impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul...
57:
(Those beings) will not see; who will be able to make those who do not see perceive [the truth] in this way (as impermanent, etc.)? 'Obscured by a mass of darkness' means covered by a mass of ignorance.
