'Appossukkatāya' means a state of being without effort, a lack of desire to teach. But why did the Buddha's mind incline in this way (not wanting to teach)? Did this Buddha not make a vow, fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) and attaining omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), saying:
'Having been liberated, I shall liberate others; having crossed over, I shall make others cross over' and
'What is the use of realizing the Dhamma here in an unknown form? Only after reaching omniscience shall I save the world together with the devas'?
Thus he made the aspiration, fulfilled the perfections, and attained omniscience, did he not?

It is true that he made such a vow; however, his mind inclined this way only due to the power of reflection. After attaining omniscience, as he reflected on the thickness of beings' defilements and the depth of the Dhamma, the thickness of beings' defilements and the depth of the Dhamma became clear to him in every aspect. Then, as he thought, 'These beings are full of defilements, extremely defiled, stained by lust, corrupted by hatred, and blinded by delusion—like a gourd full of sour gruel, like a pot filled with buttermilk, like a rag soaked in fat and oil, or like hands smeared with collyrium—how could they possibly penetrate [the Dhamma]?' his mind inclined this way due to the power of reflecting on the thickness of defilements.

'And this Dhamma is deep like the mass of water that supports the earth, hard to see like a mustard seed hidden by a mountain, and hard to understand like hitting the tip of a hair with the tip of another hair that has been split a hundred times. While I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift I had not given, no virtue (sīla) I had not guarded, and no perfection (pāramī) I had not fulfilled. Even as I, such as I am, was crushing the army of Māra, the earth did not tremble; it did not tremble as I recollected past lives in the first watch, nor as I purified the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) in the middle watch. But in the last watch, as I penetrated Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. How then will worldly people penetrate this Dhamma, which was penetrated with such difficulty even by one with sharp wisdom like me?' Thus it should be understood that his mind inclined this way also due to the power of reflecting on the depth of the Dhamma.
58:
Furthermore, the Buddha's mind inclined in this way (as if not wanting to teach) because he desired to teach only when requested by a Brahmā. Indeed, the Blessed One knew: 'If my mind inclines toward inaction, Mahābrahmā will request me to teach the Dhamma. These beings hold the Brahmā in high regard; they will listen attentively, thinking, "The Teacher was initially unwilling to teach the Dhamma, but then Mahābrahmā requested him and made him teach. Oh, how peaceful is the Dhamma! Oh, how sublime is the Dhamma!"' It should be understood that his mind inclined toward inaction because of this reason, and not because he truly did not want to teach the Dhamma.

In the word 'aññatarassa' (a certain), although it says 'a certain [one],' it should be understood as the Great Brahmā who is the chief in this universe. That Brahmā uttered the words 'The world is perishing, alas!' with such a sound that the Brahmās of the ten-thousandfold world system heard it and assembled. 'Yatra hi nāma' means 'in which world.' 'Purato pāturahosi' means he appeared together with those ten thousand Brahmās. 'Apparajakkhajātika' refers to those who have little dust of lust, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom. 'Assavanatā' means due to not hearing the Dhamma. By the word 'bhavissanti' (there will be), he shows that there will be not just one or two, but many hundreds of thousands of people who will understand the Dhamma—those who have performed meritorious deeds through the ten bases of meritorious action under previous Buddhas, whose faculties are mature, and who, like lotus flowers awaiting the touch of the sun's rays, are longing for the Dhamma teaching and are capable of entering the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya) at the end of a single verse.

'Ajjhesana' means requesting in this way three times. 'Buddha-cakkhu' (the Buddha-eye) consists of the knowledge of the high and low faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of their latent tendencies (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa). These two knowledges are called the 'Buddha-eye'; omniscience is called the 'All-seeing eye' (samanta-cakkhu); and the three lower path knowledges are called the 'Dhamma-eye' (dhamma-cakkhu). In the terms 'apparajakkha' and so on, those who have little dust of lust, etc., in their eye of wisdom, as previously explained, are called 'apparajakkha' (those with little dust). Those who have much dust are 'mahārajakkha.' Those whose faculties such as faith are sharp are 'tikkhindriya.' Those whose faculties are weak are 'mudindriya.' Those whose dispositions such as faith are good are 'svākāra.' Those who can easily be made to understand because they can well-note the explained meaning are 'suviññāpaya.' Those who see danger in the next world and in faults are called 'paralokavajjabhayadassāvī'.
59:
In this matter, the Pali text states: "A person with faith has little dust of defilement; a person without faith has much dust of defilement. ... An energetic person has little dust of defilement; a lazy person has much dust of defilement. A person with established mindfulness has little dust of defilement; a person with muddled mindfulness has much dust of defilement. A person with a concentrated mind has little dust of defilement; a person with an unconcentrated mind has much dust of defilement. A person with wisdom has little dust of defilement; a person with little wisdom has much dust of defilement. Likewise, a person with faith has sharp faculties ... a person with wisdom is one who sees danger in the next world and in faults; a person with little wisdom is one who does not see danger in the next world and in faults."

The world (loka) means: the world of aggregates (khandhaloka), the world of elements (dhātuloka), the world of bases (āyatanaloka), the world of prosperous existence (sampattibhavaloka - sugati), the world of miserable existence (vipattibhavaloka - dugati), the world of the cause of prosperous existence (sampattisambhavaloka - wholesome kamma that causes sugati), and the world of the cause of miserable existence (vipattisambhavaloka - unwholesome kamma that causes dugati).

One world: All beings subsist on nutriment.
Two worlds: Name and form.
Three worlds: The three feelings.
Four worlds: The four nutriments.
Five worlds: The five aggregates of clinging.
Six worlds: The six internal bases.
Seven worlds: The seven stations of consciousness.
Eight worlds: The eight worldly conditions.
Nine worlds: The nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).
Ten worlds: The ten bases.
Twelve worlds: The twelve bases.
Eighteen worlds: The eighteen elements.

Fault (vajja) means: all defilements, all misconduct, all volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and all kamma that leads to rebirth. Thus, in this world and in this fault, the perception of intense danger (bhayasaññā) appears clearly, just as it does for an executioner with a raised sword. Through these fifty modes, He knows, sees, understands, and penetrates these five faculties. This is the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa).

'Uppalinī' refers to a pond of blue, red, or white lotuses. The same method applies to other terms. 'Antonimuggaposīnī' refers to lotuses that grow while remaining submerged in the water. 'Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitānī' refers to lotuses that stand having risen above the water. Among them, those that stand having risen above the water, awaiting contact with the sun's rays, will bloom today. Those that stand level with the water will bloom tomorrow. Those that are still within the water and growing will bloom on the third day. There are also other lotuses, such as those born in the lake, that cannot rise above the water and will only become food for fish and turtles; these are not included in the Pali text but are mentioned in the Commentary for clarification. Just like these four types of lotuses, there are four types of persons: the ugghaṭitaññū, the vipañcitaññū, the neyya, and the padaparama. Among those four...
60:
A person who attains the realization of the Dhamma (the Four Noble Truths) at the very time a brief instruction is uttered is called an 'ugghaṭitaññū' person. A person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs when the meaning of a briefly stated Pali text is analyzed in detail is called a 'vipañcitaññū' person. A person for whom the realization of the Dhamma occurs gradually through learning the Pali text, questioning and discussing the meaning, wise attention, and associating with, following, and attending to good friends is called a 'neyya' person. A person for whom the realization of the Dhamma does not occur in that very life, even though they hear much of the Dhamma, recite it, learn it, memorize it, or teach it, is called a 'padaparama' person (Pug. 148, 149, 150, 151).

Among those four types of persons, when the Blessed One surveyed the ten-thousandfold world system, which is like a lotus pond, He saw: 'The ugghaṭitaññū persons are like the lotuses that will bloom today; the vipañcitaññū persons are like the lotuses that will bloom tomorrow; the neyya persons are like the lotuses that will bloom on the third day; and the padaparama persons are like the lotuses that are food for fish and turtles.' Even as He saw them, He saw them in every aspect: 'This many beings have the eye of wisdom with little dust of defilement; this many beings have the eye of wisdom with much dust of defilement. Among them, this many are ugghaṭitaññū persons.' Among those four types of persons, the Buddha's teaching of the Dhamma fulfills the benefit for the first three types in this very life; for the padaparama persons, however, it serves as an impression (vāsanā) for the future.

Then, the Blessed One, having known the Dhamma teaching that brings benefit to these four types of persons and having generated the desire to teach, again divided all beings in all three realms of existence into two groups: the capable (bhabba) and the incapable (abhabba). With reference to this division, it was said: 'Those beings who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma (kammāvaraṇa), possessed of the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa), possessed of the obstruction of defilement (kilesāvaraṇa), who lack faith, lack wholesome desire, and lack wisdom—these beings are incapable of entering the right path (the Path) which is of an unerring nature among wholesome states; these are called incapable (abhabba) persons. Which beings are capable? Those beings who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma... these are called capable (bhabba) persons' (Vibh. 827; Paṭis. I. 114).

Among them, setting aside all incapable persons and selecting only the capable persons with His knowledge, He divided them into six groups: 'This many are of a lustful temperament (rāgacarita); this many are of temperaments of hatred, delusion, discursive thought, faith, and intelligence.' Having done so, He thought, 'I shall teach the Dhamma.'
61:
(The Blessed One) reflected thus. The Brahmā, knowing his intention to teach the Dhamma, became joyful and addressed the Blessed One with verses. With reference to this joyful address upon knowing the intention to teach, it was said: "Then, O monks, the Great Brahmā..." and so forth.

In that text, "ajjhabhāsi" means he addressed him persistently; he addressed him by taking up and referring to a specific matter.

"Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito" means as if standing on the summit of a solid rocky mountain. Indeed, for one standing on such a summit, there is no need for stretching or craning the neck to look down. "Tathūpamaṃ" refers to the palace of Dhamma which is like that solid rocky mountain, having a rocky mountain as its metaphor. The summary meaning here is: Just as a man with vision, standing on the summit of a rocky mountain, would see the people all around, even so, O Sumedha (the Blessed One), who are wise and capable of seeing all around with the knowledge of omniscience, please ascend the palace made of Dhamma, made of wisdom, and being yourself free from sorrow, look upon the people who are immersed in sorrow and oppressed by birth and old age.

The detailed meaning here is: Suppose people were to clear a large field around the foot of a mountain, build small huts on the ridges of those fields, and light fires at night. There would be darkness endowed with four factors. Then, for a man with vision standing on the summit of that mountain and looking down at the ground, the fields, the ridges, the huts, and the people sleeping in those huts would not be visible; only the flames of the fires in the huts would be seen. Similarly, for the Tathāgata who has ascended the palace of Dhamma and looks upon the multitude of beings, those beings who have not performed meritorious deeds do not come into the range of the Buddha-eye (Buddha-cakkhu), even if they are staying in the same monastery near his right knee; they are like arrows shot in the dark of night. However, those veneyya persons (those ready for liberation) who have performed meritorious deeds come into the range of the Buddha-eye even if they are far away from the Blessed One. They appear clearly like a flame or like the Himālaya mountains. This has also been said:

"The virtuous shine from afar, like the Himālaya mountains;
The non-virtuous are not seen here, like arrows shot at night." (Dhp. 304)

"Uṭṭhehi" (Arise): He says this requesting the Blessed One to wander for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. In the terms such as "Vīra", the Blessed One is called "Vīra" (Hero) because of his possession of energy (vīriya). Because he has conquered the Māra as a deity, the Māra as death, and the Māra of defilements...
62:
...because he has conquered the Māra as a deity (devaputta-māra), the Māra as death (maccu-māra), and the Māra of defilements (kilesa-māra), he is called "Vijitasaṅgāmo" (Conqueror of the Battle). He is called "Satthavāho" (Caravan Leader) because he is capable of leading veneyya beings from the wilderness of birth and so forth to reach Nibbāna. He is called "Aṇanno" (Debtless) because he is free from the debt of sensual desire.

"Apārutā" means they are opened. "Amatassa dvārā" (The doors to the Deathless) refers to the Noble Path (Ariya-magga). Indeed, that Noble Path is like a door to Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless. He shows that "I have opened that door and set it so." "Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ" means let all beings release (or place) their faith. In the final two phrases, the meaning is: "I did not teach this profound and supreme Dhamma, though I have mastered it and can explain it well, because I was mindful of the weariness of body and speech. But now, let all people bring the vessel of faith; I shall fulfill their aspirations."

## Explanation of the Pair of Chief Disciples

"Bodhirukkhamūle" means he disappeared at the Ajapāla Banyan tree, not far from the Bodhi tree. "Kheme migadāye" refers to the forest named Isipatana. At the time when the Buddha Vipassī was enlightened, it was a park named Khema. It is called "Migadāya" (Deer Park) because it was given as a sanctuary for deer. With reference to that, it was said: "In the Khema Deer Park." Just as the Blessed One Vipassī, when going to give the first sermon, traveled through the sky and descended right there, so too other Buddhas, when going to give the first sermon, travel through the sky and descend at that very spot. However, our Blessed One, seeing the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of the Ājīvaka named Upaka, thought: "Upaka is traveling on this road; he will see me, converse with me, and then go. Later, becoming weary [of the world], he will come back and realize Arahantship." Knowing this, he traveled the journey of 18 yojanas on foot. "He addressed the park-keeper" means that upon seeing him, looking at him again and again, the park-keeper approached and said, "Venerable sir, our master has arrived," and then the Buddha addressed him.

75-6. "Anupubbī-kathā" (Gradual Discourse) means he taught the discourse in sequence: the talk on giving (dāna), followed by the talk on virtue (sīla), followed by the talk on heaven (sagga), and followed by the talk on the path (magga). Among those, "Dānakathā" means this thing called giving is the source of happiness, the root of prosperity, and the basis for the enjoyment of wealth. It is the protection, the shelter, the refuge, and the final resort for one who has fallen into distress. In this world and the world beyond, there is no support, basis, object, protection, shelter, refuge, or final resort equal to giving. In the sense of being a support, it is like a jeweled lion-throne; in the sense of being a basis, it is like the great earth.
63:
(Generosity) is like a rope for clinging, in the sense of being something to hold onto. This generosity is like a boat in the sense of crossing over suffering; it is like a brave warrior on the battlefield in the sense of providing relief; it is like a well-fortified city in the sense of preventing danger; it is like a lotus in the sense of being unstained by the impurities of stinginess and so forth; it is like fire in the sense of burning away those impurities; it is like a venomous cobra in the sense of being difficult to approach; it is like a lion king in the sense of being fearless; it is like an elephant in the sense of being powerful; it is like a white bull in the sense of being considered highly auspicious; and it is like the Valāhaka horse king in the sense of reaching the land of safety. Generosity can grant the prosperity of Sakka, the prosperity of Māra, the prosperity of Brahmā, the prosperity of a Universal Monarch, the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection, the knowledge of a Paccekabodhi, and the knowledge of Supreme Enlightenment—such talk connected with the virtues of generosity (is called Dānakathā).

Because one who gives is able to undertake virtue, He taught the discourse on virtue (Sīlakathā) immediately after the discourse on generosity. Regarding the discourse on virtue: this virtue is a support, a foundation, an object to hold onto, a protection, a shelter, a destination, and a refuge. For the prosperity of this world and the world beyond, there is no support, foundation, object, protection, shelter, destination, or refuge equal to virtue. There is no ornament like virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, and no fragrance like the fragrance of virtue. The world together with the devas, when beholding one adorned with the ornament of virtue, wearing the flower of virtue, and anointed with the fragrance of virtue, can never look enough—such talk connected with the virtues of virtue (is called Sīlakathā).

To show that this heaven can be obtained by relying on this virtue, He taught the discourse on heaven (Saggakathā) immediately after the discourse on virtue. Regarding the discourse on heaven: this heaven is desirable, lovely, and pleasant; here there is constant play and enjoyment, and prosperity is always obtained. The Cātumahārājikā devas enjoy divine happiness and divine prosperity for nine million years; the Tāvatimsā devas (enjoy it) for thirty-six million years—such is the talk connected with the merits of heaven. Even the mouth of the Buddhas is not sufficient to describe the prosperity of heaven. Indeed, it was said: "Monks, I could speak about heaven in many ways."

After enticing them with the talk on heaven, just like decorating an elephant and then cutting off its trunk, He showed that "this heaven is also impermanent and unstable; one should not have desire or lust for it." In this way, He spoke of the... of sensual pleasures, saying: "Sensual pleasures provide little satisfaction, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in them is even greater."
64:
The Blessed One taught the danger (ādīnava), the baseness (okāra), and the defilement (saṅkilesa) of sensual pleasures. Among those terms, 'danger' means fault. 'Baseness' means the state of being low or inferior. 'Defilement' means the state of beings being defiled in saṃsāra by those defilements. As it was said: "Alas, friends, beings are defiled!" Having thus threatened them with the danger of sensual pleasures, He revealed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma), meaning He revealed the virtues of monkhood. The remaining words are as explained in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta Commentary and are clear in meaning.

Regarding the word "they received" (alatthuṃ): How did they receive it? They received it through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, Monk) ordination. It is said that the Blessed One, seeing their supporting conditions (upanissaya) for receiving the miraculous bowl and robes, and seeing their past deeds such as offering robes in many previous lives, said, "Come, monks," and so forth. At that very moment, they appeared with shaven heads, wearing saffron-dyed robes, and equipped with the eight monastic requisites as if they were elders of a hundred years, and they sat down paying homage to the Blessed One.

In the words "He fully showed" (sandassesi) and so forth: He showed the benefit of this world and the benefit of the world beyond. In showing the benefit of this world, He showed impermanence, suffering, and non-self; He showed the aggregates, the elements, the sense bases, and dependent origination. In showing the arising (udaya) of the aggregate of form, He showed five characteristics; likewise for the aggregate of feeling and so forth. Similarly, in showing the passing away (vaya), He showed fifty characteristics by way of arising and passing away. In showing the benefit of the world beyond, He showed hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, and the host of asuras; He showed the prosperity of the six heavens and the nine Brahma worlds, which are the results of the three types of wholesome actions.

"He urged them to undertake" (samādapesi) means He made them take up the beautiful Dhamma, such as the fourfold purification virtue, the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and the ten bases of talk (kathāvatthu).

"He inspired them" (samuttejesi) means He thoroughly sharpened their resolve and greatly encouraged them. He spoke by making them feel as if they had attained the benefits of this world and the world beyond after repeatedly causing them to feel trepidation. When the Blessed One spoke, repeatedly causing trepidation regarding the benefits of this world—consisting of the thirty-two types of torture and the twenty-five great fears—one becomes agitated like a person whose hands are bound behind his back, who is beaten with a hundred blows at the crossroads, and who is led out through the south gate; or like one whose head is placed on the executioner's block; or like one impaled on a stake; or like one being trampled by a mad elephant.
65:
When he speaks of the benefits of the next world, it is as if one were being born in hell and the like, or as if one were experiencing the prosperity of the heavenly realm.

'Sampahaṃsesi' means he urged them by means of the virtues they had attained, or he taught by making it a matter of great benefit.

'The danger of formations' (saṅkhārānaṃ ādīnavaṃ) means that previously, he taught the danger of sensual pleasures for the purpose of attaining the path of stream-entry. But here, for the purpose of attaining the higher paths, he showed the danger and the wretchedness of formations, and the exhaustion caused by them, in this way: "Monks, formations are impermanent, unstable, and provide no relief. Monks, it is enough to become weary of all formations, enough to become dispassionate toward them, enough to be liberated from them." Just as in that case he showed the benefit of renunciation (nekkhamma) for the sake of attaining the first path, so here, for the sake of attaining the higher paths, he showed the benefit of Nibbāna in this way: "Monks, this Nibbāna is peaceful, sublime, a shelter, and a refuge."

## Description of the Going Forth of the Great Multitude (Mahājanakāyapabbajjāvaṇṇanā)

'Mahājanakāya' (great multitude) refers to the group of people who were the attendants of those two princes.

When they said, "We go to the Blessed One and the Dhamma as our refuge," they took only the two-word refuge (dvevācika-saraṇagamana) because the Saṅgha was not yet complete.

'Alatthuṃ' (they received) means they received it only through the 'Come, bhikkhu' (ehibhikkhu) ordination, just as mentioned before. This same method applies to the subsequent instances of going forth.

## Description of the Permission for Wandering (Cārikāanujānanavaṇṇanā)

When did the thought 'Parivitakko udapādi' (a reflection arose) occur? It occurred seven years, seven months, and seven days after the attainment of Enlightenment. The Blessed One was staying there while providing support to his father. The Great King also thought: "My eldest son went forth and became a Buddha; my second son went forth and became a Chief Disciple; the son of the chaplain became the second Chief Disciple; and all these remaining monks used to follow my son even when they were laypeople. All these people..."
66:
"Even now, these monks are my responsibility alone. I myself will attend to them with the four requisites; I will not give others the opportunity to attend to them." Thinking thus, he had a fence of catechu wood built on both sides of the road from the gate of the monastery to the gate of the King's palace in Rājagaha. He had it covered with mats, then draped with cloth inside, and also covered above with cloth. He had various flower-garland canopies made, as large as palm trunks, beautifully decorated with golden stars and well-suspended. On the ground below, he had ornate rugs spread. Inside, on both sides, he had water-pots filled with water and decorated with floral patterns placed. To make the entire path fragrant, he had flowers placed between perfumes and perfumes placed between flowers in jars. Then he had the time for the meal announced to the Blessed One.

Surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, the Blessed One entered the city of Rājagaha within the curtained path, and after finishing the meal, returned to the monastery. No one else had the opportunity even to see him, let alone to offer alms, to pay homage, or to hear the Dhamma. The citizens thought: "It has now been seven years and over seven months since the Teacher appeared in the world, yet we do not even get the chance to see him, much less to offer alms, pay homage, or hear the Dhamma. The King, cherishing them as 'My Buddha, my Dhamma, my Saṅgha,' attends to them himself. When a Buddha appears, he appears for the benefit and welfare of the world including the devas. Surely, hell is not hot only for the King, nor is it as cool as a blue lotus pond for others. Therefore, let us speak to the King. If he gives us the opportunity to see the Teacher, that is good. If he does not, we will even fight with the King, take the Saṅgha, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms. However, it is not possible to do this with only the citizens; let us also take a leading man as an ally."

Those people approached the General, informed him of the matter, and asked, "Lord, will you be on our side or on the King's side?" The General said, "I will be on your side, but the first day must be given to me." They agreed. The General approached the King and said, "Great King, the citizens are angry with you." When asked, "Friend, why are they angry?", he replied, "They say that only you are attending to the Teacher and they do not get the chance. They are angry because of this. Even now, if they get the chance, they will not be angry; but if they do not, they wish to fight with you, Great King." The King said, "Friend, I will fight; I cannot give up the Saṅgha of monks." The General replied, "Great King, the citizens who are your servants say they will fight with you. On whom will you rely to fight?" The King said, "Are you not the General?" He replied, "Great King, I cannot fight without the citizens."
67:
“Great King, I am not able to engage in battle (against the citizens),” the General (Senāpati) replied. Then the King, realizing that “The citizens are powerful, and even the General is on their side,” said, “Let me have the opportunity to offer alms to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha for another seven years and seven months.” The citizens did not accept this. The King reduced his request to “six years, five, four, three, two, and one year.” Even with these reductions, the citizens did not accept. He then requested for another seven days. The citizens, thinking, “It is not proper to be so extremely harsh with the King now,” granted him permission.

The King distributed the alms-offerings, which had been prepared for seven years and seven months, within only seven days. For six days, he gave alms without letting certain people see. On the seventh day, he summoned the citizens and asked, “Friends, will you be able to give such an offering?” They replied, “Is it not because of us that this alms-offering became possible for the Great King?” and said, “We shall be able to do so.” The King, wiping his tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Blessed One and said, “Venerable Sir, I intended to serve six million eight hundred thousand monks with the four requisites for the rest of my life without giving a turn to anyone else. Now, the citizens do not permit me; they are angry, saying, ‘We do not get the chance to give alms.’ Blessed One, from tomorrow onwards, please show favor to those citizens.”

Furthermore, on the second day, the General prepared a great alms-offering and stationed men all around, saying, “Guard the area so that today no one else can give even a single portion of alms-food.” On that day, the Treasurer’s wife, weeping, said to her daughter, “Dear daughter, if your father were still alive, today I would have been the first to offer alms-food to the Buddha (Dasabala).” The daughter said to her mother, “Mother, do not worry; I will arrange it so that the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, will partake of our alms-food first.”

Then, she filled a golden bowl worth one hundred thousand with pure milk-rice (pāyāsa) without any water, prepared it with ghee, honey, sugar, and so on, and covered it with another golden bowl. She surrounded that bowl with jasmine (sumana) garlands, making it look like a ball of flowers. When the Blessed One was about to enter the village, she carried it herself and came out of the city surrounded by a group of servants. Along the way, the General’s attendants said, “Mother, do not go this way.” Those with great merit possess pleasant speech (manāpa-kathā), and it is not possible to reject the words of such people even when they speak repeatedly. The Treasurer’s daughter asked, “Uncles and elder uncles, why do you not allow me to go?” They replied, “The General has stationed us here, saying, ‘Do not allow anyone else to give food (khādanīya-bhojanīya).’” She asked, “What then, do you see food in my hands?” They replied, “(We see) a ball of flowers.”
68:
“We see it,” they replied. She asked, “Does your General not even allow the offering of a ball of flowers?” They answered, “Mother, he allows it.” “If so, move aside, move aside,” she said. Approaching the Blessed One, she said, “Blessed One, please accept this ball of flowers.” The Blessed One looked at one of the General’s attendants and had him accept the ball of flowers. The Treasurer’s daughter paid homage to the Blessed One and made an aspiration: “Blessed One, as long as I am reborn in various existences, may I never live a life of hardship and distress. Like this jasmine flower, may I be loved and cherished by others wherever I am born, and may my name be Sumana.” The Teacher said, “May you be happy.” She paid homage, circumambulated Him, and departed.

The Blessed One went to the General’s house and sat on the prepared seat. When the General approached with rice-gruel (yāgu), the Teacher covered His bowl. “Venerable Sir, the Bhikkhu-saṅgha is seated in full,” he said. “Lay disciple, we have received one portion of alms-food on the way,” the Teacher replied. When the General removed the flowers, he saw the alms-food. The young attendant said, “Master, a young woman deceived me by saying it was flowers.” That milk-rice was sufficient for all the monks, headed by the Buddha. The General also gave his own offerings. After the Teacher had finished His meal and delivered a blessing (maṅgala), He departed. The General asked, “Who was it that gave that alms-food?” “Master, it was the Treasurer’s daughter,” they replied. Thinking, “That woman is wise; for a man with such a woman living in his house, the attainment of heavenly bliss is not difficult,” he brought the Treasurer’s daughter and placed her in the position of the chief wife.

On the following day, the citizens gave alms; on the day after that, the King gave alms. In this way, they began to give alms on alternate days. The King stationed spies and gave offerings that were superior to those given by the citizens. The citizens did the same, giving offerings superior to those given by the King. The palace dancers said to the young novices (sāmaṇeras), “Dear ones, please accept this; this alms-food is not made by the hands of wealthy householders who have wiped their bodies and clothes or washed the saliva and mucus of children; it is prepared purely and excellently.” On the next day, the citizens, while giving alms, said, “Dear ones, please accept this; this alms-food is not made from rice, milk, curd, or ghee collected from towns and villages; it is not made from things brought by oppressing the knees, heads, or backs of others; it is prepared only with the ghee and milk of our own cattle.” In this way, when seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed, this thought arose in the Blessed One. Therefore, it is said: “Seven years, seven months, and seven days after the Enlightenment, (this thought) arose.”
69:
"A certain Great Brahmā" refers to the very Brahmā who requested the teaching of the Dhamma. "Eighty-four thousand dwellings" means eighty-four thousand monasteries. All of these were great monasteries capable of accommodating twelve thousand monks, similar to Abhayagiri, Cetiyapabbata, Cittala-pabbata, and Mahāvihāra.

"Patience is the highest austerity (tapo)" means the patience known as endurance (adhivāsana-khanti) is the supreme practice. "Titikkhā" is merely a synonym for patience (khanti). The meaning is that endurance, which is called patience, is the noble practice. "Nibbāna is supreme" means the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme in every way. "One who harms others is not a monk" means that one who, due to a lack of endurance, oppresses, harms, or hurts others is not truly a monk. The fourth line of the verse is a synonym for the third. The synonym for the phrase "na hi pabbajito" is "na samaṇo hoti" (he is not an ascetic). The synonym for the term "parūpaghātī" is "paraṃ viheṭhayanto" (one who harms others). Alternatively, "parūpaghātī" means one who destroys virtue (sīla). Virtue is called "para" (the other/the highest) because of its noble sense. The meaning is that if a monk harms any living being and thus destroys his own virtue, he is not truly a monk. Or, one who harms others due to the absence of endurance, even intentionally taking the life of a gnat or mosquito, is not a monk. Why? Because he has not yet cast out the stain of defilements. "Because he has cast out his own stains, he is called a pabbajita (monk)"—this is the characteristic of a monk. One who does not kill but still harms others with sticks, spears, and so on, is not a samaṇa (ascetic) because he harms others. Why? Because the stain of cruelty has not been stilled. "Because of the stilling of evils, one is called a samaṇa"—this is the characteristic of a samaṇa.

In the second verse, "sabbapāpassa" means of all unwholesome deeds. "Akaraṇaṃ" means not producing them. "Kusalassa" means of the wholesome states belonging to the four planes. "Upasampadā" means attainment. "Sacittapariyodapanaṃ" means purifying one's own mind, which is achieved through the Fruition of Arahantship. Thus, by abandoning all evil through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), fulfilling the wholesome through serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā), and purifying the mind through the Fruition of Arahantship—this is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
70:
In the third verse, "anūpavādo" means not reviling or accusing anyone verbally. "Anūpaghāto" means not committing physical harm. "Pātimokkhe" refers to the supreme virtue (sīla) which protects from the dangers of the states of woe, or because it liberates the one who guards it from the fear of unhappy destinations; thus, restraint in that Pātimokkha virtue is intended. "Mattaññutā" means knowing the measure in receiving and using requisites. "Pantañca sayanāsanaṃ" means resorting to a lodging that is secluded and free from human disturbance. Here, by mentioning two requisites (alms-food and lodging), it should be understood that contentment with all four requisites is shown. "Etam buddhāna sāsanaṃ" means that this—not reviling, not harming, restraint in the Pātimokkha, moderation in consumption, and resorting to secluded dwellings to master the eight attainments—is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas. It should be understood that these verses represent the Ovāda Pātimokkha of all the Buddhas.

## Explanation of the Deities' Announcement

By this extensive explanation following the life story (apadāna) of the Blessed One Vipassī, the state of the Dhamma-element (dhamma-dhātu) being well-penetrated is revealed, as said: "Monks, this Dhamma-element has been well-penetrated by the Tathāgata." Now, to reveal the announcement of the deities, as said: "The deities also announced this matter to the Tathāgata," the passage beginning with "Ekamidāhaṃ" is spoken.

In that context, "Subhagavane" means in the forest of that name. "Sālarājamūle" means at the foot of the great Sāla tree, the chief of trees. "Kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā" means having completely eradicated sensual desire through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). Just as deities who lived the holy life under the teaching of the Buddha Vipassī came to announce, so did those who lived under the teachings of the other Buddhas. However, in the Pali text, it is presented only through the power of the Blessed One Vipassī and our Blessed One.

Among those deities, they are called "Avihā" because they do not fall away from their own prosperity. They are called "Atappā" because they do not cause distress to any being. They are called "Sudassā" because they are very beautiful and have an inspiring appearance. They are called "Sudassī" because they see well, or because their vision is excellent. They are called "Akaniṭṭhā" because they are superior to all others in their qualities and life-prosperity, and there are no "juniors" (kaniṭṭha) in that realm.
71:
At this point, the recitation sections (bhāṇavāras) should be combined and counted. For in this sutta, three bhāṇavāras are spoken by way of the life story (apadāna) of the Blessed One Vipassī. Just as they are spoken by way of the life story of the Blessed One Vipassī, so they are also spoken by way of the life stories of the Buddhas such as Sikhī and the others. However, the Pali text is abbreviated. Thus, through the power of the seven Buddhas, our Blessed One spoke twenty-one bhāṇavāras. Likewise, the Avihā Brahmās, the Atappā Brahmās, the Sudassā Brahmās, the Sudassī Brahmās, and the Akaniṭṭha Brahmās [each consist of twenty-one bhāṇavāras]; when all are combined, there are one hundred and twenty-six bhāṇavāras. In the Word of the Buddha known as the Tipiṭaka, there is no other sutta with a magnitude of one hundred and twenty-six bhāṇavāras; this sutta should be known as the King of Suttas (Suttantarāja). From here on, wishing to conclude the two connections (anusandhi), he spoke the words beginning with "Iti kho bhikkhave." All those words are clear in meaning.

## Thus the explanation of the Mahāpadāna Sutta in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya
## named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī is finished.
72:
## 2. Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta
## Commentary on the Introduction

This sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "Kurūsu", is the Mahānidāna Sutta. In this Mahānidāna Sutta, this is the explanation of the obscure terms. In the phrase "Kurūsu viharati", those called "Kuru" are the princes who rule the province. A single province that is the dwelling place of these princes is also called "Kuru" by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī). In that Kuru province (the Blessed One was staying).

The commentators say this: In the time of King Mandhātu, people from the three great islands heard that "Jambudīpa is the birthplace of noble beings such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Great Disciples, and Universal Monarchs. It is a noble island and is extremely delightful." Hearing this, they followed King Mandhātu, the Universal Monarch, as he traveled through the four great islands, preceded by the Wheel-treasure. Later, the King asked the Advisor-treasure (the eldest son treasure), "Dear son, is there any place more pleasant and delightful than the human world?" He replied, "Great King, why do you speak thus? Do you not see the power of the Moon-god and the Sun-god? Is not the place of those deities more pleasant and delightful than this human world?" Preceded by the Wheel-treasure, the King went to that celestial realm (of the Four Great Kings). When the four Great Kings heard that "King Mandhātu has arrived," they reflected, "This king is of great psychic power and majesty; it is impossible to stop him by war," and they surrendered their kingdoms. After King Mandhātu took over that celestial realm, he asked again, "Dear son, is there any place more pleasant and delightful than this realm of the Four Great Kings?"

Then the assembly informed him about the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. "Great King, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is more pleasant and delightful than this. In that heaven, these four Great Kings stand in the position of gatekeepers as attendants to Sakka, the King of Gods. Sakka, the King of Gods, is of great psychic power and majesty. These are the places of his enjoyment: the Vejayanta Palace, one thousand leagues high; the Sudhammā Hall of the Gods, five hundred leagues high; the Vejayanta Chariot, one hundred and fifty leagues long; likewise the Erāvaṇa elephant; the Nandana Grove, adorned with a thousand divine trees; the Cittalatā Grove, the Phārusaka Grove, and the Missaka Grove. There is also the Pāricchattaka Kovidāra tree, one hundred leagues high. Beneath that tree is the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, sixty leagues long, fifty leagues wide, and fifteen leagues thick, having the color of a Jayakusuma flower. Because of its softness, when Sakka sits down, half of his body sinks into it."
73:
Hearing this, the King, wishing to go to that Tāvatiṃsa heaven, sprinkled the Wheel-treasure (with ceremonial water). That Wheel-treasure stood in the sky together with the fourfold army. Then, the Wheel-treasure descended from between the two celestial realms and stood on the ground together with the fourfold army headed by the Advisor-treasure. The King went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven alone. As soon as Sakka heard that "Mandhātu has arrived," he went out to welcome him and said, "Welcome, Great King! This heaven is your own, Great King! Rule it, Great King!" and dividing the Tāvatiṃsa heaven into two parts, he gave one part to him along with the celestial dancers. As soon as the King was established in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, his human state disappeared and a divine state became manifest. It is said that when he sat with Sakka on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, the difference between them could only be known by the blinking of eyes. The gods, not noticing this, were confused and could not distinguish between Sakka and King Mandhātu. While enjoying divine bliss in that heaven, King Mandhātu ruled until thirty-six Sakkas had been born and passed away; yet, being unsatisfied with sensual pleasures, he passed away from that heaven, fell into his own garden, and died with a body affected by wind and heat.

When the Wheel-treasure stood on the ground again, the Advisor-treasure had King Mandhātu's footprint engraved on a gold plate and ruled the country, saying, "This is the kingdom of King Mandhātu." Those people who had followed from the three great islands, being unable to return to their own places, approached the Advisor-treasure and pleaded, "Lord, we came here by the power of the King. Now we are unable to return. Please give us a place to live." The Advisor-treasure gave each group a province. Among those places, the area inhabited by the people who came from the island of Pubbavideha received the name "Videha Country" according to their former designation. The area inhabited by the people who came from the island of Aparagoyāna received the name "Aparanta Province". The area inhabited by the people who came from the island of Uttarakuru received the name "Kuru Country". Because it comprises many villages, market towns, etc., it is referred to in the plural. Therefore, it is said, "He was staying among the Kurus (Kurūsu)."

In the phrase "a market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma", some teachers explain the meaning of the syllable 'dha' with the syllable 'da'. It is called "Kammāsadamma" because the Kammāsa (Porisāda) was tamed there. "Kammāsa" refers to Kammāsapāda the Porisāda (man-eater). It is said that when the wound on his foot, where it had been pierced by a stump, healed, the new flesh grew back looking like variegated wood. Therefore, he became known as "Kammāsapāda" (the one with the variegated foot). Because he was tamed in that place...
74:
That person was prohibited from being a man-eater. By whom? By the Great Being (the Bodhisatta). In which Jātaka? Some say in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka. However, these elders say it was in the Jayaddisa Jātaka. At that time, the Great Being tamed Kammāsapāda. Regarding this, it was said: "When I was the son of Jayaddisa, the offspring of the ruler of the Pañcāla kingdom, I gave up my life to free my father Jayaddisa from danger, and I also inspired faith in the small man-eater with spotted feet (Cūḷa-kammāsapāda)."

Some teachers explain the meaning using the letter 'dha' (as in Dhamma). It is said that the Kuruvattadhamma (the five precepts) of the Kuru people became 'spotted' (kammāsa) at that time. Therefore, because the Dhamma became spotted in that place, it is called 'Kammāsadhamma'. The market town (nigama) situated in that place also received this same name. Why is it not spoken of using the locative case (as a place of residence)? Because there was no monastery for residence. In that market town, there was no monastery called a vihāra for the Blessed One to reside in. Away from the market town, in a pleasant area of land well-supplied with water, there was a large forest grove. The Blessed One resided in that forest grove, making that market town his alms-resort village. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as: "In the Kuru country, there is a market town of the Kuru princes named Kammāsadhamma; he resided there, making that market town his alms-resort village."

'Āyasmā' (Venerable) is a term of endearment and a term of respect. 'Ānando' is the name of that elder. 'Ekamantaṃ' (to one side) is an adverbial use of the neuter gender (bhāvana-napuṃsaka-niddesa), as in the phrase "the moon and sun revolve unevenly (visamaṃ)," and so on. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as: he sat in such a way that, when sitting, he was sitting appropriately and suitably. Alternatively, this accusative case 'ekamantaṃ' is used in the sense of the locative case. 'Nisīdi' means he approached and entered nearby. For wise people, being skilled in sitting, approach a person worthy of respect and sit in an appropriate place. This Venerable Ānanda was also one of those wise people; therefore, he sat in an appropriate place.

How does one sit so that it is called sitting in an appropriate and suitable place? It is by sitting while avoiding the six faults of sitting. These six faults are: sitting too far, too near, upwind, on a high place, directly in front, and directly behind. If one sits too far away, one must speak with a loud voice if one wishes to talk. If one sits too near, it causes physical contact. If one sits upwind, one disturbs the other with one's body odor. If one sits on a high place...
75:
If one sits on a high place, it shows a lack of respect. If one sits too closely directly in front, one must look eye-to-eye when one wishes to look. If one sits too far behind, one must turn one's neck when one wishes to look. Therefore, this Venerable Ānanda also circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, paid respects with great reverence, and avoiding these six faults of sitting, he sat in front of the Blessed One's right knee. Entering within the six-colored Buddha-rays, Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, sat down as if diving into clear liquid lac, as if wrapping himself in a golden cloth, and as if entering the midst of a canopy of red lotus flowers. Therefore, it is said, "He sat to one side."

At what time and for what reason did this Venerable approach the Blessed One? It was in the evening for the purpose of asking a question regarding Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). It is said that on that day, this Venerable, for the sake of favoring the families, wandered for alms in the village of Kammāsadhamma as if laying down a bundle of a thousand pieces of wealth at every house door. Having returned from the alms round, he performed the major and minor duties for the Teacher. When the Teacher entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭī), he paid respects and went to his own place for the day's rest. After having his disciples perform their duties and seeing them depart, he swept his day-quarters, spread out a piece of leather, took water from a water-pot, cooled his hands and feet with the water, and sat down cross-legged, entering the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala-samāpatti). Then, emerging from the attainment at the designated time, he applied his knowledge to the law of Dependent Origination. Starting from the beginning, "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be," to the end; from the end to the beginning; from both ends to the middle; and from the middle to both ends, he contemplated the twelve factors of Dependent Origination three times. As he contemplated in this way, Dependent Origination became so clear to him that it appeared as if it were very superficial and plain.

Furthermore, he thought: "This Dependent Origination has been described by all Buddhas as 'deep and appearing deep.' To me, however, who am a disciple established in partial knowledge, it appears superficial, clear, and evident. Does it appear superficial only to me, or to others as well?" Then this thought occurred to him: "Now, let me take this question and ask the Blessed One. Surely, the Blessed One, making this the occasion, will show me by teaching a discourse (sutta), as if lifting Mount Sineru like a porch. For when the Buddhas reach these four subjects—Vinaya regulations, the various planes of existence, Dependent Origination, and various philosophical views—their lion's roar is great, their knowledge penetrates, the greatness of the Buddha-knowledge becomes evident, and that teaching is extremely profound."
76:
The greatness of [the Buddha's] wisdom is evident; the teaching is profound, connected with the three characteristics, and associated with emptiness (thus thought Ven. Ānanda). Although Ven. Ānanda usually approached the Blessed One a hundred or even a thousand times a day, he never did so without a cause or reason. On that day, however, taking this problem [with him], he thought: "I will approach this Gandha-elephant-like Buddha and listen to the elephant-cry of his wisdom; I will approach this lion-like Buddha and listen to the lion's roar of his wisdom; I will approach this Sindh-horse-like Buddha and observe the swift stride of his wisdom." Having so reflected, he rose from his day-rest, shook out his leather sitting-mat, took it, and approached the Blessed One in the evening. Therefore, it is said: "He approached in the evening for the purpose of asking a question about Dependent Origination."

In the phrase "yāva gambhīro," the word "yāva" is used in the sense of exceeding a measure. Because it exceeds [ordinary] measure in depth, it means "exceedingly profound." "Gambhīrāvabhāso" means that it appears or manifests as being profound. For some things are shallow but appear deep, like old water turned black by rotten leaves. Such water, though only knee-deep, appears as if it were a hundred fathoms deep. Some things are deep but appear shallow, like the clear water in the Jewel River (Maṇigaṅgā). Such water, though a hundred fathoms deep, appears to be only knee-deep. Some things are shallow and appear shallow, like water in a pot or similar vessels. Some things are deep and appear deep, like the water of the great ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru. Thus, water receives these four designations. However, in the case of Dependent Origination, this is not so. This Dhamma receives only one designation: it is both deep and appears deep. [Ānanda thought:] "Venerable Sir, it is wonderful, Venerable Sir, it is marvelous, that while this Dhamma is of such a nature, it yet appears to me as if it were very clear (shallow)." Expressing his amazement in this way, he asked the question and then sat down in silence.

The Blessed One, having heard Ven. Ānanda's words, thought: "Ānanda speaks of this problem, which is the domain of the Buddhas, as being clear to him—as if he were stretching out his hand to grasp the peak of existence (bhavagga), or as if he were striving to split Mount Sineru to extract its marrow, or as if he wished to cross the great ocean without a boat, or as if he were striving to overturn the earth to take the essence of the earth. I shall now tell him of its profound nature." Thinking thus, he spoke the words beginning with "Mā hevaṃ."

In that context, in the phrase "Mā hevaṃ," the syllable "ha" is a mere particle (nipāta). The meaning is "Do not say so." The Blessed One spoke these words "Mā hevaṃ" to the venerable Ānanda both for the purpose of exalting him and for the purpose of rebuking him.
77:
## Explanation of Exaltation (Ussādanā)

In that context, the Blessed One, exalting [Ānanda], said: "Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and clear knowledge. Because you possess such great and clear wisdom, even this profound Dependent Origination appears to you as if it were clear. However, it should not be considered clear to others; it is indeed deep and has a profound appearance."

In this matter, [the commentators] provide four similes. It is said that there was a great wrestler who had grown strong on the taste of good food for six months and had constantly practiced and exerted himself. He was well-practiced in lifting the heavy stones used by wrestlers at festivals. While going to the battlefield, he was shown a wrestler's stone on the way. He asked, "What is this?" When told, "It is a stone lifted by wrestlers," he said, "Bring it here." When they said, "We cannot lift it," he went there himself, asked, "Where is the heavy part of this stone?" and lifting two stones with both hands, he tossed them like playing-dice (or soap-nuts) and went on his way. In this simile, although the stone was light to the great wrestler, it should not be said to be light to others. Like the great wrestler who grew strong on good food for six months, the venerable Ānanda has fulfilled the aspirations (pāramīs) for a hundred thousand aeons. Just as the stone was light to the wrestler because of his great strength, so too Dependent Origination is clear to the Elder because of his great wisdom. However, it should not be said that this Dependent Origination is clear to others.

In the great ocean, the fish named Timi is two hundred yojanas long; the Timingala fish is three hundred yojanas long; the Timipingala fish is four hundred yojanas long; and the Timirapingala fish is five hundred yojanas long. The four types of fish—Ānanda, Timinanda, Ajjhāroha, and Mahātimi—are each one thousand yojanas long. Among them, the simile is shown only by means of the Timirapingala fish. It is said that when that Timirapingala fish moves its right ear, the water moves in an area of five hundred yojanas. It is the same when it moves its left ear, its tail, or its head. When it moves both ears, strikes the water with its tail, and tosses its head to and fro to play, the water in an area of seven hundred or eight hundred yojanas boils up like water placed in a pot on a stove. Water in an area of about three hundred yojanas is unable to cover the back of that fish. That fish might say: "They say this great ocean is deep, deep; where is its depth? We do not even get enough water to cover our backs." In that simile, although the great ocean is shallow to the Timirapingala fish which has such a massive body, it should not be said to be shallow to other small fish. In the same way, although Dependent Origination is clear to the Elder who is endowed with great wisdom, it should not be said to be clear to others.
78:
The King of Garuḍas is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. The right wing of that Garuḍa King is fifty yojanas long, and likewise, the left wing is fifty yojanas long. The wing-fringe is sixty yojanas. The neck is thirty yojanas. The beak is nine yojanas. The feet are twelve yojanas long. When that Garuḍa King begins to demonstrate the wind from his wings, an area of seven or eight hundred yojanas is insufficient. That Garuḍa King might say, 'They say this sky is infinite, infinite; how can it be infinite? We do not even find enough space to stretch the wind of our wings.' In that case, it is said that the sky is small for the Garuḍa King who possesses such a great body, but it cannot be said to be small for other small birds. In the same way, it is said that for the Elder who is endowed with wisdom, the Law of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is shallow, but it cannot be said to be shallow for others.

Rāhu, the Lord of Asuras, is four thousand eight hundred yojanas tall from the tips of his toes to the tips of his hair. The span between his two arms is one thousand two hundred yojanas. In thickness, he is six hundred yojanas. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are each three hundred yojanas; likewise, his mouth is three hundred yojanas. Each finger joint is fifty yojanas; likewise, the space between his eyebrows is fifty yojanas. The forehead is three hundred yojanas. The head is nine hundred yojanas. For that Lord of Asuras who has descended into the great ocean, the deep water reaches only to the level of his knees. That Lord of Asuras might say, 'They say this great ocean is deep, deep; how can it be deep? We do not even find enough water to cover our knees.' In that case, it is said that the great ocean is shallow for Rāhu who possesses such a body, but it cannot be said to be shallow for others. In the same way, it is said that for the Elder who is endowed with wisdom, the Law of Dependent Origination is shallow, but it cannot be said to be shallow for others. With reference to this meaning, the Blessed One said, 'Do not say so, Ānanda; do not say so, Ānanda.'

Indeed, for the Elder, although the Law of Dependent Origination is deep, it appears as shallow due to four reasons. What are the four reasons? They are: the perfection of previous requisites (pubbūpanissayasampatti), having resided with great teachers (titthavāsa), being a Stream-enterer (sotāpannatā), and being very learned (bahussutabhāva).

## Pubbūpanissayasampattikathā

It is said that one hundred thousand eons ago, a Teacher named Padumuttara appeared in the world. His city was named Haṃsavatī, and the King was named Ānanda...
79:
The father was King Ānanda, and the mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was named Prince Uttara. On the very day his son was born, the Prince departed in the Great Renunciation (mahābhinikkhamana), became a monk, and while practicing the great struggle, he gradually attained Omniscience (sabbaññuta). After uttering the solemn utterance (udāna) beginning with 'Aneka jāti saṃsāraṃ,' he spent seven days on the Bodhi-throne in bliss, and then extended his foot, thinking, 'I shall set it upon the ground.' At that moment, a great Paduma lotus burst through the earth and arose. Its petals were ninety cubits, the filaments were thirty cubits, the pericarp was twelve cubits, and the pollen was the volume of nine jars. The Teacher, in height, was fifty-eight cubits tall. The span between his two arms was eighteen cubits, his forehead was five cubits, and his hands and feet were eleven cubits. As soon as he stepped on the twelve-cubit pericarp with his eleven-cubit foot, the pollen, the volume of nine jars, rose up to fifty-eight cubits and fell all around like scattered powder of cinnabar and realgar. Because of his stepping upon the lotus, the Blessed One became famously known as 'Padumuttara.' Devela and Sujāta were his two Chief Disciples (aggasāvaka). Amitā and Asamā were his two Chief Female Disciples (aggasāvikā). Sumana was his attendant. The Blessed One Padumuttara, wishing to show favor to his father, resided in the royal capital of Haṃsavatī surrounded by one hundred thousand monks.

He had a younger brother named Prince Sumana. The royal father gave that prince a fief village at a place one hundred and twenty yojanas away from Haṃsavatī. That prince would occasionally come to visit his father and the Teacher. One day, there was an uprising in the border region. Prince Sumana sent word to the King, saying, 'The border region is in turmoil.' The King sent back a message, 'Why did I place you there?' The Prince went out, suppressed the rebels, and sent word again to the King, 'Great King, the province is now peaceful.' The King was very pleased and said, 'Let my son come quickly.' That prince had a thousand ministers. Along the way, the prince consulted with those ministers, 'My father is pleased; if he grants me a boon, what should I take?' Some suggested taking elephants, horses, chariots, provinces, or the seven treasures. Other ministers, however, said, 'Sirs, you are the sons of the lord of the earth, so wealth is not difficult for you to obtain; even if obtained, all this must be left behind. Only merit can be taken along. Therefore, when the Great King grants a boon, take the boon to serve the Blessed One Padumuttara for the three months of the Rains Retreat.' The Prince said, 'You are my good friends who desire my welfare; I did not have such a thought, but you have brought it about. I shall do exactly that,' and he went to his father. When he paid homage to his father, the King embraced him, kissed his head, and said, 'Dear son, I grant you a boon.' The Prince said, 'Great King, very well; please grant me the boon of the opportunity to serve the Blessed One with the four requisites for three months.' The King said, 'Dear son, I cannot grant that boon; I will give other boons.' But the Prince said, 'Great King, kings do not have two words; please grant only this boon, I desire no other.' The King said, 'Dear son, the intentions of the Buddhas are difficult to know; if the Blessed One does not wish it, what will happen even if I give it?' The Prince replied, 'Very well, I shall find out the Blessed One's intention,' and he went to the monastery. At that time, the Blessed One had finished his meal and entered the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi). Prince Sumana was at the assembly hall.
80:
(The prince) paid homage, and the father also embraced him, kissed him on the head, and said, "Dear son, I grant you a boon." When this was said, he replied, "It is well, Great King. Great King, I wish to serve the Blessed One with the four requisites for three months and make my life not in vain. Please grant me this very boon." When it was said, "Dear son, that is not possible; choose another boon," he replied, "Sire, for those of the warrior caste (Khattiyas), there are no two words. Grant me this very boon; I have no need for any other." The King said, "Dear son, the minds of the Buddhas are hard to know. If the Blessed One does not wish it, even if I grant it, what will happen?" The prince replied, "It is well, Sire. I will come to know the mind of the Blessed One," and he went to the monastery.

At that time, the Blessed One had finished his meal and entered the Gandhakuti (Perfumed Chamber). The prince went to the monks who were seated in the assembly hall. They asked him, "Prince, why have you come?" "I have come to see the Blessed One. Please show me the Blessed One," he replied. They said, "Prince, we do not get to see the Teacher at any moment we desire." He asked, "Venerable sirs, who then gets to see him?" They replied, "Prince, the one named Sumana Thera gets to see him." He asked, "Venerable sirs, where is that Elder?" Having asked for the Elder's dwelling place, he went there, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One. Please show him to me." The Elder said, "Come, Prince," and taking him, he left him in the courtyard of the Gandhakuti and ascended to the Gandhakuti.

Then the Blessed One said to the Elder, "Sumana, why have you come?" He replied, "Venerable sir, the prince has come to see the Blessed One." "In that case, monk, prepare a seat," he said. The Elder prepared the seat, and the Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The prince paid homage to the Blessed One and exchanged friendly greetings. The Buddha asked, "Prince, when did you arrive?" "Venerable sir, I arrived while you were entering the Gandhakuti. However, the monks said, 'We do not get to see the Blessed One at any moment we desire,' and sent me to the Venerable Sumana Thera. The Elder, however, showed you to me with just a single word. Venerable sir, I think the Elder is very dear (intimate) in your Dispensation." The Buddha said, "Yes, Prince, this monk is dear in my Dispensation." "Venerable sir, by doing what does one become dear in the Dispensation of the Buddhas?" he asked. "Prince, by giving gifts, undertaking virtue, and performing the Uposatha observance, one becomes dear," he replied. "Venerable sir, I also wish to be dear in the Buddha's Dispensation like the Elder. Please accept my invitation for the three-month rains retreat." The Blessed One, considering whether there would be benefit by going there and seeing that there would be, said, "Prince, the Tathāgatas delight in seclusion..."
81:
"...delight in seclusion," he said. The prince said, "I understand, Blessed One; I understand, Sugata (Well-Gone One)." He then said, "Venerable sir, I will go ahead and have a monastery built. When I send word, please come with a hundred thousand monks," and having received the promise, he went to his father and said, "Sire, the Blessed One has given me his promise. When I send word, please send the Blessed One to me." Having paid homage to his father, he departed. He had a monastery built at every league (yojana), and having traveled the distance of one hundred and twenty leagues, he searched for a site for a monastery in his own city. Seeing the garden of a householder named Sobhana, he bought it for a hundred thousand and spent another hundred thousand to have a monastery built. In that monastery, he had a Gandhakuti built for the Blessed One, and for the remaining monks, he had huts, caves, and pavilions built for their night and day quarters. Having constructed a surrounding wall and completed the gatehouse, he sent word to his father: "My task is finished; please send the Teacher."

The King offered a meal to the Blessed One and said, "Blessed One, Prince Sumana's task is finished; he awaits your arrival." The Blessed One set out, accompanied by a hundred thousand monks, staying in the monasteries at every league. Hearing that "The Teacher has arrived," the prince went out for one league to welcome him. Honoring him with flowers and such, he led him into the monastery and said:

"The garden named Sobhana,
Which I bought for a hundred thousand,
And built for a hundred thousand,
O Great Sage, please accept it."

Thus he offered the monastery. On the day of entering the rains retreat, he gave gifts and, having called his wife, children, and ministers, he said, "This Blessed One has come to us from afar. The Buddhas are those who honor the Dhamma, not those who honor material things. Therefore, for the three months of the rains, I will wear only two cloths, undertake the ten precepts, and stay right here with the Blessed One. You all should provide alms to the hundred thousand Arahants in this same manner for the three months of the rains."

Staying in a place similar to the dwelling of Sumana Thera, the prince observed all the major and minor duties the Elder performed for the Blessed One and thought, "In this place, this Elder is exceedingly dear and beloved. It is fitting that I too should aspire to this very position." As the Pavāraṇā ceremony drew near, he entered the village, gave a great gift for seven days, and on the seventh day, placed sets of the triple robes at the feet of the hundred thousand monks...
82:
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he said, "Venerable Sir, starting from the time I built and offered monasteries at every interval of a league along the journey, whatever merit I have performed was not done out of a desire for the prosperity of Sakka, the prosperity of Māra, or the prosperity of Brahma. It was done only out of a desire to be an attendant of a Buddha. Therefore, Venerable Sir, may I also become an attendant of a Buddha in the future, just like Sumana Thera." Having said this, he prostrated himself with the fivefold touching and paid homage.

The Blessed One, reflecting, "The heart of this clansman is indeed great; will his wish be fulfilled?" perceived, "In the future, one hundred thousand aeons from this present one, a Buddha named Gotama will arise; he will indeed be the attendant of that Buddha." Thus, He said:

"May all that you wish for and aspire to be fulfilled,
May all your intentions be fulfilled, like the full moon on the fifteenth day."

Upon hearing those words, the prince thought, "The Buddhas do not speak double words (their words are never otherwise)," and on the very second day, he acted as if he were following closely behind that Blessed One, carrying His bowl and robes. Having performed acts of merit for a hundred thousand years during that Buddha's era, he was reborn in the celestial realm. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he also performed an act of worship by offering his upper garment to a Thera who was wandering for alms, so that the Thera could receive the bowl. Being reborn again in the celestial realm and passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī and built leaf-roofed hermitages for eight Paccekabuddhas, provided them with jeweled bowl-rests, and attended to them with the four requisites for ten thousand years. These are the well-known accounts.

That future Ānanda, who had been performing acts of merit for a hundred thousand aeons, was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta. Passing away from there, he took rebirth in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan. In due course, after the Buddha's Great Renunciation and attainment of Supreme Enlightenment, when the Buddha first returned to Kapilavatthu, he departed along with Prince Bhaddiya and others while the princes were ordaining to be the Buddha's retinue. He then ordained in the presence of the Blessed One. Before long, after hearing a Dhamma discourse from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Thus, this venerable one was endowed with the perfection of previous supporting conditions (pubbūpanissaya). Because of being endowed with such previous supporting conditions, even the profound Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) appeared to the Venerable Ānanda as if it were clear and plain.
83:
## Titthavāsa-ādi-vaṇṇanā
Titthavāsa refers to the repeated learning, listening, questioning, and memorizing in the presence of teachers. This residence with teachers (titthavāsa) was extremely pure for the Venerable Ānanda; therefore, this profound Dependent Origination appeared to him as if it were clear and plain.

For those who are Stream-enters (Sotāpanna), the Law of Conditionality (paccaya-ākāra) naturally appears clear and plain, and this Venerable Ānanda was a Stream-enterer. For those of great learning (bahussuta), just as couches and stools become visible when a lamp is lit inside a room of four cubits, the distinction between mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) becomes clear. This Venerable Ānanda was the foremost among those of great learning; due to the power of that great learning as well, the profound Law of Conditionality appeared to him as if it were clear and plain.

## Paṭiccasamuppāda-gambhīratā
In that context, Dependent Origination is called profound in four ways: profundity of meaning (attha-gambhīratā), profundity of the law (dhamma-gambhīratā), profundity of teaching (desanā-gambhīratā), and profundity of penetration (paṭivedha-gambhīratā).

Among those four, the nature of aging and death (jarā-maraṇa) arising and repeatedly occurring due to the cause of birth (jāti) is profound... the nature of mental formations (saṅkhāra) arising and repeatedly occurring due to the cause of ignorance (avijjā) is profound. This nature is called the profundity of meaning (attha-gambhīratā).

The nature of ignorance being the cause for mental formations is profound... the nature of birth being the cause for aging and death is profound. This nature is called the profundity of the law (dhamma-gambhīratā).

In some discourses, Dependent Origination is taught in forward order (anuloma); in some, in reverse order (paṭiloma); in some, in both forward and reverse order; in some, starting from the middle in forward, reverse, or both forward and reverse orders. In some, it is taught with three connections and four groups (tisandhi catusaṅkhepa); in some, with two connections and three groups (dvisandhi tisaṅkhepa); in some, with one connection and two groups (ekasandhi dvisaṅkhepa). This nature is called the profundity of teaching (desanā-gambhīratā).

The nature of ignorance as not knowing, not seeing, and the inability to penetrate the Truth is profound. The nature of mental formations as constructing, accumulating, being with lust, and being without lust is profound. The nature of consciousness (viññāṇa) as being empty of self, without effort, not transmigrating, and the manifestation of rebirth-linking is profound. The nature of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) as arising together, being distinct, being indistinct, inclining towards an object, and being subject to change is profound. The nature of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) as being predominant, being the world, being doors, being the field of occurrence, and being the takers of objects is profound.
84:
The nature of contact (phassa) as touching, impacting, coinciding, and meeting is profound. The nature of feeling (vedanā) as experiencing the flavor of the object, as pleasure, pain, or equanimity, as non-self, and as the mode of experiencing is profound. The nature of craving (taṇhā) as delighting, clinging to the object, flowing like a river, entangling like a creeper, being like a river of craving, and being difficult to fill like the ocean of craving is profound. The nature of clinging (upādāna) as grasping, taking wrongly, attending to, misinterpreting, and being difficult to overcome is profound. The nature of existence (bhava) as conditioning, accumulating, and casting into the four modes of birth, five destinations, seven stations of consciousness, and nine abodes of beings is profound. The nature of birth (jāti) as arising, being born, descending, manifesting, and appearing is profound. The nature of aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) as exhaustion, decay, breaking up, and transformation is profound.

Thus, the nature of ignorance (avijjā) and so forth is profound; and the penetration by which ignorance and so forth are penetrated according to their own characteristics is profound. This should be known as the profundity of penetration (paṭivedhagambhīratā). All this profundity appeared to the Venerable Ānanda as if it were clear and shallow. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to encourage him with wisdom (or to uplift him), spoke the words beginning with "Mā hevaṃ" (Do not say so). The intention here is: "Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and clear knowledge; therefore, even the profound Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) appears clear to you. Thus, do not say, 'Does this Dependent Origination appear clear only to me, or to others as well?'"

## Description of the Rebuke (Apasādanāvaṇ္ဏနာ)
Regarding the word "apasādento" (rebuking), the intention is: "Ānanda, do not say, 'To me, Dependent Origination appears very, very clear.' For if this Dependent Origination appears very clear to you, why did you not become a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) by your own nature? Why did you penetrate the Path of Stream-entry only by standing in the method given by me? Ānanda, is it that only Nibbāna is profound, while Dependent Origination (paccayākāra) has become clear to you? If it is so clear, why do you not realize the fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala) by uprooting the four defilements: the gross fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill-will, the gross underlying tendency to sensual lust, and the underlying tendency to ill-will? Why do you not realize the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala) by uprooting those same four defilements in their subtle form? Why do you not realize Arahantship (arahatta) by uprooting these eight defilements: the five fetters such as lust for form, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance?"
85:
Why do you not penetrate the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa) like Sāriputta and Moggallāna, who fulfilled perfections for one incalculable (asankhyeyya) and a hundred thousand aeons? Why do you not penetrate the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhiñāṇa) like the Private Buddhas (Paccekabuddhas), who fulfilled perfections for two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? If, according to your view, this Dhamma appears clear in every way, why do you not realize Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) like the Buddhas, who fulfilled perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? Do you not desire these distinguished attainments? Look at your error. You are a disciple standing in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), yet you say of the extremely profound Dependent Origination, "It appears clear to me." These words of yours are contrary to the speech of the Buddhas. It is not proper for such a monk to speak words contrary to the speech of the Buddhas.

Ānanda, for me, while striving to penetrate this Dependent Origination, four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons have passed.
