To realize this Dhamma, there is no gift I have not given, no perfection I have not fulfilled. While I was striving, saying "I shall penetrate Dependent Origination," and crushing the army of Māra, this great earth did not shake even two inches. Likewise, while I was accomplishing the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsañāṇa) in the first watch, and the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) in the middle watch, this earth did not shake. But in the last watch, at the time of dawn, as soon as I saw, "Ignorance conditions mental formations in nine ways," the ten-thousandfold world system resounded like a bronze gong struck with an iron rod, and it shook like a drop of water on a lotus leaf struck by the wind. Thus, Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is profound and has a profound appearance. Ānanda, because of not understanding... not penetrating this Dhamma... they do not transcend [the round of rebirth].

"This Dhamma" means this law of conditionality (paccayadhamma). "Because of not understanding" means not understanding through the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). "Because of not penetrating" means not penetrating through the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā) and the full understanding by abandoning (pahānapariññā). "Become like a tangled ball of thread" (tantākulakajāta) means becoming confused like a ball of thread spread out by weavers. For example, a ball of thread that is poorly kept and bitten by mice becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to join end to end or beginning to beginning, thinking "This is the end, this is the beginning." In the same way, beings stumble, become confused, and are especially disturbed in this Dependent Origination, unable to make this Dependent Origination straight. In that example of the thread, it might be possible to make it straight through human effort; but except for the two types of Bodhisattas (the future Paccekabuddha and the future Sammāsambuddha), other beings cannot make this Dependent Origination straight by themselves. However, I shall make that confusion clear. If a tangled ball of thread is soaked in gruel (kañjiyā) and combed with a hog-bristle brush, the knots and tangles here and there...
86:
Indeed, except for the two Bodhisattas (the future Paccekabuddha and the future Sammāsambuddha), other beings are not able to straighten out Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) by their own nature. For example, just as a tangled skein of thread, when treated with rice-scum and combed with a bristle-brush, becomes knotted and clumped in various places; in the same way, these beings, having stumbled in the conditions and being unable to straighten out the conditions, become tangled and knotted through the power of the sixty-two kinds of wrong views. All those who rely on any kind of wrong view are simply unable to straighten out Dependent Origination.

'Kulāgaṇṭhikajātā' means that the thread treated with rice-scum by weavers is called 'kulāgaṇṭhika'. 'Kulā' refers to weaver-birds; some teachers say that 'kulāgaṇṭhika' refers to the nest of that bird. Just as both of those are so tangled that it is difficult to untangle them to match end to end or root to root, this should be applied in the same way as the previous method.

'Muñjapabbajabhūtā' means becoming like muñja grass and like pabbajja grass. When a rope made by pounding those grasses becomes old and falls somewhere, and one picks it up, it is very difficult to untangle those grasses to match end to end or root to root, saying 'this is the end, this is the root'. Even that rope might be straightened out by human effort; however, except for the two Bodhisattas, other beings are not able to straighten out Dependent Origination by themselves. Thus, this generation, being unable to straighten out Dependent Origination and becoming tangled through the power of wrong views, cannot transcend the round of rebirth (saṃsāra), which consists of the states of deprivation (apāya), the bad destination (duggati), and the downfall (vinipāta).

In that context, 'apāya' refers to the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, the ghost realm (peta), and the host of asuras. All those are called 'apāya' because of the absence of 'aya', which means growth or happiness (or merit). Likewise, they are called 'duggati' because they are the destination of suffering. They are called 'vinipāta' because they are a state of falling away from the accumulation of happiness. The other term is defined as:

'The continuous and uninterrupted succession of the aggregates (khandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) is called saṃsāra.'

They cannot transcend all that suffering of the states of deprivation and the round of rebirth. Instead, taking up death and rebirth repeatedly—from death to rebirth and from rebirth to death—within the three realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, they are like a ship tossed by the wind in the great ocean, or like an ox yoked to a machine...
87:
...wandering around in the round of rebirth. It should be understood that the Blessed One said all this desiring to admonish the Venerable Ānanda.

## Exposition of Dependent Origination

Now, since this Mahānidāna Sutta is connected only with these two phrases: 'Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is profound' and 'It has become like a tangled skein', the Blessed One, wishing to begin the discourse to show the profound nature of the mode of conditions (paccayākāra) through this sequence: 'Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is profound', said: 'Is there aging-and-death due to this-conditionality?' and so on. In that text, this is the meaning: the condition for this aging-and-death is called 'this-condition' (idappaccaya). Therefore, is there aging-and-death because of this-condition? When asked, 'Is there indeed a condition for aging-and-death, from which condition aging-and-death would arise?', Ānanda, a virtuous and wise person should not act as one does when asked 'Is the soul the same as the body?', where the question must be set aside (thapanīya) and one must remain silent, or where it must be said 'This has not been declared (abyākata) by the Tathāgata'. Instead of falling into such silence or non-explanation, just as when asked 'Is the eye permanent or impermanent?', one must categorically say 'Impermanent', so too one must categorically say 'It exists'. Again, when asked 'Due to what condition does aging-and-death occur? What is the name of that condition from which aging-and-death arises?', one must say 'Aging-and-death occurs due to the condition of birth (jāti)'. This is the meaning of how it should be said. This method applies to all terms.

Regarding the statement 'Contact occurs due to the condition of name-and-form (nāmarūpa)', when it is said 'due to the condition of the sixfold sense base (saḷāyatana)', it only includes the six kinds of resultant contact (vipāka-phassa) such as eye-contact. In this Mahānidāna Sutta, however, the Blessed One spoke this because He wished to show the specific resultants—namely wholesome, unwholesome, and functional contacts—which were both included and not yet included by the term 'due to the condition of the sixfold sense base', and also to show other specific conditions for contact beyond the sixfold sense base. What did the Blessed One explain by this turn? He explained the causality (nidāna) of the conditions. This sutta is called the Mahānidāna Sutta because it is taught by making the conditions free from tangles and clusters.

Now, to show the true, unerring, and invariable nature of those various conditions, He said: 'Thus it was said: "Aging-and-death occurs due to the condition of birth"' and so on. In that text, 'pariyāyena' means by way of cause. 'Sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ' is a combination of two particles. Its meaning is: in every way, entirely, in all respects...
88:
The meaning is: "If birth were not to occur in any way at all, in any manner whatsoever." The meaning of 'becoming' (bhava) and so forth should also be understood in this same way. 'Kassaci' is an indefinite term, referring to any being among devas and so forth. 'Kimhici' is also an indefinite term, referring to the occurrence in any of the nine types of becoming, such as the sense-sphere becoming (kāmabhava). 'Seyyathidaṃ' is a particle (nipāta) used in the sense of analyzing a meaning that has been stated indefinitely; its meaning is: "I shall analyze for you the meaning of what was stated as 'kassaci kimhici'."

Then, wishing to analyze that meaning, He said: "Whether for devas as devas," and so forth. In that text, "for devas as devas" refers to the birth (jāti) of the aggregates for the sake of attaining the state of a deva; it is because of the birth of those aggregates that devas are called "devas." The meaning of all terms should be understood in this way: "If birth were not to occur in any way at all." Here, 'deva' refers to devas by rebirth (upapatti-deva). 'Gandhabba' refers to deities residing in the roots and trunks of trees. 'Yakkha' refers to non-human beings (amanussa). 'Bhūta' refers to all beings that have been born. 'Pakkhi' refers to all creatures with bony wings, leathery wings, or feathered wings. 'Sarīsapa' refers to all creatures that move by crawling on the ground. 'Tesaṃ tesaṃ' refers to those various devas, gandhabbas, and so forth. 'Tadatthāya' means for the sake of attaining the state of a deva, gandhabba, and so forth. 'Jātinirodha' means the cessation of birth, or the absence of birth.

All terms such as 'hetu' are merely synonyms for 'cause' (kāraṇa). A cause is called 'hetu' because it moves or proceeds (hinoti) for the sake of its own fruit. It is called 'nidāna' because it delivers the fruit as if saying, "Here, take this." It is called both 'samudaya' and 'paccaya' because the fruit arises (samudeti) from it and proceeds by depending on (paṭicca) it. This method applies everywhere. Furthermore, in the phrase 'yadidaṃ jāti', 'yadidaṃ' is a particle. Its meaning should be understood in all instances according to the gender (liṅga). Here, however, its meaning is: "this birth which is such." For birth is a condition for aging and death by way of decisive support (upanissaya).

In the term 'becoming' (bhava), the scope of location is defined by the word 'kimhici'. Therein, the sense-sphere becoming (kāmabhava) should be understood as including everything from the Avīci hell below to the Paranimmitavasavatti heaven above. This method is appropriate for rebirth-becoming (upapatti-bhava). However, in this sutta, it is appropriate for kamma-becoming (kamma-bhava). For that kamma-becoming is a condition for birth only by way of decisive support. In the terms 'clinging' (upādāna) and so forth, it should be understood that the word 'kimhici' is used only to define the location of occurrence.
89:
In the phrase 'upādānapaccayā bhavo' (with clinging as condition, becoming), sense-desire clinging (kāmupādāna) is a condition for the three types of kamma-becoming and the three types of rebirth-becoming. Likewise, the remaining types of clinging should be understood as conditions for the twenty-four types of becoming. In the primary sense (nippariyāyena), twelve types of kamma-becoming are obtained here. Clinging is a condition for those kamma-becomings by way of conascence (sahajāta) and decisive support (upanissaya).

'Rūpataṇhā' refers to craving for forms. This same method applies to craving for sounds (saddataṇhā) and so forth. That craving is also a condition for clinging by way of conascence and decisive support.

In the phrase 'vedanāpaccayā taṇhā' (with feeling as condition, craving), resultant feeling (vipāka-vedanā) is a condition for craving by way of decisive support. Other types of feeling are conditions in other ways.

Having thus shown the prior craving which is the root of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭamūla), the Blessed One now wishes to show manifest craving (samudācarataṇhā) through nine terms—like one who, striking someone on the back or seizing them by the hair, drives the screaming person off the path—and thus said: "So it is, Ānanda, that with feeling as condition, craving arises," and so forth. Therein, craving is of two kinds: seeking-craving (esanātaṇhā) and sought-craving (esitataṇhā). The craving by which one seeks and searches for wealth by traveling along goat-paths, spike-paths, and so forth, is called seeking-craving. The craving that arises when that sought and searched-for wealth is obtained is called sought-craving. Both are merely designations for manifest craving. Therefore, craving conditioned by feeling is of two kinds. 'Seeking' (pariyesanā) means searching for objects such as forms; it occurs only when there is craving. 'Gain' (lābha) means the acquisition of objects such as forms; it occurs only when there is seeking. 'Decision' (vinicchaya), however, is fourfold by way of knowledge, craving, views, and thought.

Among those four, "One should know the knowledge for deciding happiness; having known the decision for happiness, one should pursue internal happiness"—this is 'decision by knowledge' (ñāṇa-vinicchaya). As it is said, "Decisions are of two kinds: decision by craving and decision by views," the one hundred and eight maneuvers of craving are called 'decision by craving' (taṇhā-vinicchaya). The sixty-two views are called 'decision by views' (diṭṭhi-vinicchaya). In this sutta, however, the word 'decision' (vinicchaya) refers to 'thought' (vitakka), as in: "Sakka, lord of devas, desire has thought as its source." Indeed, after obtaining a gained object, one decides whether it is desirable or undesirable, good or bad, only through thought.
90:
“This much of wealth will be for the sake of visual objects; this much for the sake of sounds and other objects; this much will be for me; this much for others; this much I will enjoy; this much I will store up”—thus one specifically distinguishes. Therefore, it is said: “Dependent on gain, decision-making (vinicchaya) arises.”

In the object thought of with such unwholesome thought (akusala-vitakka), weak lust and strong lust arise. In this context, this is indeed called craving (taṇhā). ‘Desire’ (chanda) is a designation for weak lust. ‘Indulgence’ (ajjhosāna) is the making of a strong decision as “I” and “mine.” ‘Possession’ (pariggaha) is the act of taking possession by the power of craving and views. ‘Stinginess’ (macchariya) is the inability to tolerate sharing with others. For that very reason, the ancient teachers say regarding its word-definition: “Because it occurs as ‘Let this wonder be for me alone, let it not be a wonder for others,’ it is called macchariya.” ‘Protection’ (ārakkha) is guarding well by means of closing doors, securing in boxes, and so forth. ‘Adhikaraṇa’ is a name for cause; thus ‘ārakkhādhikaraṇa’ means because of the cause of protection.

In ‘taking up the rod’ (daṇḍādāna) and so forth, the grasping of sticks, spears, etc., to restrain others is called ‘taking up the rod.’ The grasping of weapons such as single-edged blades is called ‘taking up weapons’ (satthādāna). ‘Quarrel’ (kalaha) is quarreling by body or by speech. The initial opposition is called ‘strife’ (viggaha). The subsequent opposition is called ‘dispute’ (vivāda). “Tuvaṃtuvaṃ” (thou-thouing) is saying “you, you” with disrespectful speech.

Now, in order to show that habitual craving (samudācara-taṇhā) also by the reverse method, the teaching is concluded by beginning with “ārakkhādhikaraṇa.” Therein, ‘sensual craving’ (kāma-taṇhā) is craving for visual objects and so forth, arising by the power of lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. ‘Craving for existence’ (bhava-taṇhā) is lust accompanied by the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi). ‘Craving for non-existence’ (vibhava-taṇhā) is lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi). These two things are the craving that is the root of the round (vaṭṭa-mūla-taṇhā) and habitual craving (samudācara-taṇhā). Although they reach a single nature by way of the characteristic of craving, they become two groups by way of the root of the round and habitual occurrence, and they have a single convergence due to the cause of feeling (vedanā). It means they have the same cause as feeling.

Convergence (samosaraṇa) is of three kinds: convergence by way of descent (osaraṇa-samosaraṇa), convergence by way of co-nascent (sahajāta-samosaraṇa), and convergence by way of condition (paccaya-samosaraṇa). Among these, “All those things converge in desire (kāma)” is called convergence by way of descent. “Friends, these things have desire as their root, contact as their origin, and feeling as their convergence (in a single object)” is called convergence by way of co-nascent. “By two ways, they have a single convergence due to the cause of feeling” should be understood as convergence by way of condition.
91:
All contacts such as eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa) are only resultant contacts (vipāka-phassa). Among those resultant contacts, if the four supramundane resultant contacts are excluded, the remaining contacts are thirty-two. In this context of “Dependent on contact, feeling arises,” contact is a condition for feeling in many ways.

“Ānanda, by whatever modes...” In this passage, the dissimilar natures of feeling and other states are called “modes” (ākāra). When those very modes are well-shown, they are called “marks” (liṅga) because they make known the various hidden meanings. They are called “signs” (nimitta) because they are the cause of recognizing each respective nature. They are called “designations” (uddesa) because they are to be pointed out in such and such ways. Therefore, the meaning here is: “Ānanda, by whatever modes... by whatever designations there is a description of the mental body (nāma-kāya), which is a collection of mental states. When there is the mode of experiencing, the mark of experiencing, the sign of experiencing, and the designation ‘feeling’ in feeling; when there is the mode of perceiving, the mark of perceiving, the sign of perceiving, and the designation ‘perception’ in perception; when there is the mode of volitional activity, the mark of volitional activity, the sign of volitional activity, and the designation ‘volition’ in mental formations; when there is the mode of cognizing, the mark of cognizing, the sign of cognizing, and the designation ‘consciousness’ in consciousness—then there is the description of the mental body as ‘This is the mental body.’ If those modes and so forth in feeling and other states, which are the causes for the description of the mental body, were absent, would designation-contact (adhivacana-samphassa) be evident in the physical body (rūpa-kāya)? Would that mind-contact (mano-samphassa) named designation-contact, which arises in the mind-door based on the four mental aggregates, be evident in the physical body, or would it arise based on the five sensitive materialities (pasāda-rūpa)?” Thus He asked. Then the Venerable Ānanda, just as one would not accept the appearance of a ripe mango from a rose-apple tree when there is no mango tree, did not accept the arising of that mind-contact from the physical body and said, “No, Bhante.”

In the second question also, the meaning of modes and so forth should be understood by way of the mode of being oppressed (ruppana), the mark of being oppressed, the sign of being oppressed, and by way of the designation “matter” (rūpa). “Impingement-contact” (paṭigha-samphassa) is the contact that arises based on the material aggregate (rūpakkhandha) which is capable of impingement. Here too, just as one would not accept the appearance of a ripe rose-apple from a mango tree when there is no rose-apple tree, the Elder did not accept the arising of that impingement-contact from the mental body and said, “No, Bhante.”
92:
The third question is spoken of by way of both (Name and Form). In that question, just as the Elder Ānanda would not accept the spontaneous appearance of mangoes or jambu fruits in the sky, he did not accept that both types of contact could arise in the absence of Name and Form, and thus he replied, "No, indeed, Bhante."

Having thus shown the respective causes of the two types of contact, he now begins the fourth question to show that both of them, without distinction, have Name and Form as their cause: "By whatever aspects, Ānanda..." "Yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ" means that this Name and Form occurring in the six doors is the very root cause, the very support (of contact). For in the eye-door and so on, the eye-sensitivity and the like, as well as the visible objects and the like, are "Form" (rūpa); the associated aggregates are "Name" (nāma). Thus, this fivefold contact is indeed contact having Name and Form as its cause. In the mind-door as well, the heart-base and the form which is the object are "Form"; the associated states and the non-form which is the object are "Name". Thus, it should be understood that mind-contact (manosamphassa) also has Name and Form as its cause. Name and Form is a cause for that contact in many ways.

"Na okkamissatha" means if it did not occur by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), as if entering and proceeding (into the womb). "Samuccissatha" means if rebirth-linking consciousness were absent, would the remaining pure Name and Form alone combine and proceed in the mother's womb in the form of the kalala-embryo and so on? "Okkamitvā vokkamissatha" means having entered by way of rebirth-linking and then departing by way of death (cuti); the meaning is that it would cease. That cessation does not occur merely by the cessation of that (rebirth-linking) mind, nor by the cessation of the second or third bhavaṅga minds thereafter. For thirty kamma-born rupa arise together with the rebirth-linking consciousness. While those rupa persist, sixteen bhavaṅga minds arise and cease. During this interval, there is no danger (death) for the child who has taken rebirth, nor for the mother. This is indeed called "anokāsa" (no opportunity for death). If the rupa that arose with the rebirth-linking consciousness are able to provide support for the seventeenth bhavaṅga, the process continues and the lineage is connected. If they are not able, the process does not continue, the lineage is not connected, and this is called "vokkamati" (departing). With reference to this, it was said: "Having entered, it were to depart."

"Itthattāya" means for this state, meaning for the state of the complete five aggregates. "Daharasseva sato" means while being just a tender young child. "Vocchijjissatha" means (would be cut off).
93:
Would growth, development, and abundance be cut off? (Upacchijjissatha vuḍḍhiṃ virūḷhiṃ vepullaṃ): If consciousness were cut off, would pure Name and Form alone arise and reach growth by way of the first stage of life, development by way of the middle stage of life, or abundance by way of the last stage of life? Or would it reach growth, development, and abundance by reaching ten years, twenty years, a hundred years, or a thousand years? This is the meaning.

"Therefore, Ānanda..." because consciousness is the cause of that Name and Form during the taking of rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, during the stay in the womb, during the exit from the womb, and during the period of its occurrence such as the ten-year period and so on; therefore, this very consciousness is the root cause, this is the support for Name and Form, namely, consciousness. For example, a King wishing to subdue his retinue might say: "Who made you the Sub-king? Who made you the General? Was it not I who did so? If I had not done so, would you have become Sub-king or General by your own nature? We would then know your power." In the same way, consciousness is the cause of Name and Form. In terms of meaning, it is as if consciousness says to Name and Form: "Who made you Name? Who made you Form? Who made you what is called Name and Form? Was it not I who did so? If I, acting as the precursor, had not taken rebirth-linking in the mother's womb, would you have become Name or Form or Name and Form? We would then know your power." That consciousness is a cause for Name and Form in many ways.

"Dukkhasamudayasambhavo" means the origin of the mass of suffering. "Yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ" means this Name and Form is the root cause, the support for consciousness. For example, the King's men, wishing to subdue the King, might say: "Who made you King? Was it not we who did so? If we did not remain in the position of Sub-king or General, would you alone be King? We would then see your kingship." In the same way, Name and Form, in terms of meaning, as if saying to consciousness: "Who made you the rebirth-linking consciousness? Was it not we who did so? If you did not depend on the three (mental) aggregates and the heart-base rupa, would you be called rebirth-linking consciousness? We would then see your status as rebirth-linking consciousness." That Name and Form is also a cause for consciousness in many ways.

"Ettāvatā kho" means when consciousness assists Name and Form, when Name and Form assists consciousness, and when these two are proceeding by way of mutual conditionality...
94:
By this much, [a being] may be born, or age, or die, or pass away, or reappear; and the modes of birth and so forth, or the repeated rounds of death and rebirth, may be known.

'Path of designation' (adhivacanapatha) refers to the path of usage where only the sound is emphasized without referring to the meaning, such as in names like "Sirivaḍḍhaka" or "Dhanavaḍḍhaka." 'Path of language' (niruttipatha) refers to the path of usage that arises by way of indicating a cause, such as "he is 'sato' (mindful) because he remembers" or "he is 'sampajāno' (clearly comprehending) because he knows well." 'Path of concept' (paññattipatha) refers to the path of usage that arises by way of making things known in various ways, such as "he is wise, skilled, sharp-witted, subtle, or a knower of others' doctrines." Thus, by these three terms, only the aggregates (khandhas), which are the basis for designations and so forth, are spoken of.

'Sphere of wisdom' (paññāvacara) refers to the five aggregates which are to be entered and known by wisdom. 'The round turns' (vaṭṭaṃ vattati) means the round of saṃsāra turns. 'This state of being' (itthatta) refers to this mode of existence, which is a name for the five aggregates. 'For the purpose of designating' (paññāpanāya) means for the purpose of designating names. The meaning is that by designating names such as "feeling" or "perception," the five aggregates are also known through the mutual assistance of this much consciousness and name-and-form. "This name-and-form together with consciousness" refers to this name-and-form which proceeds in mutual dependence with consciousness. This is the concluding statement here.

## Description of the Designation of Self

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the connection to the phrase "Deep is this dependent origination, Ānanda, and deep it appears," now begins the teaching "By how much, Ānanda..." wishing to show the connection to the phrase "It has become like a tangled skein." In that teaching, regarding the phrases "Ānanda, [designating] a material self that is finite," etc., whoever takes an undeveloped kasiṇa sign as the self designates a material, finite self. One who attains various kasiṇas designates that self as sometimes blue or sometimes yellow. One who takes a developed kasiṇa sign as the self designates a material, infinite (ananta) self.

Alternatively, whoever removes the undeveloped kasiṇa sign and takes either the space-concept touched by the sign, or the four mental aggregates occurring there, or just the consciousness among them as the self, designates an immaterial, finite self. Whoever removes the developed kasiṇa sign and takes either the space-concept touched by the sign, or the four mental aggregates occurring there, or just the consciousness among them as the self, designates an immaterial, infinite self.
95:
In the phrase "In that [context], Ānanda" (tatra Ānanda), "tatra" means among those four types of people with wrong views. "Or now" (etarahi vā) means only in the present life, and not designating anything beyond this. This is said in terms of the view of annihilationism (uccheda). "Or what will be there" (tatthabhāviṃ vā) means that which will always exist in the next world. This is said in terms of the view of eternalism (sassata). "Though it is not so" (atathaṃ vā pana santaṃ) means while having a nature that is not true (distorted). "For the sake of being so" (tathattāya) means for the sake of being true. "I will prepare" (upakappessāmi) means I will accomplish or bring about. By this, the Buddha shows the opposing views.

Specifically, an annihilationist thinks: "Although the self of the eternalist is not true in its nature of being non-perishing, I will make it true in the nature of annihilation (perishing). I will make him understand the eternalist view [as false] and make him adopt only the annihilationist view." The eternalist also thinks: "Although the self of the annihilationist is not true in its nature of being impermanent, I will make it true in the nature of eternalism (permanence). I will make him understand the annihilationist view [as false] and make him adopt only the eternalist view."

"This being so" (evaṃ santaṃ kho) means while things are thus, they designate a material, finite self. "Material" (rūpī) refers to one who has attained a material kasiṇa jhana. "The underlying tendency of the view of a finite self lies latent" (parittattānudiṭṭhi anuseti) means this wrong view that "the self is finite" repeatedly underlies. That view does not underlie like a vine or a creeper, but should be understood to underlie in the sense of not yet being abandoned by the Path. "It is fit to say" (iccālaṃ vacanāya) means it is appropriate to say that such a view underlies that person. This method should be understood in all cases.

In the word "immaterial" (arūpī), the meaning should be understood as one who has attained an immaterial kasiṇa jhana or one whose object is the mental aggregates. Through this sequence of teaching, sixteen types of people with wrong views regarding the self are shown: four who attain [jhana], their four disciples, four speculators (takkika), and their four disciples.

## Description of the Non-designation of Self

Having shown those who designate a self, the Buddha now says "By how much, Ānanda..." to show those who do not. Who are those who do not designate? All noble persons (ariya puggala) do not designate a self. Also, worldlings (puthujjana) who are learned and bear the Three Pitakas, Two Pitakas, or One Pitaka; or even a Dhamma-preacher who has well-determined and learned at least one Nikaya; or one who has begun insight meditation (vipassanā)—they do not designate a self. The reason is that for these noble ones and others, in the counterpart sign (paṭibhāgakasiṇa), there is only the knowledge "counterpart sign." In the mental aggregates, there is only the knowledge "mental aggregates."
96:
## Commentary on the Contemplation of Self

Having shown those who do not designate a self, He now wishes to show those who do. They designate it by repeatedly viewing it through the power of wrong view. Their repeated viewing occurs because the twenty-fold identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) has not yet been abandoned. Therefore, to show that twenty-fold identity view, He said again, "To what extent, Ānanda," and so forth.

In that passage, by the words "or feeling," He taught the identity view based on the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). By the words "My self does not experience," He taught the identity view based on the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). By the words "My self experiences, for the nature of feeling is my self," He taught the identity view based on the aggregates of perception (saññā), formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa). This is because these three aggregates experience by being associated with feeling. For these three aggregates, the nature of feeling is inseparable.

Now, wishing to show the faults in those three doctrines, He said, "In that case, Ānanda," and so forth. In that passage, "in that case" refers to those three types of persons with wrong views. "At whatever time, Ānanda," and so forth, is stated to show the faults such as the self sometimes existing and sometimes not existing for whichever person views a particular feeling as the self.

In the terms "impermanent" and so forth: they are called "impermanent" (anicca) because they do not exist after having been. They are called "conditioned" (saṅkhata) because they are produced by coming together through various causes. They are called "dependently arisen" (paṭiccasamuppanna) because they arise only through appropriate causes depending on various conditions. All the words such as "exhaustion" (khaya) are synonyms for "dissolution" (bhaṅga). Whatever breaks up also gets exhausted, vanishes, fades away, and ceases. Therefore, He said "subject to exhaustion," and so forth.

"My self has disappeared" means it has reached the state of being gone. The meaning is that my self has vanished and ceased. If it is asked whether "This is my self" occurs to a single person in all three times, why would it not? For one with wrong view, there is no stability, like a stake driven into a pile of chaff; like a forest monkey, they grab one thing and let go of another. "Intermingled with impermanence, pleasure, and pain" means that specifically, one who views a particular feeling as the self views an impermanent, pleasant, and painful self. One who views feeling as the self without distinction views it as intermingled...
97:
...views the self as having the nature of arising and passing away. Indeed, feeling is of three kinds and has the nature of arising and passing away. This person with wrong view also views that feeling as the self. Because of such a view, that person's self reaches the state of being impermanent, and many feelings also come to arise in a single moment. That person admits that their self is impermanent, yet the arising of many feelings in a single moment does not exist. Referring to this meaning—that many feelings do not arise in a single moment—He said, "Therefore, Ānanda, for this reason, it is not fit to view 'Feeling is my self'."

In the phrase "Friends, where," in things like a palm-leaf fan or a window, which are called the mere aggregate of form, there is no experience of feeling at all. "In that (absence of feeling)" means in that palm-leaf fan or window devoid of feeling, would the conceit (ahaṃkāra) "I am" arise? "Therefore, Ānanda" means because the mere aggregate of form does not rise up and say "I am," therefore, by this clearly contradictory reason, the wise do not approve of viewing feeling as self. "In that (absence of feeling), would 'This I am' occur?" means among the three aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness which have the nature of feeling, would even one state be fit to be called "This is I"? Or, when those three aggregates cease along with the cessation of feeling, would "This I am" or "I am" arise? Then Ven. Ānanda, not accepting the existence of "I" in that teaching—just as one does not accept the sharpness of a rabbit's horn—said, "No, Bhante."

What is taught by this sequence of the Dispensation? The discourse on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭakathā) is taught. When the Buddha teaches the vaṭṭakathā, in some suttas He teaches with ignorance as the head (avijjāsīsena), in some with craving (taṇhāsīsena), and in some with wrong view (diṭṭhisīsena). Among these: "Monks, the first beginning of ignorance is not known; it is not the case that 'Before this, ignorance did not exist, but it arose later.' Monks, this is said. However, it is known that ignorance arises due to this condition." Thus, it is taught with ignorance as the head. "Monks, the first beginning of craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is not known; it is not the case that 'Before this, craving for existence did not exist, but it arose later.' Monks, this is said. However, it is known that craving for existence arises due to this condition." Thus, it is taught with craving as the head. "Monks, the first beginning of the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi) is not known; it is not the case that 'Before this, the view of existence did not exist, but it arose later.' Monks, this is said. However, it is known that the view of existence arises due to this condition." Thus, it is taught with the view of existence as the head. Here too, it is taught with wrong view as the head.
98:
A person with wrong view, grasping feelings such as pleasure as the self, wanders continuously through all types of existence, modes of birth, destinations, stations of consciousness, and abodes of beings, passing away from one and being reborn in another, by the power of the wrong comprehension of the notions of 'I' and 'mine' (conceit and craving). Like a boat tossed by the wind in the great ocean, such a person is unable even to lift their head from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa).

Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the round of rebirths through this sequence of discourse to the person with wrong view who is confused about the law of dependent origination, now wishing to teach the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), said: "When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu..." and so forth.

Furthermore, because the Blessed One is skillful in teaching, he did not refer to a person whose mind is distracted by new work (navakamma) and the like, having set aside meditation. Instead, he began by referring to a person who dwells practicing the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) in accordance with the Buddha's instructions, saying: "He does not regard feeling as the self," and so forth. Such a bhikkhu defines all form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—as "impermanent"; this is one kind of comprehension (sammasana). He defines it as "suffering"; this is one kind of comprehension. He defines it as "non-self"; this is one kind of comprehension. By the power of the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa) taught in this manner, because it is applied to all phenomena of the three planes, he does not regard feeling as the self, nor does he regard other phenomena such as perception (saññā) and mental formations (saṅkhāra) as the self. Such a bhikkhu, not regarding things in this way, does not grasp anything in the world of the aggregates and the world of formations, such as form and other phenomena, as "my self" or as "belonging to my self."

Because he does not grasp, he is not agitated by the agitation (or longing) of craving, wrong view, and conceit. Being unagitated, he attains parinibbāna within himself through the extinction of defilements. To show the occurrence of the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā-ñāṇa) in such an Arahant who has extinguished defilements, the Buddha said: "Birth is exhausted," and so forth.

"Thus is his view" means that the view of the Arahant who is thus liberated from defilements is of such a nature. There is also a variant reading: "iti'ssa diṭṭhi." This means that for the Arahant who is thus liberated from defilements, such is his view. To say that [the Arahant has a view] is not appropriate. Why? Because if it were so, it would mean that "the Arahant knows nothing." To say that the Arahant who has been liberated by knowing thus "knows nothing"...
99:
...is not appropriate to say. For that very reason, at the end of all four methods, the Buddha said: "For what reason is that?" and so forth.

In that passage, "As far, Ānanda, as there is designation" (yāvatā ānanada adhivacanaṃ) refers to the entirety of usage known as designation-concepts. "As far as there is the path of designation" (yāvatā adhivacanapatho) refers to the entirety of the aggregates, bases, or elements which are the basis for designation. This method should be understood in all instances. "The sphere of wisdom" (paññāvacaraṃ) refers to the five aggregates which are to be comprehended by wisdom. "Having directly known that" (tadabhiññā) means having known that collection of phenomena such as designation-concepts with higher knowledge. What did the Blessed One show by this sequence of teaching? He showed only the connection (anusandhi) to the phrase "tangled like a ball of thread."

## Explanation of the Seven Stations of Consciousness

Now, the person described as "one who does not designate" (na paññāpeti) becomes what is called "one liberated in both ways" (ubhatobhāgavimutta) as he proceeds through the path of insight to Nibbāna. The person described as "one who does not regard" (na samanupassati) becomes what is called "one liberated by wisdom" (paññāvimutta) as he proceeds. Therefore, to show the liberation from the round and the names of those two bhikkhus mentioned below, the Buddha said: "There are, Ānanda, these seven stations of consciousness," and so forth.

In that context, the word "seven" is spoken in terms of rebirth. The four stations of consciousness taught in the Saṅgīti Sutta in terms of objects of consciousness will be mentioned later. It is called a "station of consciousness" (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) because consciousness stands there; this is a designation for the aggregates which are the support for rebirth-consciousness. "And two bases" (dve ca āyatanāni) refers to two places of residence. In this context, "base" (āyatana) is intended as a place of residence. For this reason, the Buddha will later say: "The base of non-percipient beings and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the second." Why are all these included? It is for the purpose of encompassing the round of rebirths without remainder. The round of rebirths does not reach its end through the stations of consciousness alone or the bases alone, but it does so through the power of existence (bhava), mode of birth (yoni), destination (gati), and abode of beings (sattāvāsa). Therefore, all these are included.

Now, wishing to analyze that meaning in sequence, the Buddha said: "Which are the seven?" and so forth. In that context, "seyyathāpi" is a particle used for illustration; it means "just as people." Among the infinite number of humans in the infinite world-systems (cakkavāḷa), there are no two people who are exactly alike in terms of complexion, shape, and so forth. Even if there are twins in some place who are similar in complexion or shape, there is still a difference between them in terms of looking, glancing, speaking, laughing, walking, standing, and so forth.
100:
Therefore, [humans] are said to be those with diverse bodies. Since the perceptions associated with the rebirth of these humans are triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless, they are also said to be those with diverse perceptions.

"Some devas" refers to the six heavens of the sense sphere. Among those devas, some have blue bodies, while others have various colors such as yellow. Their perception is either double-rooted or triple-rooted; there is no rootless perception.

"Some vinipātikas" refers to those such as the ogresses Uttaramātā, Piyankarāmātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and other mansion-dwelling ghosts (vemānika petas) who are exempt from the four woeful states. Their bodies are diverse in terms of color—such as yellow, white, black, or dark green—and in terms of being thin, stout, short, or tall, just like humans. Their perception is also diverse, being triple-rooted, double-rooted, or rootless, similar to humans. However, these vinipātikas do not have great power like the devas; they have little power like poor humans and live suffering from the difficulty of finding food and clothing. Some suffer during the waning moon and are happy during the waxing moon. Therefore, they are called "vinipātika" because they have fallen away from a state of total happiness (or from a body that is the source of happiness).

Among those vinipātikas, those with triple-rooted rebirth have the potential to realize the Four Noble Truths. For example, the ogress Piyankarāmātā, upon hearing the Venerable Anuruddha reciting the Dhamma at dawn, said to her son:
"Do not make a sound, Piyankara; the monk is reciting the Dhamma verses.
If we understand and practice the Dhamma, it will be for our welfare and happiness.
Let us exercise restraint toward living beings, and let us not knowingly speak what is false.
Let us train ourselves in good virtue; thus may we be released from the ghostly realm."
After persuading her young son in this way, she attained the Fruit of Stream-entry on that very day. Uttaramātā also became a Stream-enterer just by listening to the Buddha's Dhamma.

"Brahmakāyika" refers to the Brahmapārisajja, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā. All of them are born through the first jhāna. Among these Brahmas, the Brahmapārisajja are born through a limited first jhāna and have a lifespan of one-third of an incalculable aeon (asankheyya-kappa). The Brahmapurohita are born through a medium first jhāna, have a lifespan of half an aeon, and their bodies are more expansive. The Mahābrahmā are born through a superior first jhāna, have a lifespan of one full aeon, and their bodies are extremely expansive. Thus, it should be understood that these Brahmas are "diverse in body but uniform in perception" (nānattakāya ekattasaññī) because their rebirth perception is uniform through the power of the first jhāna.

Just as these Brahmas have diverse bodies but uniform perception, it should be understood that beings in the four woeful states also have diverse bodies but uniform perception. Indeed, in the hells, some beings have bodies one gāvuta in size, some half a yojana, and some one yojana. Devadatta's body was as large as one hundred yojanas. Among animals, some are small and some are large. Among ghosts (petas), some are sixty cubits tall.
101:
Just like the Brahmas, the beings in the four woeful states are the same. In the hells, the physical forms (attabhāva) of some beings are one gāvuta, some half a yojana, and some one yojana in length. Devadatta's physical form was one hundred yojanas. Among animals, some are small and some are large. In the realm of ghosts, some are sixty cubits, some seventy cubits, and some eighty cubits in length. Some are beautiful, and some are unattractive. The Kālakañjika Asuras are the same. Furthermore, among these ghosts, those named Dīghapiṭṭhika are as long as sixty yojanas. However, the perception (recognition) of all beings in the woeful states consists only of unwholesome resultant rootless consciousness. Thus, although beings in the woeful states differ in their bodies, they are uniform in perception, and thus they are designated as "diverse in body but uniform in perception" (nānattakāya ekattasaññī).

"Ābhassara" (Radiant) means that the radiance from the bodies of these Brahmas spreads and flows out in flashes, like flames breaking away from a torch. Among them, according to the fivefold method, those born from developing the second and third jhānas to a limited degree are called Parittābha, with a lifespan of two aeons. Those born from developing them to a medium degree are called Appamāṇābha, with a lifespan of four aeons. Those born from developing them to a superior degree are called Ābhassara, with a lifespan of eight aeons. Here, however, all are taken as Ābhassara according to the highest division. The bodies of all these Brahmas have the same expansiveness, but their perception is diverse because it may consist of only sustained thought (vicāra) without initial thought (vitakka), or it may lack both initial and sustained thought.

"Subhakiṇha" (Lustrous) means being suffused with beautiful radiance, or having a solid mass of beautiful bodily radiance. The radiance of these Brahmas does not go out in flashes like that of the Ābhassara Brahmas. In the fivefold method, they are born as Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇha Brahmas with lifespans of 16, 32, and 64 aeons respectively, through the power of the fourth jhāna. Thus, it should be understood that all these Brahmas are uniform in body and uniform in perception through the fourth jhāna perception. The Vehapphala Brahmas also belong to the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). The non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) are not included in this station of consciousness because they lack consciousness, but they are included in the abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).

The Pure Abode (Suddhāvāsa) Brahmas stand on the side of liberation (vivaṭṭapakka) and thus do not exist at all times; they do not appear in the world during a Buddha-empty interval of a hundred thousand aeons or an incalculable period. They only appear when Buddhas arise within a period of sixteen thousand aeons. They are like the encampment (khandhavāra) or the Migadāya forest of the Blessed One who has turned the Wheel of Dhamma. Therefore, they do not belong to either the stations of consciousness or the abodes of beings. However, according to the discourse cited by the Elder Mahāsīva, "Sāriputta, that is not an abode of beings...", the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas are said to enter only the fourth station of consciousness or the fourth abode of beings.
102:
Regarding the Sutta (M. Ni. 1.160) which states, "There is hardly any place where I have not lived during this long period of time, except for the Suddhāvāsa heavens," Mahāsīva Thera says that the inhabitants of the Suddhāvāsa realms also belong to the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti) and the fourth abode of beings (sattāvāsa). This statement is accepted because it is not contrary to the Sutta.

The meaning of the terms beginning with "sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" has already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. As for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ), just as it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" due to the subtlety of perception, it is also neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness due to the subtlety of consciousness. Therefore, it is not mentioned among the stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti) but is mentioned only among the spheres (āyatana).

"Tatra" means in those stations of consciousness. "Tañca pajānāti" means he knows that station of consciousness. "Tassā ca samudayaṃ" means he also knows the cause of that station of consciousness by the method such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form." "Tassā ca atthaṅgamaṃ" means he also knows the cessation of that station of consciousness by the method such as "with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form." "Assādaṃ" means he also knows the gratification of that station of consciousness thus: "Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on form... dependent on consciousness, this is the gratification (assāda) of consciousness." "Ādīnavaṃ" means he also knows the danger of that station of consciousness thus: "That form... that consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change; this is the danger (ādīnava) of consciousness." "Nissaraṇaṃ" means he also knows the escape from that station of consciousness thus: "The removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for form... for consciousness, this is the escape (nissaraṇa) from consciousness." "Kallaṃ nu tena" means is it appropriate for that monk to delight in that station of consciousness through the power of craving, conceit, and views as "I" or "mine"? In this manner, it should be understood in all sections. Where there is no form (in the formless realms), the origin (samudaya) should be applied by way of the four aggregates; where there is no consciousness (in the realm of non-percipient beings), it should be applied by way of a single aggregate. The phrase "due to the arising of nutriment, due to the cessation of nutriment" should also be applied here.

"Yato kho Ānanda bhikkhu" means when, Ānanda, a monk. "Anupādā vimutto" means one who is liberated without clinging through the four types of clinging. "Paññāvimutto" means one who is liberated by wisdom. The meaning is one who is liberated by causing the non-occurrence of the mental body (nāmakāya) and the physical body (rūpakāya) through the power of wisdom alone, without having realized the eight liberations (vimokkha). Such a person is either a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) or one who attains Arahatship while established in one of the jhānas such as the first jhāna...
103:
...and there are five types of such persons who have reached (Arahatship). It is also stated: "Who is the person liberated by wisdom? Here, a certain person does not dwell having touched the eight liberations with his mental body, but having seen with wisdom, his taints are destroyed; this person is called one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutto)."

## Aṭṭhavimokkhavaṇṇanā

Having thus shown the conclusion and the name of one type of monk, the Buddha said, "Ānanda, there are these eight (liberations)," and so on, to show the conclusion and the name of the other type (the one liberated in both ways). In that context, for what reason is it called liberation (vimokkha)? It is called liberation because of the sense of being fully released from opposing states and because of the sense of fully inclining (adhimuccana) towards the object. What is this sense of inclining? It is being well-released from opposing states and well-inclined by way of delight in the object. It means occurring in the object without restraint and without anxiety, like the sleeping of a young child who has relaxed his limbs in his father's lap. This meaning does not exist in the final liberation (the attainment of cessation), but it exists in all the preceding liberations.

In the phrase "rūpī rūpāni passati" (possessing form, one sees forms), the fine-material jhāna produced by way of the blue kasiṇa etc., in one's own internal hair etc., is called "form" (rūpa); because he has that form-jhāna, he is called "possessing form" (rūpī). "Bahiddhā rūpāni passati" means he sees external forms such as the blue kasiṇa with the eye of jhāna. By this, the four fine-material jhānas are shown for a person who has produced jhāna in kasiṇas based on both internal and external objects. "Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī" (unperceptive of form internally) means one who has no perception of form internally; the meaning is a person who has not produced fine-material jhāna in his own hair and so on. By this, the fine-material jhānas are shown for a person who, having performed the preliminary work (parikamma) on external form-kasiṇas, produces jhāna only externally.

By the phrase "subhanteva adhimutto hoti" (he is resolved only on the beautiful), the jhānas produced in very pure color-kasiṇas such as the blue kasiṇa are shown. In that state, although the reflection "it is beautiful" does not exist within the absorption (appanā), because the person who dwells having made a pure and beautiful kasiṇa his object reaches the state of being described as "resolved on the beautiful," this teaching was given in this way. However, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga it is said: "How is it that one is resolved only on the beautiful and thus it is a liberation? Here, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness... because loving-kindness has been developed, beings are not repulsive. He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity... because equanimity has been developed, beings..."
104:
(The objects) are not repulsive. Thus, "one is intent only on the beautiful"—this is said to be a deliverance (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

Everything that should be said regarding the words "sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" and so forth has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. "This is the eighth deliverance" means this deliverance called the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called the eighth and supreme deliverance because of the absolute purity and liberation of the four mental aggregates.

Anuloma means from the beginning to the end. Paṭiloma means from the end to the beginning. The phrase anulomapaṭiloma is spoken in terms of moving back and forth without stopping at any particular attainment because of being extremely proficient in the attainments. Yatthicchaka is a term indicating the place, meaning in whatever place one desires to enter. Yadicchaka is a term indicating the attainment, meaning whichever attainment one desires to enter. Yāvatiicchaka is a term indicating the duration, meaning for however long a duration one desires to enter. Samāpajjati means one enters into such and such an attainment. Vuṭṭhāti means one emerges and stands from that attainment.

Ubhatobhāgavimutta (one liberated in both ways) means one who is liberated by two parts: liberated from the material body (rūpakāya) by the formless attainments, and liberated from the mental body (nāmakāya) by the Noble Path. This has also been said: "Upasīva, just as a flame tossed by the force of the wind goes out and cannot be designated, so too the sage, liberated from the mental body, goes out and cannot be designated" (the Buddha said).

That ubhatobhāgavimutta person is of five kinds: four kinds who emerge from one of the formless attainments such as the base of infinite space and reach the fruit of Arahantship, and one kind who, being a Non-returner (Anāgāmī), emerges from the attainment of cessation and reaches the fruit of Arahantship. Some teachers, however, say: "Since the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere also has two factors and is accompanied by equanimity, and the formless sphere jhānas are the same, therefore, one who emerges from the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere and reaches the fruit of Arahantship is also called ubhatobhāgavimutta."

This question regarding the ubhatobhāgavimutta arose below the Lohapāsāda (Brazen Palace) and, relying on the commentary of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷasumana, reached a decision after a long time.
105:
It is said that at the Giri-vihāra monastery, a certain monk who was a student of the Elder Tipiṭaka Sumana heard that question from a Piṇḍapātika (alms-collector) Elder and said: "Friends, while our teacher was explaining the Dhamma below the Lohapāsāda, no one had ever heard this meaning before."

When asked, "Venerable sir, what did the Elder say?", (he replied): "Although the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere has two factors and is accompanied by equanimity, and although it can suppress the defilements, it occurs only in the vicinity where defilements arise. These defilements, in the five-constituent existence, occur depending on one of the objects such as the color blue; and the fine-material sphere jhāna does not transcend that object. Therefore, only the person who, having removed all matter (rūpa) and suppressed the defilements by the power of the formless jhānas, reaches the fruit of Arahantship is called ubhatobhāgavimutta." This, friends, is what the Elder said.

Having said this, he cited this sutta: "And what person is liberated in both ways? Here, a certain person dwells having touched the eight deliverances with his mental body, and having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsavas) are exhausted. This person is called one liberated in both ways."

"And by this liberation in both ways, Ānanda" means "Ānanda, from this liberation in both ways." All the remaining words are clear in every respect.

## The Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta is finished.
